speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called-

Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) if his attention has been called to an item which appears in Saturday's Free Press, and which is also referred to in this morning's Ottawa Citizen, in regard to the release of one Thomas Riley from Kingston Penitentiary. It is reported in both articles that there were two Rileys in that institution and that the one who was sentenced about a year ago to fifteen years for manslaughter was by mistake released for the other Riley. If this is true it certainly reflects very strongly on the administration or management of that institution. I would ask the minister if his attention has been called to this fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My attention was
brought to the fact. What happened was this: an application was made on behalf of Thomas Riley, convicted of manslaughter in April, 1913, and sentenced to seven years. After consideration of the case a recommendation was made and was acted upon by His Royal Highness the Governor General approving an order for the release of this man, whose offence was, as I have stated, with all the circumstances on the face of it. Unfortunately there was in the same penitentiary another Thomas Riley who had been sentenced likewise for manslaughter in April,

1914, and. who had been sentenced to"fifteen years. I should say that the one difference between the two men, and this is where the very unfortunate error occurred, was that the man who had been sentenced to fifteen years had a middle initial in his name; his name was Thomas M. Riley. When the. order went from the Secretary of State's Department to the warden it contained no information in regard to the individual, but described him as Thomas M. Riley. Thomas M. Riley was, upon that order, discharged, although the recommendation approved by His Royal Highness was for the discharge of the other man. The "M" got slipped into the papers because of a report that was on the files on the question of the deportability of the fifteen-year man. The incident is, of course, most regrettable. What it makes most clear is that in the communication of these orders more care should be taken to give not only the man's name, but every circumstance surrounding him so as to make a mistake of identity impossible. I 'do not know that it is going to help things to direct public attention to it, but I may inform the House that steps are being taken to re-arrest and return to the penitentiary the man for whose discharge no order of His Royal Highness was issued and who, through this unfortunate combination of circumstances, in effect escaped from the penitentiary. We have initiated steps to remedy the mistake that occurred.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are you going to ask for extradition?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have given instructions that the matter be taken up from that point of view.
I presume the minister is going to let out the right man?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not at all an unnatural presumption. [DOT] Most assuredly there is a proper order for the discharge of that man, and the proper action would be to discharge him. The mere fact that the message unfortunately did not convey the correct information should not prejudice the man whose discharge was ordered.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to rise to a matter of privilege. I am sorry that the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) is not in his seat this morning, because I desire to direct the attention of the House to some remarks he is reported to have made on Saturday last in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. There is an article in the London Advertiser of vester-day headed, " Appeal for Blood-suckers," and containing the report of a speech delivered by the hon. member for West Lamb-ton. Speaking at a Liberal convention held in the city of London last Saturday, to nominate a candidate for the Dominion House, he said:
Then along- comes the Finance Minister, White, a very practical farmer is Mr. White, having come direct from an office in Toronto, and he says to you farmers: " Pay a little more, have a little more patriotism and a little more production and pay more blood money in order that the suckers may be kept going."
Then of this 5 per cent. The Tories have been shouting " Royalty." They always have. They have the only Simon pure brand of loyalty concealed about them. The Grits are disloyal. They want annexation. They are not British subjects.
The Tories did not oppose reciprocity on economic grounds-they couldn't,

so they came to you farmers and said that while reciprocity would give you bigger markets and better prices you should not vote for it because if it carried it would weaken the bonds of the Empire and Canada would become annexed to the United States.
They waved the flag. They called themselves the paragon of loyalty and called on Ontario to look at them. Ontario did look and it must have been through a magnifying glass for we were left with a shattered 13. However, I have no fault to find. It was foolish but every man's destiny is his own. Ontario was afraid of the bugbear of loyalty.

How loyal are the Tories of to-day?
What do the Conservatives say? Do they show consistency? Their arguments of loyalty don't go. The arguments that they are Tories from the ground up are aocepted. They called on the British-born not to support the Liberal party because it was disloyal and would not support the British Empire. What will the British-born do now?
Last week I heard your present representative, S. F. Glass, endeavouring to justify the seven and a half per cent increase. He said: " If it wasn't for this row would we satisfy the manufacturers?" (Laughter.) In that one short sentence the whole trend of the policy of the Tories is shown. It is " fatten up the manufacturers and don't worry about the farmer. He will come."
If my hon. friend (Mr. Pardee) were in the House now, I should like to ask him if he has been correctly reported; and judging from the construction of the sentences, I rather believe he has not. But I do want to say that every word in that statement, from beginning to end, both in its sentiment and its construction, is absolutely false, and Hansard will show that I was not properly quoted. The object no doubt was to prejudice me before the farmers who were present. I take this opportunity, if the hon. gentleman is reported correctly, to say that the statements he made are absolutely false and without a tittle of foundation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
With reference to the
practice which seems to be somewhat prevalent of late, of reading newspaper articles in the House as a question of privilege, I wish to say that it is not a question of privilege, and cannot by any stretch of the imagination be properly regarded as privilege. All the same, it is the right of an hon. member to refer to such statements and to contradict them.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House again went into committee, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair, on Bill No. Ill, to enable Canadians on active military service during the present war to exercise their electoral franchise.-Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Bill has been reprinted so as to have inserted certain amendments and alterations, some as the result of discussion in committee, and some as the result of further consideration on our part. Yesterday there was distributed a reprint in which there were a number of clerical errors, and in which there was inserted a section which I might describe as a tentative section looking to give effect to a suggestion which emanated from the right hon. leader of the Opposition. This section was inserted by mistake, because I did not inltend to have it inserted in the Bill until after I had had an opportunity of submitting it to the right hon. gentleman. I do not want to suggest that I am not willing to carry out the suggestion of the right hon. gentleman if we can agree upon the best form in which to carry it out; but, by reason of the errors requiring to be corrected and the insertion of this section, I have caused a correct reprint to be made, and I will have copies of the Bill as reprinted handed around. It is substantially the same as the reprint issued yesterday, with the exception that the section to which I have referred is omitted, the other alterations being merely verbal corrections. I understand that we have dealt with the first two sections; but, if it is desired to take them up again, I have no objection.
Is the first section the same as the first section in the original Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no alteration in the first section.
What about the second section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no alteration
in the second section. The committee will notice that a heading has been inserted between the first section and the second section. This is the distinction between the portions of the Bill which deal with volunteers outside of Canada and the portions of the Bill which deal with volunteers in Canada. The dispositions with regard to the latter begin with section 4.
There are certain changes in the first section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To what effect?
Certain words have been dropped out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no change in
the section as it passed the committee on Saturday, although there is a change in the section as originally drafted.
There is a change in the printing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not indicated in what the change consists.
Do I understand my hon. friend to say that the first section in the reprint is the same as the first section in the original Bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, but there is no change in it as it passed the committee on Saturday last.
That may be true, but I am speaking about the Bill as first printed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The first section in the Bill as originally introduced was amended in the committee on Saturday last, and the first section as now printed is the section as it passed the committee iin accordance with the amendments made.
On section 1-soldiers entitled to vote:
Has the minister made a distinction between the volunteers and the regulars?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: According to the first section the word " volunteer " covers any person serving in the military forces of Canada at the present moment.

Is schedule A, which describes the manner in which the soldier is to vote, applicable to section 1 of the Bill? Schedule A corresponds with section 2, but section 1 does not say anything as to how volunteers in Canada are to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are dealing now with volunteers outside of Canada, and we shall deal in due [DOT] course with volunteers in Canada. The form A of ballot is exactly the form of ballot used in every election in Canada. To put it beyond doubt that the ballot as printed reproduces the actual ballot, I will, if the committee will consent, instead of the printing in the Bill, put upon the official copy one of the actual ballots.
I want to make it quite clear that the soldiers of both classes are to use exactly the ballot that is used in Canada, save that a soldier voting outside of Canada, instead of having a ballot on which the names of the candidates are, will have a ballot the spaces of which will be filled in the manner provided in schedule A. There is no difference in the form itself; the difference between the ballot actually used under the Dominion Elections Act and this ballot consists in the fact-and the difference exists only with regard to overseas votes-that instead of names of candidates being printed in the white spaces, the words found upon the form are to be printed. In every other respect the ballot is absolutely the ballot used under the Dominion Elections Act.

I think the statement which my hon. friend the Minister of Justice has made, that his mind has been moving towards acting upon the suggestion made by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition with regard to adopting some provision which will make the Bill more satisfactory to all parties and perhaps throw around d-t safeguards which it is recognized ought to be thrown around the taking of the ballots of absent electors, is certainly calculated to make one believe that it will be .possible for us all to agree upon a measure having that end in view. It is a little embarrassing, because my hon. friend has had the Bill reprinted with a clause looking to the appointment of scrutineers or commissioners, and another printed leaving that out. It is difficult to discuss the provisions of a new Bill-for this is practically a new Bill-across the floor of the House without having had time to study it. I would suggest, in view of these new provisions and of the suggestion the hon. gentleman has made, that it might be well to appoint a small committee,
representing both sides, to go into thi3 matter. I think that the idea of scrutineers and commissioners is a good one; it provides safeguards which are acceptable. I should think, .however, that the powers of the commissioners should go somewhat further than the amendment provides, and that they should have in a large measure the control of the taking of the vote. If the . Minister of Justice and the right hon. leader of the Opposition could get together, probably a Bill could be framed that would be acceptable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to the clause to which the hon. member refers, I have already explained that it was a little premature to print it, for I understood that it was drawn as a tentative clause. I had a few words in consultation with the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) about it, and it seemed to me it did not quite meet his views, and was not, perhaps, as practical as I would like to see it. I had not expected that it would appear in the reprinted Bill; and, inasmuch as there were other clerical errors, I had these corrected also and the Bill reprinted in that form.
I am in hopes that, with discussion, we may be able to draft a clause that will be satisfactory and that will give effect to his suggestion as I understood it.
As to the suggestion that the Bill should be dealt with by a small committee, I think that might be a proper course. But I am in hopes also that there are a large number of the provisions in the Bill on which we can agree in Committee of the Whole. In that way we can greatly limit the scope of the deference made to the special committee. Perhaps, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) would accept this modification of his suggestion, we might act upon it. We might go through the Bill, allowing to stand for reference to a special committee such clauses as require more careful consideration.

If clause 1 is still open for discussion, I wish to reiterate my objection to the proviso. First, I would urge the same reason I gave before-that this makes a double qualification and, owing to the amendment the hon. gentleman has made this proviso is unnecessary to give a fair and reasonable opportunity to vote. Another reason against this is that the hon. gentleman has made a third qualification. I submit that that is mixing it up too much. I quite approve of the third qualification; but when he has the first qualification, that

of the place of enlistment, and also the third, that of voting within the electoral district where the man belongs, there is no need, I submit, for this proviso. I do not wish to make a motion to strike it out, but simply to put myself on record.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-distribution of ballot papers:

I observe that the ballots are to be sent to the commander of the forces in Bermuda, and later on it is provided that the commander of the forces in Bermuda is to control the handling of the ballots. I thought it was understood that the commander of the forces was not to have the handling of the ballots, but that under a later section it was provided that the balloting should be done under the paymaster. Is it not in order to make the same provision in regard to Bermuda as in regard to the other forces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, the paymaster of the Canadian expeditionary forces is in England so that we could not very well bring the Bermuda forces under the general provisions under which the ballots would emanate from the chief paymaster. And, as regards Bermuda, after all, we have only to deal with one regiment of 982 men. It would be a very extraordinary system to send these ballots to the paymaster and all the more so because he does not pay these men, as I understand if. He is chief paymaster of the Canadian expeditionary forces, but I understand that the men in Bermuda do not form a part of these forces. They are doing garrison duty there, having been detached for that purpose. If it is thought that the commanding officer is a particularly objectionable man to do this duty, I suppose we could say that the paymaster of that one particular regiment should distribute the ballots. The hon. member will understand that the only thing the commanding officer has to do with these ballots is to distribute them to the officers commanding companies; that is the beginning and end of his work; the rest is done by the officers commanding companies and the volunteers to whom they distribute the ballots. The commanding officer is the mere instrument of handing out the ballots to the officers who are to take the votes.

I do not see that it
makes any difference whether the ballots are sent to the commanding officer or to the paymaster. The objection that I have, and the objection that I believe the people will have, is that under this legislation 
there will be an indiscriminate circulation of ballot papers by the commanding officer or paymaster among the officers commanding squadrons, companies and batteries, and that the soldiers will vote higgledy-piggledy, if I may use the expression, without any guarantee that the votes shall he properly recorded. There will be no supervision; it will be done simply as the commanding officer may wish to have it done, if he has strong political convictions and desires to have the votes recorded in favour of the party in which he may have an active interest. Is a man commanding a company, because he is in uniform, going to conduct the casting of these ballots more properly than a man <at home, who is not in uniform? There is no supervision over his conduct; he may do exactly what he likes. As I stated in the few remarks that I made on the second reading of this Bill, when the ballots are returned to a close constituency and it is found that the vote of the soldiers changes the result in that constituency, ill-feeling will be engendered. It is because of this probability that I am strongly opposed to this Bill. There is no safeguard; we simply say that because a man is wearing the King's uniform he will be more honest than he would be if be were at home. In elections at home all precautions are taken; we have scrutineers; we have agents; every safeguard surrounds the casting of the vote before a deputy returning officer, who is just as honest as if he were in uniform. I see no reason why similar safeguards should not surround the voting of the soldiers. It is proposed, however, to place the matter in the hands of men who are in a position to suit themselves as to their actions, without the restrictions of any safeguards whatever.

Has the minister taken
into consideration the advisability of placing the ballot within the affidavit itself, so that there shall be only one document?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We cannot very well have the ballot and the affidavit in one document, but as it is now proposed, the affidavit will be endorsed upon the envelope which contains the ballot.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
So far as the first clause of section 2 is concerned, I have no objection. The ballots are simply sent to the High Commissioner in London, and to the commander of the forces in Bermuda.
I presume that the provisions of the law as it exists to-day will be observed, so far as they can be observed, under this Bill, and that there is a disposition to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is a provision
that this Bill is to be read as one with the Dominion Elections Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
ballots. It seems to m'e that this would-be a very much better method than that provided in the Bill, which allows the ballots to be sent out broadcast to the different paymasters, to be delivered in turn to the commanders of squadrons, companies and batteries. The regulations should provide that the ballots must always be in the charge of the commissioners or their deputies, whom they might
12 noon, appoint from time to time.
This seems to me a very much better provision. At all events, I throw out the suggestion for the consideration of my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At first glance I should be very apprehensive that the constitution of a civilian body of this kind might be looked upon as an invasion of the field of the military authorities. The plan as outlined in the Bill has proceeded upon the assumption that w-e were keeping ourselves within our own scope, although I think some hon. gentlemen said that we were going, too far in the invasion of the field that ought to be reserved exclusively to the military authorities. Generally speaking, this Bill is to provide for a clear recognition by law of the right of the soldiers to vote, and to provide a method by which that right may be exercised. In the carrying out of that plan we do not propose to send to the military forces any officers of our law such as has been suggested by the hon. gentleman, but to provide the men who are there already in their military capacity with the means by which they themselves can provide the machinery for voting. Now to constitute a commission which will name a large number of officers -and they might select them from the military men, I suppose; I do not know precisely how they would proceed about it-seems to me at the first glance to involve the introduction into the army there of some civilian body which is going to carry on operations. The members of that civilian body, being non-military men, will in no way be under the control, as military men, of the authorities there. I am just pointing this out as what occurred to me at first glance, but I am not saying that it is necessarily impossible to act upon the suggestion of my hon. friend. It might be possible to reduce the number of hands that these ballots will have to pass through. It occurs to me that if provision is made for the ballots being sent at the outset to the chief paymaster instead of to the secretary of the High Commissioner, we would at all vents avoid one transmission. If that were adopted, we would have just these two transmissions: the ballots would be in the possession of the chief paymaster, and would be passed by him to the regimental paymasters, and from them to the company officers. Of course the ballots should be kept carefully and not be distributed indiscriminately. It is not proposed to make any indiscriminate distribution; the ballot is to get to the man who is going to use it only after he has taken the necessary affidavit. The thing that is going to pass through these people's hands is a blank ballot. Now, any person can get printed any number of these blank ballots, so I do not quite see what is the serious danger in having some of these blank ballots in the hands of the officers. Why, I have here half a dozen blank ballots myself.

Before they went out
would you not have them certified to and given an official character?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I take it, they will acquire their official character by the affidavits on the envelopes in which the ballots will be sent to the Clerk of the -Crown in Chancery.

Are you not going to
make some provision to prevent the indiscriminate printing of ballots? Will there not be something to identify the ballots as offiicial when sent to the secretary of the High Commissioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In distributing these
ballots we shall have all the provisions that are made with regard to the distribution of other ballots. I have half a dozen ballots here, and there is nothing to prevent me from going to a printing office and getting them absolutely reproduced. These ballots become official and acquire a value which makes it necessary to preserve them when once they have been used in connection with an election. I do not quite see that there is a tremendous danger in putting them in the hands of the paymasters, when somebody who is not a paymaster at all can go and get any number printed. Of course, he would have to have them printed on the paper prescribed by the statute.
Mr. PU-GSLEY: They might be stamped by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery before they left his office.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That might be done, but it seems to me that the natural effect of that is to give them an official character,

which makes it dangerous if anybody gets possession of them.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is all we get by giving them out with a stamp on them. We make it a dangerous thing, but if the ballot be a ballot pure and simple, its value begins only when it has attached to it that which makes a vote out of it. Its value begins therefore when it has been voted upon and when it is encased in the envelope with the necessary affidavits taken before the proper officer. I quite agree with hon. gentlemen who have spoken. But let us take the other suggestion. Commissioners, we will say, are going to have charge of these ballots. The commissioners will distribute them to I do not know how many scrutineers and deputies. I cannot help but think that there is a greater danger in such a system as that. It has been argued that a man with his uniform on is no better than a man with his uniform off. If it is better to have scrutineers than that the ballots should go through the hands of an officer it is not because they go through the hands of men who do not wear a uniform. I think we may assume that a uniformed man and a man without a uniform are on a footing of equality in that respect.
The scrutineers are a check on each other; it does not matter whether they are honest or dishonest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are not discussing what is going to happen when they go to take the vote; we are discussing the comparative safety of ballots going through the hands of people. They have to go through somebody's hands. What is the advantage of these somebodies not being soldiers? There is the disadvantage of introducing a large civilian element in this matter. What did seem to me as the result of the suggestion of my right hon. friend and as the result of the brief conference I had with him, as being a reasonable and useful thing, was that we should appoint a commission whose business it would be to be representative of the respective parties and who will be placed in a position where they could, each as representative of a party, secure in connection with the giving of this vote to each of the parties respectively the protection that h-secured under the system here to each of the candidates by the provision which entitles the candidates to have a representative in each of the polling booths. Instead of providing for six commissioners as suggested, and which on reflection I think is an entirely unwieldy and unworkable number, if we provide for the appointment 'of two commissioners, one on the nomination of the Prime Minister and one on the nomination of -the leader of the Opposition, and give them all the powers that are given to scrutineers with the further power of appointing agents who would be entitled to exercise the powers of the commissioners themselves, then we will create a system whereby each of the parties is enabled to secure to itself in connection with the vote the very same protection that the law provides in connection with our voting here by allowing each of the candidates to have a representative who may be present ait the different operations that are provided for here and perform the same functions that scrutineers would perform here. Something on this line would seem to me to be as far as we could go and after all it creates a situation where a military officer who is the returning officer will perform his operations in the presence of the representative of each of the parties. One cannot make imperative requirements any more than imperative requirements are made under the law -here. Under the law here there is no absolute requirement that the scrutineer shall be present. On the contrary, there is an express provision that the absence of the scrutineer shall not affect the validity of anything. All the law does is to recognize the right of each candidate to provide some one to act as his representative, but the law does not insist upon the presence of that man as being essential to the validity of that which is done. Why need we go farther than the law here goes with the result of providing very cumbersome machinery and creating the possibility of very considerable delay in the taking of the votes?

Would it be provided in the Bill that there shall be a fixed day or hour for taking the vote in any particular Tegiment, so that the scrutineers may be on hand at the proper time and so that there will be no possibility of the vote being taken before or after a certain time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, the Bill does not make such provision, and I do not think it could do so without creating a situation which will make the taking of the vote impossible or make it imply some encroach-

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: ment upon the performance of military duty. As I understand the provision of the Bill with reference to the taking of the votes, they will be taken as they can conveniently be taken. T:hfe officer commanding the company-and that officer will only have a comparatively small number of ballots, only as many ballots as there are men in the company-shall, under the Act, furnish a ballot to any volunteer who presents himself before him, asks for a ballot for the purpose of voting and makes the affidavit that is required. Thereupon the soldier may mark- his ballot, but under the system I have been trying to outline I fancy that in all probability-I do not see how it could work otherwise-these agents that the commissioners would name would be men or officers in the different companies, and, being brother officers and soldiers, I can hardly believe that thte officer who was going to take the votes would be endeavouring to run away from ohe scrutineers or that there would be any attempt on his part to prevent them from exercising the powers conferred upon them. After all, I think they would all get on in the perfectly amicable way in which scrutineers representing different candidates in a polling booth in this country get on together. I think we would be able to take each other's word about arranging one thing and another, and I think we would be justified in doing that in the case of military men. ft seems to me that a scheme of that kind might be worked out. I would be glad to act on the suggestion of the hon. member to refer some of these matters to a small committee. However, there are other sections of the Bill which we might go on with in Committee of the Whole.
If the minister is going to have any portion of this Bill discussed by a small committee it would save a great deal of time if he would let the whole Bill go to that committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Even after such a committee has performed its duties there are other clauses in the Bill which would have to 'be taken up by the Committee of the Whole, and we might as well discuss them now. We can reserve for a special committee such matters as this committee thinks call for further consideration.

Is there anything in the Bill to deal with a situation such as this: suppose a shell comes along and destroys a number of these ballots after they have .been marked, is there any
	I
machinery jn the Bill to have the ballots marked again by those who had previously marked them? That is a perfect possibility. The soldiers enjoy their leisure in the trenches in reading their letters and writing their letters, with shells flying over their heads all the time, and I suppose the minister has imagination enough to conceive that the place where the soldiers .are enjoying such leisure as men at war have, is a place where a poll might be taken. If you do not take the ballot in such a place, you would have to take the soldiers outside the firing line for the purpose of your election at the front. If a poll were taken there and a hunch of the ballots were marked and a shell destroyed the whole hunch, has the minister any arrangement for dealing with that situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. No more is there
any arrangement provided by law under the Election Act, for what is to happen if the polling-booth should be struck by lightning and all of the marked ballots destroyed, which is a thing that may happen. I am striving to contend with the practical difficulties which surround the taking of this vote, hut I really cannot undertake to overcome the forces of nature in order to prevent all of the tilings that might happen by reason of the conditions under which this vote is going to be taken. It is a soldiers' vote and it will be taken under war conditions, and just as the soldier himself has to take the risk of what may happen, I am afraid that the soldiers' ballots will have to take the risk of what may happen to them.

Does the Minister of Justice not think that if he were to have a general election in Canada on a day when lightning were likely to be as frequent as shells are on the battle-field, that he would postpone the election from that particular day? I am almost certain he would, especially if he was going to be the returning officer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If the Government will not accept the suggestion made by my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) to have a commission, of course we can go on with the Bill, but if the Government leaves that point undecided, there is no use going on to consider the section, because the idea embodied in the amendment of the hon. member is that the commission should make regulations subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. The Minister of Justice sees no inconvenience in having ballots distributed promiscuously, but

the law as it exists takes precaution against the promiscuous distribution of ballots, and for very good reasons. These restrictions as to the distribution of ballots were inserted in the law, because if an agent wanted to bribe an elector he would give him a ballot previously marked to deposit in the box and get the voter to bring back the original ballot, so as to ensure that the person bribed would deliver the goods. The suggestion of my hon. friend provides that regulations shall be made by this commission. Are we to have a counterfoil on these ballots? Are we to have a poll-book as in the ordinary elections? The Minister of Justice wants to make a commissioned officer the returning officer.
In all probability the officer, if he is an English officer, will be very much embarrassed as to what his duties are. He will have no conception of them; the work will be something very new to him and he will be a very poor returning officer I am sure; but if we have scrutineers on either side, he then can be instructed as to his duties. If, however, my hon. friend were to agree to the suggestion made by my hon. friend from St. John that we should have a special committee appointed, it would certainly obviate a number of difficulties, and we would have more satisfactory legislation than we would otherwise have.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The suggestion has often been made by hon. gentlemen opposite that it is proposed to distribute ballots promiscuously. I have not heard of any such intention, nor do I find it in the provisions of -the Bill. In the ordinary course, the ballots go to the deputy returning officer who is bound to keep them in his possession until he hands them out one by one to the voters who desire to record their votes. In the present case it is proposed to use the military organization for the same purpose, and ballots are to be delivered to the commanding officer of each unit, the smallest unit being selected; that is to say, companies, squadrons and batteries. The commanding officer of any particular company, squadron or battery, does not distribute the ballots indiscriminately; what he does is to hand a ballot to any soldier who comes before him and makes an affidavit showing that under the provisions of this Bill he is qualified to vote. Apart from that the commanding officer has no authority whatever to deliver a ballot to any person at all, just as the deputy returning officer has no authority to deliver a ballot except to a voter whose name is upon the list and
who comes into the polling booth and demands the right to exercise his franchise, so that there is no promiscuous distribution of the ballots under the provisions of this Bill. The purpose of this Bill is simply to use, , as necessarily one must use, the military organization for the purpose of giving the soldiers at the front or in Great Britain the right to Tecord their votes. In framing the Bill, the committee were inspired with the belief, which I think might very well be supported by hon. members on both sides of the House, that we could not anticipate that men serving their country at the front under conditions which have been described by the hon. member for Red DeeT (Mr. Clark) could have their minds taken up with the desire to commit a fraud in the exercise of the franchise under the provisions of this Bill. It is perfectly obvious that if the men at the front are to have the right to exercise the franchise, one must give to the officers who are commanding them and to the men themselves some credit for reasonable honesty and for a desire to carry out the provisions of this Bill as they are intended to be carried out. If we start with the premise that every officer or man at the front is filled with and animated by a desire to commit a fraud in the exercise of his franchise, of course very wide precautions will be necessary; but after all, whatever precautions you take, either in this Bill or in any other Bill concerning the exercise of the franchise, the legitimate carrying out of its provisions depends in the last analysis upon the men selected to carry them out. You may legislate from to-day until the 31st day of December and in the end, whatever provisions you enact and whatever safeguards you provide, the result will depend upon the honesty and the integrity of the men carrying out the provisions of any legislative measure, and I defy this House or any other House to make legislative provisions with regard to the exercise of the franchise which cannot be defeated by dishonest men. Therefore, the whole question seems, in my judgment, to depend upon whether we may with reasonable confidence rely upon the commanders of the units to discharge the duties imposed upon them by this Bill in an honest way and without any desire to commit a fraud.
If we are entitled to have that confidence in them, then it seems to me that the Bill contains reasonably sufficient safeguards; if we are not entitled to have that confidence in them, then I believe that no safeguards that we can insert will in the last analysis prevent fraud from being committed. I have not the slightest idea as to the political

opinions of the officers of the various units and I do not know who they are. They were not selected by reason of their political opinions, and I have every confidence that whether they are of one political party or of the other, (they will, under the conditions which have been described be disposed to discharge this duty in an honest and patriotic way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The fact that we insist upon taking such precautions as regards military life as are taken in civil life does not imply that there is any discrimination against the members of the army any more than there is discrimination against men in civil life. No one has answered the objection put forward by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) that a uniform does not make a man honest. Whether a man wears a uniform or not, it is human nature all the same, so that we are certainly doing nothing extraordinary in asking that the same precautions which are taken in civil life should be taken as regards military life. Does any one contend that in military life less precaution should be taken than in civil life? Military life is no better than civil life and civil life is no better than military life; human nature is the same in both cases. I am glad to hear from my right hon. friend that there is to be no promiscuous distribution of ballots, and that the volunteer can have the ballot only when he comes and asks for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He asks for it when
he makes the affidavit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I suppose my right hon. friend has in mind subsection 3 of section 2, part of which reads as follows:
And such officers shall give each volunteer under their respective commands making the affidavit in form B before such officer, a ballot paper.
This is a change from the original Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is a new provision and it satisfies me. It is a new precaution which has been inserted, showing that the suggestion we have made is not frivolous but serious. All that we can ask under this Bill is that the same precautions should be taken as if the soldiers were voting in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We are perfectly willing to take any precautions except to the extent of making the Bill unwork-

able. The difference between the right hon. gentleman and myself is this:	The basis
upon which this Bill was reported by the committee is that under the exceptional conditions in which the soldiers are to exercise their franchise, we must have regard to military considerations, and that the best that we can do is to utilize the military organization for the purpose of giving these men the right to vote. If we superimpose upon that a proposal which will create an organization for the purpose of supervising the exercise by these men of their franchise, of such a character that it cannot be properly worked out under the military regulations which govern at the front, we might as well pass no legislation at all. Subject to that consideration, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is disposed, as I am, to establish every possible safeguard. But I think that is a matter which might very well be considered in the informal committee that has been alluded to. In the meantime, the Minister of Justice thought, and I myself think, that we might make some progress with the provisions of the Bill.

It would be as impossible for my right hon. friend to prove that all men into whose hands these ballots would fall are honest as it would be unreasonable for any person on this side of the House to argue that all the men into whose hands they may fall are dishonest. That is not the purpose of this discussion. Under the Elections Act as it stands, the Minister of Justice knows perfectly well the principle is to limit the circulation of ballots to as few persons as possible. For that reason, when an election is held in Canada under this Act the ballots are first of all placed in the custody of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. This also is proposed to be done under the Bill now before the committee. When they leave the custody of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery they go to certain designated officers, the returning officers for the several constituencies in Canada. All these officers are under the jurisdiction of the law of Canada and subject to well-understood penalties if they fail to carry out their duties. Here you begin to have a departure under this proposed Act. These men in Canada distribute the ballots to certain deputy returning officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They have to go into
the hands of printers in every constituency in the Dominion.

I am assuming this is
to be done by those who are recognized under our Act as persons responsible for the custody and proper distribution of ballots when the election is held in Canada. Now, the difference between this and the method proposed in the Bill is very marked. The ballots go to other hands and ultimately fall into the custody of people who cannot be designated and are absolutely unknown. This discussion thus far has proceeded on the assumption that all the officers into whose hands these ballots will go are Canadians. I do not so understand the matter. From the discussion which took place the other day, and from the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), possibly repeated by some other gentlemen, I understand that the Canadian troops are dispersed through many regiments and may be under the command of British officers-I mean officers from England, Ireland, Scotland or Wales. They may be under the command of Australian, New Zealand or other officers for aught I know. I venture to say that these officers, if they come from any other country than Canada would be very apt to decline to be bothered with carrying out the details of an election in the face of the tremendous task in which they are engaged. I think that if a request of this kind were made of these officers they would say they were there for carrying on the business of war for the Empire and not for the purpose of carrying on the business of elections for the people of Canada. These seem to me, at any rate, to be practical objections to what has been proposed. Dealing more particularly with the subsection to which the right hon. leader of the Opposition called attention, 1 would suggest that if that subsection is to be proceeded with, the distribution of the ballots should be entrusted to the several regimental paymasters, and that they should not be further distributed after coming to the hands of these officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In this country, no doubt, we try to take care of the ballots. Before I go into that, I concede-it was conceded from the outset-that if the view be taken that the soldier cannot vote unless we can have identically and absolutely the precautions taken under the Dominion Elections Act, of course, we shall have to drop the Bill. But it seemed to us that something must be conceded in order to make it possible for the soldier to vote, and it is just because we cannot have him vote
under all the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act that it is necessary to pass this Bill. Let us contrast how the ballots are handled in this country with the way they are going to be handled under this Bill. The ballots here are in the hands of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, and from him they go to the returning officers all over the country. Then they go into the hands of printers in every constituency in this Dominion. When they come back from the printers they go into the hands of deputy-returning officers, of whom there would be in each constituency, on the average, I suppose, fifty or sixty. Now, contrast this with what will happen under this Bill. From the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery these ballots will go to the chief paymaster and from him to the several regimental paymasters. That will not be more men than, I doubt that it will be as many as,, there are returning officers in Canada. From these the ballots go to the company or battery commanders, each of whom, as I understand it, commands approximately 250 men. But we here have a returning officer for an average of between 200 and 300 voites. So that, proportionately to the number of voters, we are not exceeding the number of deputy-returning officers in the handling of these ballots. This means that these ballots will go through fewer hands than we are willing that they should go through in dealing with a similar number of voters in Canada. It is conceivable, of course, that some of these people may not be honest; it is conceivable-and I am afraid that we have had evidence of it -that all the men who handle ballots in Canada are not trustworthy under all circumstances. They are human, as has been said, and we have to take them as they are. The question comes back to this: Is it of sufficient importance that we should secure to the soldiers the right to vote to justify our modifying our law in some respects and foregoing to some extent the protection that we seek in the holding of an election in time of peace at home. It does seem to me that it is worth while to make some sacrifice. However we do want to reduce that sacrifice so long as the Act can be made workable. So far, I think, I have accepted every suggestion that has been made-certainly every one that seemed to me at all practicable-looking to greater security. The last one that has been made, it seems to me, cannot be given effect to and at the same time give effect to the soldier's right to vote.

I do not think that the Bill is in any sense open to the reproach that it provides for a more promiscuous scattering of ballots than takes place under the Dominion Elections Act. Indeed, I think that neither under the Dominion Elections Act nor under this Bill can it be said that there is or will be any promiscuous distribution of ballots. The soldier does not get a ballot until he takes the affidavit. While I am willing to give credit to other hon. gentlemen for a number of suggestions which they have made, I must say that that particular improvement is the result of my own consideration of how it might work if you handed the ballot out otherwise than to the man who is going to vote. When he gets the ballot, he does not go away with it; he then and there marks his ballot and returns it. The provision is that the officer must be in such a position that he can see that the voter marks the ballot which he receives, and returns it; so that I think we have done what is humanly possible to be done in that regard. As I say, I am quite willing to consider further whether we can so arrange that it may be possible to provide people who shall have authority to be present,'wherever it is practicable for them to be present, to keep an eye on the carrying out of these provisions.

My hon. friend will know, from his experience as the able and courteous chairman of the committee which drafted this Bill, how much faster progress can be made when discussing matters informally in committee than can possibly be made in a committee such as this, even taking it for granted that there is a general desire to make headway. In connection with the observations which my hon. friend has just made, this distinction should be pointed out: for any irregularity which may be committed in Canada, a remedy is provided by law, but for any irregularity which may be committed elsewhere, there is no remedy. Irregularities, I believe, occur through ignorance or carelessness just as frequently, possibly, as they do through deliberate intent. Did I understand my hon. friend to say that all the ballots, before being sent away, should bear the stamp of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Inasmuch as the Bill which we are now passing is to be read as one with the Dominion Elections Act, such provisions as now exist with regard to what shall be stamped on the ballots will apply to the operation of this proposed legislation.
I take it, therefore, that the ballot mentioned in this Bill is the ballot described in

the Dominion Elections Act. As to the suggestion that this could be better dealt with in a small committee, I have already said that I think subsection 4 ought to stand to be dealt with by the sub-committee. If that meets with the view of the committee, I suggest that subsection 4 be allowed ,to stand for that purpose, and that we proceed to the consideration of other clauses which will not, I think, not give rise to any questions necessitating such action.

I think that the suggestion that a small committee be appointed is a good one. I think the suggestion made by the Minister of Justice should be acted upon, namely, that the opinions of hon. gentlemen be taken down so that the committee will have the benefit of their views with regard to these different sections. I understood the Minister of Justice to say that section 4 only should be referred to a committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is as far as we
have gone. If there are any suggestions with regard to matters contained in previous sections, I should be glad to hear them.

I think that in sections 2 and 3 there are some matters that may require consideration by such a committee. We have arrived at the position where both parties are practically united on the principle of this Bill; both parties are united in their support of giving the soldiers an opportunity to vote. We now come to consider the method by which that shall be done, and it seems to me that the machinery whereby the soldiers will be given an opportunity to vote should be made as direct and as simple as possible. Surely it ought not to be difficult to give these men an opportunity to register their votes before proper officers. We cannot apply to their voting the whole election machinery used in civil life, but we can rely on the assumption that officers commanding these regiments, companies and units will honestly carry out the duties imposed upon them. Officers who are in command of a certain number of men and who have other officers under them, realizing the necessity of their possessing the respect and confidence of the men over whom they have control, would surely do nothing which would cause the men to lose that confidence in them. It seems to me to be proper that the ballots should be given to the chief paymaster, because he has direct communication with every officer and with all men in the expeditionary force. I think

it is advisable that a change be made in the section whereby it will be provided that the officer taking the ballots shall make a list of the men who have voted, such list to be returned in the envelope with the ballots. It would be very easy for the officer, as the soldier votes, to put down his name and the number opposite his name, and to put that number on the envelope containing the soldier's affidavit. The ballot, of course, will be in a separate envelope. I would point out also that this section says that the ballots shall be delivered by the paymaster to the officers commanding squadrons, companies, and batteries, who shall deliver them to the soldiers under their command. Sometimes, in the absence of the commanding officer, the next senior officer takes command, and I suggest that in order to cover this point, it might be provided that the ballot be delivered by the paymaster to the officer commanding, or, in his absence, to the senior officer in charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is section 3 that provides that, if for any reason the officer charged with such duty is unable to perform it, it shall be performed by the officer next below him in rank.

I had not noticed that.
I see that it is provided that the paymasters shall deliver the ballot papers to the officers commanding squadrons, companies and .batteries. Now, the medical officers are neither a battery, a company nor a squadron; and to cover them I think we ought to insert the words "and units" after "companies and batteries." If we provided that the ballots should be distributed also by the officers commanding medical units, we should cover the men in our hospitals, which are in charge of officers with the honorary rank of colonel. I think we ought to make the officers commanding absolutely responsible for having these ballots sent forward, marked and collected.
At one o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

There are one or
two more suggestions that I would like to call to the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice. Looking over paragraph 3 of section 2 I find there is a very good provision made in regard to the channel that may be used in forwarding the ballots. It is provided that the paymasters' department 156
shall distribute the ballots. It seems to me that the same channel should be used in collecting the ballots from the officers commanding the different units in different places so that there will be no delay in having these packages collected and returned. Another point is that there ought to be a limit to the time at which the polling is to take place. Before recess I pointed out that an officer commanding a company might have 220 men under him, that an officer commanding a battery might have 240 men under him, that these officers are therefore very busy men, especially when on active service and very important duties devolve upon them. It is quite right that the ballots should be sent to the commanding officer but he should have authority to authorize or employ other officers under him to carry out the duties prescribed in the Act. There are always one or two officers in the orderly room who might be available for doing this particular work and he might appoint the assistant adjutant, or some other officer under his command, to carry out these duties. It is going to take a long time to receive 220 affidavits and it is imposible for the commanding officer to do it himself. It should be provided that in the event of the officer commanding not being able to act himself the next senior -should act. It would be better to authorize the commanding officer to appoint some other officer to carry out this duty if necessary. In the ordinary way, when an officer commanding is required to do so and so it does not mean that he himself, personally, does it. I have no doubt that in this discussion efforts are being made by hon. members to make the Bill perfect, and I think we should be able to provide machinery direct and simple in character to carry out the wishes of the House. In regard to the suggestion made by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), that it might be advisable to have a commission of two, one representing the Government and one representing the Opposition, I would not go so far as my hon. friend because I would not like this commission to interfere with the disposition of the ballots through the channel which has been decided upon, that of the paymaster. I could see the advisability of having a commission whose duty it is to see that the work is carried out properly, that is to have general supervision over it. Explanations and information might be required by the officers charged with this duty, and it would be necessary for them to write to some one. Whom would they



write to? If they were a little slow in taking in their instructions they would not know whom to apply to. A commissioner on the spot could give all the necessary directions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The suggestions made by my hon. friend are worthy of very careful consideration. I understand that the hon. member first points out that if we distribute these ballots to the officers commanding squadrons, companies and batteries, that might leave unprovided for some other bodies that would not come within the description. Of course we want to cover everybody as far as we possibly can do it.
I have had some consultation with my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence as to what might be added to meet that desire and he thinks we would reach everybody if we added to the words " squadrons, companies and batteries," the words, " or of any line of communication or administrative unit." I understand that would cover hospitals and men engaged otherwise. I also understand that the word " unit " might extend to a much larger body of men than a company or squadron. What we had in mind was to endeavour to reach the officer who would have a reasonable number of people under his command. If that addition would meet the view of my hon. friend I would 'be quite happy to amend the Bill to that extent. As to the officer keeping a list, no doubt it would make the matter more perfect, but I think we ought to bear in mind the conditions that will exist when this vote is being taken and we have to be a little on our guard not to impose so many detailed operations on the officer as to make it impossible for him to carry out the directions. The advantages of a list no doubt are considerable, but on the other hand when all the votes of the company are to be deposited in a bag or other receptacle and forwarded, bearing on the outside the affidavit of the man who gives the vote, it will be a very simple procedure. We have provided that these envelopes shall be returned to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery and he has to keep a record of them. Whether there would be* sufficient gained from that list to compensate for the additional duty imposed on the officer appears to me to be perhaps open to question.
As to the return of the ballots through the same channel as that through which they are sent, a good deal of consideration has been given to that idea. The consideration that led us to the conclusion that it would

be better that they should be posted direct after the voting by the officer who took them was that it is objectionable that the ballots should pass through too many hands, and whatever force there might be in the objection when you are dealing with an unmarked ballot becomes greater when you are dealing with a ballot that has been actually marked. It seemed to us that it would be wiher that the ballots should pass as directly as possible from the officer who took the vote to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. Ultimately they will have to get into the post office, and it did seem to us that the earlier they got into the post office the better. In reference to what the hon. member has said as to the officers commanding these companies, squadrons and batteries, appointing others to do the work, you see there again that you are increasing the number of people who are going to handle these ballots. After all, at home we give to one deputy returning officer complete control of the voting of between 200 and 300 voters, and all the operations, as far as possible, have to take place between eight in the morning and five in the afternoon.
On the other hand, under the system provided, the votes may be taken at the time that is most convenient, and the Bill does not propose, nor do I think it desirable or possible, to fix that this shall be done on a particular day or at a particular time. It ought to be reasonably possible for the officers to take the vote of those who desire to vote. I have with my colleagues given the best consideration possible to the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John and my view is confirmed that an endeavour to create machinery such as he suggested would in all probability, result in making the plan unworkable. I feel impelled to say that I do not find it possible to accept that suggestion. If something in the nature of what I endeavoured to outline, namely, the making of it possible for scrutineers to be authorized to be present, I would be disposed to acquiesce in the wisdom of letting that be considered by a small committee, such as has been suggested.

Suppose a number of
these ballots have been marked and received in due course by the returning officer, and it is evident that those who have made affidavits are not on the voters' list for a particular district, nor were they residents of that locality at the time they enlisted, will these votes be counted, and would the defeated candidate have to resort to a protest and recount in order to strike them out?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I take it that such
ballots would be in the same position as any other ballots that have been cast at an election, and I do not see that we can make a provision whereby the returning officer could adjudge whether the affidavits upon which these men had been allowed to vote were true or false. An analogous situation would arise if at the counting of the ballots in an ordinary election it were established that fifty men had voted who were not qualified. In an election held at home there would be no right in the returning officer to strike these names off, and I do not see that we could provide here for a system under which with regard to the absent soldier a trial could he had then and there and a determination reached as to_whether he told the truth in the affidavit he made. After all, what would occur in this case is what would occur in an ordinary election held at home.

In the ordinary case, a
man's name is on the list or he could not vote; but I venture to say that there will not be 20,000 men, out of the 100,000 men on active service, whose names will be on any voters' list. You can have the man in Canada arrested for perjury at once, but under the provisions of this Bill a man may make any affidavit he likes and he is immune of the- law.

These men enlisted in September or October, and at that time the courts were proceeding to revise the lists for 1914. I can well recollect that at many places the objection was raised that the men were not there at the time, and the judge very properly said that the men were at home when the application was made and that the fact that they went to Valeartier only temporarily disarranged their residence, so that he allowed their names on the list. The hon. gentleman is very wide of the mark when he says that not 20,000 out of the 100,000 soldiers would he found on the lists of last year.

I want to protest against
the statement of the minister that there was some suggestion on our side that the commanding officer at Bermuda was not a person to be trusted. That is not the question before us. The question is: Is he the proper person to be charged with this responsibility? In the following section, my hon. friend, in dealing with the votes in other parts of the world, says that he is not the proper person, and I see no reason why the com-1561
manding officer at Bermuda should have a responsibility laid upon him that is not to be laid upon commanding officers elsewhere. My hon. friend says that the chief paymaster cannot be as conveniently employed for Bermuda as he can for the European situation. It is not necessary that the chief paymaster shall be employed; there is a paymaster for the forces at Bermuda, I presume, and if my hon. friend will make the paymaster at Bermuda the recipient of the ballots, he will have the section in that particular on all fours with the other proviso.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not see that it makes the slightest difference, if there is a regimental paymaster at Bermuda, whether the ballot goes to the commanding officer or to the paymaster. So far as we are concerned, the matter is not worth while discussing.
Let me disagree, then, with the right hon. the Prime Minister, because I think the matter is worth while discussing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I said, "So far as we are concerned." I was not speaking for the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend wants to be quite certain that at all times there will be a paymaster at Bermuda, I can, of course, delay the Bill in order to ascertain this point. The hon. gentleman seems to think that it is important whether the commanding officer or the paymaster receives the ballots. Ifithatisthe case, I will try to find out whether or not there is a paymaster at Bermuda; but there will always he a commanding officer-that is the one advantage that we have. I am not in a position to say with any certainty that there will always be a paymaster actually available. The commanding officer is a general term; no matter if the man who generally commands is absent, there will always be a man commanding, and we have a certainty that we shall have an official person who will always be available.
That is the only reason for the difference. In the other case, r.-e reason why wa fell upon the paymaster wras that by taking the general paymaster for the entire force, wa got a man who had a regular system of communication with the entire expedi- . tionary force. It was not because he happened to be paymaster that he seemed to be desirable; it was simply because he was the man who had the entire organization ready to carry out the work. This argument would not apply to the paymas-

ter at Bermuda who would be purely a regimental paymaster, just like any other officer of the regiment.

There were reasons put, forward by the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. H. H. McLean) why the commanding officer should not be used. These reasons apply just as much to the men in Bermuda as they do to any other place, and I am only suggesting that; the section be amended to make the terms correspond in effect with the like provisions elsewhere in the Legislation. As to whether the matter is important or not, it has been suggested that there are less than 1,000 men in Bermuda, and if those 1,000 men are entitled to vote in the province of Nova Scotia, I do not think I need impress upon the House that those are enough votes, if properly directed, to change the electoral complexion of that province. I have seen tremendous issues decided by a less number of votes than that; I have seen elections carried by the vote of the deputy returning officer, and important issues resulting from that condition. It is not for this House to consider lightly the question whether votes shall be properly counted or not; for be it remembered that this is not a question of the right of the men to cast their votes-no one disputes their right-but whether those votes are going to be cast under proper conditions and with the guarantee that, having been cast under proper conditions, they shall be properly counted. It is desirable that the individual citizen shall have the right to vote whether he is a soldier or not, but it is essential to the welfare of the state that the result of the voting shall be the fair expression of the mind of the people according to the well-understood and well-defined rules laid down and worked upon before and during the election. The proposal of this Bill is that a certain separate condition shall be established that there shall be votes cast under different conditions from those under whicn the rest of the votes shall be cast. A new feature is projected into our elections, and the minister says: You must not accuse us of improper motives in connection with the projection of this new system of voting and of counting votes. We have to take things as we find them and if it is possible to switch the whole of the elections in Canada by the manipulation of the votes cast by the men overseas,-and I maintain it is- then I maintain further that this Government has no right nor claim to be released

from the suspicion that it has within its ranks the men who will be willing to do that. For the sake of the credit of the Government let us have such provisions in this Bill as shall remove the Government from suspicion. If the minister cannot provide such provisions then he has no right to ask that this Parliament shall place in the hands of himself and his colleagues the power of counting tneir opponents in or out of office as they please to manipulate those votes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have said all that 1
can usefully say with regard to the line of argument in which the hon. member sees proper to persist. Therefore I trust he will not think me discourteous if I do not say anything further.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken as to the personnel of these men in Bermuda. This regiment is recruited in part from the permanent force in Halifax, but it is also recruited, in considerable part, if I am not mistaken, from Vale artier camp.
Several there are from Ontario.
That does not affect the principle.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would interfere to this extent: If you undertook to establish polls you would have to establish the polls for many different constituencies. I think about 400 of these men are from a force assembled at Valcartier and gathered from all over the Dominion. Therefore the conditions do not seem to be such as to make it practicable for the vote to be taken in the ordinary way.

The answer of my right hon. friend does not furnish any reason why my suggestion should not 'be carried out under clause 5 of the Bill. If the men in Bermuda were in large degree recruited from Valcartier, the regiment would still be in the same position as one mobilized anywhere in Canada. There is no reason why the system applied to volunteers here in Canada should not be worked in the case of volunteers in Bermuda.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It might possibly be
worked out in Bermuda, but it does involve some anomalies arising out of our issuing a writ to an officer to go beyond the limits of Canada to perform the duties *f a returning officer. We should have no more authority over his proceedings outside of Canada than we have over those
of these other officers concerned. If it be true-j do nolt discuss it-that we cannot punish the people for offences committed in France, we cannot deal more effectually with those who have committed offences in Bermuda. When we came to the actual making of distnetions under this Bill, we found a natural line of difference running between that class of soldiers who are within Canada and that class of soldiers who are outside of Canada. That indicates one system for one class and a different system for the other. Those in Bermuda may be under different conditions from those in other places outside of Canada in relation to this Bill, but they are more like the soldiers outside of Canada than like the soldiers inside Canada. It is to be remembered that all our soldiers outside of Canada are not, and will not be at the time of an election should one be held, in the field of active hostilities. We have soldiers in England for long periods at a time, and it may happen that many will be in England at the time of an election, should one take place. If this system can be adopted for soldiers generally outside of Canada, I fail to see what advantage there would be in distinguishing between those who happen to be in Bermuda or in England and those who happen to be in countries nearer to or actually within the scene, of war. We must draw the line somewhere, and it seems to me we have drawn it at the proper place. Further than that, the practical difficulties of carrying out Canadian law in Bermuda with regard to the prepartion of ballots and so on, it se<_ms to me, would be considerable, and we might get ourselves into complications that would be hardly desirable and run risks otherwise unnecessary for the sake of making a separate arrangement with regard to one regiment of soldierk amongst all those outside of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Another consideration I mentioned a moment ago. The regiment at Bermuda is anxious to go to the front, and may go to the front. It is not improbable that they may be sent before an election is held, if it should be held. Therefore, we might have a force in Bermuda made up of men gathered from all over Canada, in which case the observations of my hon friend from Pictou would not apply.

The Bill provides that the ballots shall be separate from the affidavits. I think it is worthy of considers

tion whether the affidavit and the ballot should not form one document-one .paper. Let the ballot paper be quite large, and the blank form of affidavit be printed on the back. In that way we should be sure that the ballot paper marked by the voter himself was the one accompanying the affidavit.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then, how are you go-iiig to preserve the secrecy of the ballot if we act on the hon. gentleman's suggestion, the man's name will appear in the affidavit on the back of the ballot?

My hon. friend knows
that a distinct law, different entirely from the law that governs the taking of the vote' in Canada is being provided. It is very important I think that there should be no switching of the ballot, no separation of the ballot from the affidavit of the man who has marked the ballot. The hon. gentleman has stated that we must trust those who have charge of the ballots. I am inclined to think that the commanding officers will not like to be bothered very much in connection with the taking of these votes, and that they will be very glad to avail themselves of the services of any Canadian commissioned officers who may be present to assist in the taking of this vote.
