If you have the ballot entirely apart from the affidavit, there is nothing in the world to prevent anybody who may be so minded from marking a ballot in a different way from that in which the soldier marked his, and substituting it for the one which the soldier actually marked. It does seem to me that wTe ought to provide a safeguard against that. If we are going to give the soldiers the right to vote in this peculiar way, we want to be assured, not merely that the soldier shall make an affidavit and mark his ballot, but that the ballot which he does mark will eventually find its way into the box of the returning officer. My hon. friend says that it is our duty to allow those who have gone to the front the right to exercise their franchise. But we owe a duty also to the people of this country, and it is that the expression of their will, as shown by the ballots which they cast, shall not be defeated by the use of ballots which were not marked by the soldiers. These fraudulent ballots, although not marked by the soldiers, will be counted when they reach the box of the returning officer. If you provide that the affidavit shall be on the back of the ballot, you add another safeguard against the switching of ballots and the substitution of fraudulent ballots for genuine ones. It does seem to

me that that would be a proper provision to make. My hon. friend says that we ought not to be suspicious, because if men are honest they will not do the thing which we suspect may possibly be done. We do know, however, from our past experience in connection with elections in Canada, that men who in their ordinary business relations are regarded as men of honour and integrity, do things in connection with the carrying on of elections which they would not do in connection with their own business. There are many Canadian politicians at the front, and officers will be just as good politicians at the front as they were at home. I venture to say that there have been no more active partisans in Canada than very many of the officers who are now serving in the Canadian expeditionary force. They are none the worse for that, but we should remove as far as possible any opportunities for wrong-doing in connection with the marking of the ballots. By this section it is provided that the soldier makes the affidavit and puts his ballot in an envelope, on the back of which the affidavit is endorced. He hands that to the officer; the officer then takes charge of it, and the moment the soldier puts his ballot in the envelope and hands it to the officer, any control which he had over it is gone, and there is nothing to prevent the marking another ballot in a different way from that in which the soldier marked his, and the substitution of it for th -*>
V,allot so bona fide marked by the soldier. 1 suggest to my hon. friend that the possibility of that condition arising ought not to be permitted. I regret very much that the minister has not seen fit to accept the suggestion for the appointment of an independent and non-partisan commission to take charge of the whole operation of the voting of the soldiers, and to make regulations which might be found necessary from time to time. These regulations would only become operative when approved by the Governor in Council. I feel quite sure that if that method were adopted it would prove satisfactory, and that the people would be assured that the ballots counted represented the true expression of the opinion of our boys at the front. The amendment which I suggested provided that one commissioner should be appointed upon the nomination of the Prime Minister, the other upon the nomination of the leader of the Opposition. The Governor in Council would act upon those nominations, and if either of these gentlemen should decline to nominate, the Governor in

Council might make the appointments. In order to prevent any difficulty that might arise by reason of differences of opinion, my amendment suggested that the persons named should nominate a third commissioner, and that if they should not agree upon a third commissioner within the short period of ten days, that third commissioner should be appointed by the chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada. I do not know whether or not I suggested it in my amendment, but I would have them sworn properly to discharge their duties, so that we would have an independent, sworn tribunal to make regulations, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. They could appoint their deputies, scrutineers and assistants, and I believe that the scheme would be worked out in a satisfactory manner, and would result in all persons who desired to vote and who were entitled to do so being given a fair and reasonable opportunity to cast their ballots. The minister makes the suggestion that in some way this would seem like intruding officials into the military system of the Empire. Surely that would be no greater intrusion than the passing of an act which maKes it the duty of the commanding officer to take charge of and distribute these ballots to the voters; to take the affidavits of the voters; to see that the ballots are marked and put into envelopes and that the envelopes are then sent in a package to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. If one is open to that objection, the other is open to the same objection. It seems to me, therefore, that the argument which my hon. friend makes against the commission on that ground is untenable. But there is another amendment which I think might very well be adopted in connection either with the mode of procedure suggested by my amendment, or with the method suggested by the Bill, and that is, that before taking proceedings under the Statute the consent of the Secretary for War should be obtained. I think that as a matter of courtesy and to ensure the harmonious working out of the details of the Bill that would be a most desirable provision to insert. I can see no possible objection to such a provision, and I think it would be much better to do that than for this Parliament to impose certain duties upon British or Canadian officers, whoever it may be-and now they are all members of the British Army, and under control of the British War Office. The Secretary for War would then know that
in the opinion of this Parliament it was considered desirable to give the Canadians who are fighting at the front the opportunity of exercising their franchise, but that at the same time this Parliament recognized that these soldiers and officers were all now a part of the British Army and under the control of the British War Office, and that before taking proceedings which might by any possibility interfere with the morale or the discipline of the army the Bill should be submitted to him, and his approval obtained. So far as the Secretary for War is concerned, that would remove every possiDle objection against the procedure which is provided for in the Bill, or against that which is proposed in my amendment. I am sure that upon consideration the Minister of Justice will consider it desirable to make an amendment of that kind, whether he adopts the provision contained in my proposed amendment or not.
Just one word as to the certificates. I see that my hon. friend has left certificate C in the same form in which it was when the Bill was before us on a previous occasion. I suppose that is because he is providing that the affidavit shall be on the back of the envelope, by which the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery will be able to tell to what electoral district the voter is alleged to belong. But that eliminates altogether any inquiry by the person making the affidavit as to whether the man is really a resident and entitled to vote as he alleges. The only thing the officer has to certify to is the name of the man, and the rank and name of the corps in which ne is serving. He is not compelled to make an inquiry-	'

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman read the whole affidavit?

I am not sure that 1 have. By reason of the kaleidoscopic changes that have been made in the Bill from time to time, almost from
4	p.m. hour to hour, it is impossible for one to be absolutely sure that he has read every line of it. To what does my hon. friend refer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Certificate C provides that the officer shall certify that " according to the best information at my disposal I believe that the statements made in the affidavits are true;" and one of the statements in the affidavit is the statement as to the man's place of residence and his qualifications. The 'objection taken the

other day was that the affidavit was not put on the hack of the envelope, and I was quite willing to recognize the force of that. This certificate has not been changed in the kaleidoscopic changes that have taken place in this Bill, as the hon. member says. This is just as it was. It is -simply completed by the fact that the affidavit is on the outside. As to the changes that have been made in- the Bill, they have been made because, as I said at the outset, I wanted to avail myself of every suggestion that it was possible to meet; and it does not strike me as the most courteous way of recognizing one's efforts in that direction to have these mere or less sneering references to the fact that this Bill has been changed, especially as it has been- changed only by virtue of an earnest desire to meet every suggestion that could from any point of view be looked upon as reasonable.

I do not think I was sneering at the efforts of my hon. friend. I was simply stating facts. By the changes he has made my hon. friend admits that the Bill when first brought down was very objectionable indeed. My hon. friend yesterday afternoon had a B-ill distributed which contained certain changes. I looked that over. Then this morning another printed Bill was distributed, eliminating the changes that -had been made in the previous printed Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: One change.
And a most important one. Therefore, I think I am fairly correct iin describing as kaleidoscopic the many changes that have taken place in so short a time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I accept the explanation.

My hon. friend claims great credit for showing a sincere desire to meet our views. Is it not rather that he is showing a desire to get a perfect Bill? Certainly he should not be willing to have a bad Bill simply for fear he might meet our views. All that we are trying to do is to make suggestions for remedying the striking defects in the Bill as originally presented to the House. Some of us believe that the whole thing is wrong. But I believe that the majority of us on this side of the House, probably all of us, would like to see the Bill go through if it were possible to give the soldiers votes in any reasonable manner. Speaking for myself, I am anxious to have the Bill go through provided the proper safeguards can be thrown around the
[Mi-. Doherty.]
voting; but we should remember that it is proposed to give votes to men whose only qualification is that they shall have resided thirty days in this country. In the case of ordinary elections most of the provinces require the voter to have resided in this country for -a period of at least twelve months. We should be careful to see that the expressed will of the people of Canada who are compelled to vote under the present law, and subject to all the safeguards which surround the voting, is not defeated by bogus ballots which may be put in, or by ballots marked by people at the front who have no right to vote. Unless proper safeguards are provided, the ballots which come back may not be the genuine ballots of the soldiers who marked them, and consequently would not express the real view of the soldiers at the front.
I think my hon. friend has met my objection as to the form of the certificate; although it does seem to me that to make that certificate oi any value it ought to be expressly provided in the statute that it shall be the duty of the person taking the affidavit to make inquiry and satisfy himself that the statements contained in the affidavit are true. But the statute seems to be entirely silent as to that, and considering all that the officers at the front are required to do, one can very well understand that they might easily sign the certificate without realizing that they were expected to satisfy themselves as to the truth or otherwise of the statements made in the affidavit.

The minister stated that a soldier had to ask for the ballot. I find in line 7 of para. 2 of sec. 2 that the commanding officer

shall provide with a ballot paper and envelope each volunteer under respective commands entitled to vote and who makes the affidavit in form B before such officer.
There is nothing in that to say that the soldier shall have to ask for a ballot to entitle him to vote. I confess that after listening to this debate for a day or two I cannot see what objection the Government would have to the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). All we ask is that this vote be absolutely fair as between the two parties. I see no reason why the Government should refuse to make it fair. It struck me that if there were two commissioners appointed, who might have these officers as their subs, or whatever you might call them, and whose duty it

would be to see that the vote was properly and systematically carried out, it would be possible to take a fair vote. One of these commissioners could be appointed by each party, and that would do away with the ill-feeling and protests that are bound to arise under this Bill. It is all right to talk about the officers being perfectly honest.
It is all right to say that to-day, but if tomorrow it does not suit my hon. friends opposite they will say the opposite.
What do you say?

As far as I am concerned, the officers are reasonably honest, just the Same as the rest of us, but no more so and no less so. When it comes to election time we know that there are a great many people who, while they will not do business in a dishonest way, will at least smile and pass along something that they call smart at election time. I believe that things sho'dd be done in elections just as they are in business-absolutely straight, no matter where it is or when it is. In this case the minister thinks we are a little suspicious *n this side of the House I am not naturally suspicious, but I confess that I do not like to have voting done for me under the direct control of a strong partisan, even if he is an officer, on the opposite side of politics. I have no doubt that my hon. friends on the other side of the House will make the same objection exactly to a strong partisan who might be on my side of polities. It will work both ways. Why refuse to put the Bill in as good a shape as possible by providing for the appointment of two or three men whose business it will be, if you are going to worry the soldiers about voting, to see that this voting is properly done. That applies more especially, in my judgment to the Bermuda soldiers. The Bermuda soldiers are no more on active service than the soldiers in Ontario. They are simply garrison soldiers and there is no difficulty in sending a commissioner there to see that the voting is properly carried out. There is nothing I can possibly see to hinder that being done in reference to the Bermuda soldiers; nor is there any difficulty in reference to the soldiers at the front. If the War Office will allow you to have these men vote at all they will allow you to send commissioners there to see that the vote is properly taken. They may not allow it at all. I do not know anything about the rules of the War Office. It seems to me ridiculous for you to ask men, who are over
there fighting for the Empire, to bother their heads about voting. That is the last thing I would dream of if I were in their places. But if you are bound to have it done why not have it properly systematized and looked after in order that it may be fair to all parties? The soldier would be the last man to suggest that he should be allowed to vote in such a way that when the votes come back to this country there will be nothing but protests and lawsuits over the voting and that is what this Bill means if it is allowed to go through in its present form. Why not accept the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John? It is a perfectly reasonable suggestion. There may be suspicions on the other side of the House as to my hon. friend's suggestion but I do not see in what way they are justified. We are asking for no party advantage whereas the Bill gives my hon. friends opposite a very great party advantage. Personally, I see no reason why the men in Canada should not be allowed to go back to their homes to vote if they are within a reasonable distance. The minister has arranged-and I think it is very much better than it was before-that the voting shall be carried out under proper supervision at the places where these men are at present drilling. In Ontario the distance is not so far and the expense of carriage is not so great that the men should not be permitted to go to their respective homes to vote. With reference to men from the West, the voting can be done as the minister proposes in the Bill. Why not adopt, for those in Bermuda and in Europe the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John and also why not adopt what my hon. friend suggested this morning- that there should be a small committee of three from the other side of the House and two from our side to put this Bill into such a shape that we can all agree upon it and let us get it passed if we are going to pass it. The 'minister says that we should go over the Bill and pick out the clauses that we disagree about, and that a small committee can be appointed to consider them. That only wastes time, because the basis of the Bill is the whole thing, and the basis is as to how these men are going to be allowed to vote both in Europe and here. Once that is arrived at the other clauses would not cause much trouble to the House. If my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is in earnest in desiring to go on with the Bill why does he not accept the proposition of my hon. friend from St. John and offer

to have a commission appointed that will arrange the details and see that the vote is carried out properly and, in the meantime, appoint a small committee of the House to get the thing worked down to the best form and all agree on it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In regard to the last
observation of my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), I have endeavoured to explain the reasons why I do not think the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John is acceptable or feasible. They may or may not carry conviction to the mind of the hon. gentleman, but, of course, they will be no stronger if I repeat them. In regard to his reference to a small committee, I have intimated my willingness, not to I'efer to a small committee that suggestion, but that the matter be referred to a small committee if something "on the line of the plan which I endeavoured to outline this morning be acceptable. I understood from the response of the hon. member for St. John that it was not acceptable; so I do not quite see what is to be gained by going to a committee with a suggestion, which, from our point of view, is not acceptable, and when the principle which I would be disposed to carry out is not acceptable from the point of view of the hon. member for St. John.
Is clause 4, which provides for the appointment of scrutineers, to be considered as part of the Bill we are now considering?-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That clause was drafted for the purpose of submitting it to the leader of the Opposition, with a view of seeing how far it carried out what I understood to be a suggestion made by him, and contrary to what I contemplated it was included in the reprinted Bill. As an alternative to that clause, the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) was put forward, and for reasons that seemed to me and to my colleagues to be sufficient we did not feel that we could accept that suggestion. On the other hand the suggestion I outlined this morning which was in some respects in line with that clause, does not appear to be acceptable to my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) and to other hon. gentlemen opposite, and, therefore, it does not seem useful that we should appoint a small committee to consider two suggestions in regard to each of which part of the committee would go in, having arrived at a conclusion that it

would not accept the suggestion of the other part.
Is the minister open to consider a proposal by which a clause should be inserted in the Bill which would guarantee supervision of the voting in some way by representatives of both political parties?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If there is any reason to suppose that would be satisfactory, I would be very glad to consider it.	It
might be possible that there should be appointed two commissioners, one representing each political party, who would have the power of scrutineers, with the further power of delegating this power to such persons as they might select, and that the persons so selected should be entitled to be present at any voting and to perform the duties that might be performed by the representative of a candidate if the vote were taken at home. Of course, there would have to be a provision that the absence of these scrutineers would not nullify the proceedings; it would be for the parties to use their own diligence to provide scrutineers.

Provided sufficient
notice were given?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would be the business of these commissioners to keep^ themselves informed. I do not think it would be possible to impose on the officers who might be called on to take the vote the obligation to notify the scrutineer every time.
A day might be fixed for the taking of the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would consider that
absolutely impracticable.
How could you have the scrutineer present?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not asking to have the scrutineers, but I think tliere might be some advantage in providing scrutineers, and if that would meet the view of hon. gentlemen opposite in any degree, I would be glad to accept it. If it is considered not desirable to have anything at all because you cannot get as perfect a system of scrutineers as you could get in Canada at an election, then I cannot conceive of a system which would be as perfect as the system we have here.
Why not let the commis-sioneers take the vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We may have 50,000
men-

You will not vote them
all one day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have given my reasons why I do not think it possible that the commissioners could take the vote, and I do not see the usefulness of my discussing that matter over and over again. When you get into the position when an officer commanding 250 men or thereabouts is in the position of a returning officer, and you afford to the representatives of the party an opportunity to select a scrutineer from among these 250 men, and you provide that these two men would be legally entitled to be present when'voting is going on, I think you will have gone as far as you can. It will be for the diligence of these scrutineers and for the good faith and camaraderie which we must count upon to exist among officers and men in the same company, to so arrange matters that so far as convenient it would be possible for these men to be present when the votes are being taken. I am not here to press that upon hon. gentlemen opposite, but it has been suggested that there is lack of supervision under the provisions of this Bill, and if a proposition along these lines would be considered to be an improvement from the point of view of supervision, I would be glad to co-operate in putting it into shape.

Would the minister be
willing to provide that it shall be the duties of the officers, in whose presence the ballots are to be marked, to notify as far as possible these commissioners or scrutineers, so that they should have an opportunity of being present? Otherwise it would be simply a farce to apply what was intended to be a safeguard, and then have the voting done and the ballots returned without the scrutineer knowing when the voting took place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My feeling with regard
to the officers whom we are asking to do this work is that we are not imposing this work upon them. They need not do it if they do not want to do it, and I quite realize that we cannot force them to do it. Under the circumstances I am not disposed to ask them to do anything more than is necessary because we have to count upon their goodwill in this matter in a very large measure. The very things that make it difficult for the scrutineer to be present at each of the polls make it equally difficult for the officeT to give notice. Is it not fairer that the
scrutineer, who is the representative of a party, should do the running around in order to find out when it is necessary to be present, than that you should impose upon the officer the obligation of keeping track of the scrutineer to see that he is present? Do we in this country say:	Mr. Deputy
Returning Officer, if the scrutineer chooses to go out and be absent, you will send for him before you take a vote? In this country the right of a candidate is the simple right to have a representative, although of course he knows when the polls are going to be held, and the candidate, if he chooses, will send the scrutineer to the polling booth and take chances on his diligence and attention. If for instance my scrutineer is taken suddenly ill on the morning of the election, the law does not ask the deputy returning officer to stop until he gets my scrutineer to the polling booth.

The scrutineer knows
the day and the hour of the election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, he knows the day and the hour of the election. I do not know how often it is necessary for me to argue that conditions at the front are not going to be identical with conditions in Canada. It is a surprise to me that hon. gentlemen should find it necessary to point out so frequently things that are perfectly obvious, such as that things are going to be different at the front, when we all know that. What I am willing to do, so far as it depends upon me to do it, is to accept any proposal or suggestion foT making it possible for the parties at their own diligence to supervise the voting, and it does not seem to me to be so difficult a thing as it seems to be considered by some hon. gentlemen. What strikes me is that after the scrutineer is appointed, hon. gentlemen do not think that he ought to make some diligence. He is there as the representative of a party; he is given full power to watch and go around and see when votes are to be taken and inquire; but hon. gentlemen seem to think that nothing is up to him; but that we must go to the officer, who is acting purely because this law asks him to enable people to vote, and impose on him, because we make scrutineers possible, the necessity of his running after the scrutineers. For my part, in pointing out the sort of suggestion that I am prepared to accept, I think I have gone as far in reason as I can go in the direction of endeavouring to secure fairness, and I do not think it is possible for me to go further without creating a situation where you are going so to embarrass this voting

as to make it practically impossible to have the voting carried on.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am quite prepared to give my hon. friend credit that he is willing to go as far as he can, but he has given a very severe blew to the Bill. He realizes himself that we have no control and no power ever the men who are entrusted with the carrying out of this legislation. In this country we cannot compel a man to become a returning officer or a deputy returning officer; but when a man accepts the position, we can compel him to do what the law says that he shall do. My hon. friend takes the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John that we should have scrutineers, but he realizes himself that scrutineers will be of no avail and can do no good for the purposes we have in view, if they are not notified as to the day on which the polling is to take place. The minister says: I am powerless; I cannot prescribe any duty to the officer to whom I am entrusting the polling. That shows exactly the weak point in this Bill, and that is why the minister should have accepted the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John to create a commission with power to take the vote. Here we are putting upon the statute book a Bill which, when it becomes law, simply gives a pious recommendation to the commanding officers that they should do right; but if they do not choose to act, we have no power over them.

My hon. friend the minister is making a general proposition, in regard to the voting which is to take place outside of Canada, which is not based on an accurate knowledge of conditions in the places in which the voting is to take place. There is no reason in the world why the men who vote in Bermuda should not vote on a certain stated day under regular conditions, with scrutineers and parties notified, because they are under peace conditions; they are not doing anything in Bermuda except mounting guard, and their votes could be taken without the slightest difficulty.
The same as in Ontario.

Yes, and the same as at Halifax. The same thing applies to the men at Shorncliffe and the other places in England. The men there are drilling; they go through the regular routine of preparation every day, and by proper arrangement all the men in England could vote on one particular date. When you come to the men on the continent, I quite agree

with the hon. Minister of Justice that you get into an unknown land, because no one can tell what is going to happen, and our control over the officers who are to take the ballot becomes entirely chimerical. The Minister of Justice, however, having gone so far in stating his position, must recognize the absolute necessity and the fairness of the representations of both parties as to the actual casting of the ballots in Bermuda or in England; otherwise his proposition is of no value at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not making a
proposition; my proposition is the Bill as it stands.

My hon. friend
knows that it is quite apparent to the House that the general proposition which he has submitted to us to enable soldiers in Bermuda or in England to vote in this peculiar way is most anomalous, and that there is no reason why some solution of the problem should not be submitted. My hon. friend is willing to have a discussion on his Bill as a basis, but he does not want to discuss the proposition put forward by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) of having a commission to undertake the carrying out of the vote at the different places. Being desirous of having satisfactory legislation enacted as regards this matter, I would point out in all sincerity that my hon. friend is failing to recognize the conditions existing in Bermuda, which I pointed out when the right hon. the Prime Minister was here, because there is no doubt that in Bermuda you can take the vote just as it is provided in subsection 5 to take the vote of volunteers in Canada. The difficulty and uncertainty to which my hon. friend refers as arising as to the colonel or commanding officer taking the vote, need not arise in Bermuda. Why should not we have scrutineers and other persons to carry on the election properly? And the same in England. If he is candid -and I believe he is-and wishes to find some solution to tois problem, why not take the suggestion he himself has made of providing reasonable scrutineering of the votes in these two countries? When you come to dealing with conditions at the front, we are left unguided by military authority. I think the Minister of Militia should have been in the House to discuss this Bill. He has seen active service, and can tell us how far this will be likely to work out properly. I do not know much about military matters, but I think there are many military informalities in this

Bill, and that it will not work out. When you cross the Channel you come to an unknown land so far as the affairs under this Bill are concerned. What will or will not take place there, neither the Minister of Justice nor anybody in the Government, nor any one in this House, knows anything, nor can he predicate anything of the conditions there. But, before you cross the Channel, while you are still in England, there is no reason why the vote should not be taken under reasonable scrutineering. As to the hon. gentleman's remarks about this matter as a proper subject of discussion, I think he should be willing to extend the basis of discussion, and not seek to confine us within the narrow limits he has indicated. I am satisfied that he cannot make a reasonable answer to the distinction I draw between these soldiers who are not, and those who are, in the field of active hostilities.

There is nothing to
prevent an election meeting being held in Bermuda and the electors informed-or misinformed-as to the issues involved in the election. They could hear any member of the Cabinet who wished to address them. They are nearer to Ottawa than are the electors of Vancouver. You go from here to New York overnight, and twenty-four hours after that you are in Bermuda. When you get there you find conditions absolutely identical with those under which it is proposed soldiers shall vote in Canada. But the unfortunate part of this whole matter is that the people of Canada have no assurance that the vote will be taken in France and Belgium. The Prime Minister has told us that the War Office is the centre of our whole operations, and of everything being done in consultation with the War Office. But if we had assurance that the vote woulu be taken in Belgium and France we would have more satisfaction in discussing the Bill. We are discussing a Bill that may never be acted upon, and that, I think, is lowering to the dignity of the Parliament of Canada. When we enact laws we should be in a position to know that they will not become a dead letter but will be respected and carried out. We order the officers in France and Belgium to take this vote. But they are officers of the British army and not under our control; if the rules of the army prevent it, the vote will not be taken. This will not redound to the credit of Parliament and of the people of Canada. This is one very weak point in the Bill. Another is that no assurance is given us that the vote that
we receive here will be the vote cast by the soldier. I have no doubt that, taken on the whole, the Canadian boys in the army will cast an honest vote guided by the best information which the circumstances allow them to receive. But we have no assurance that the vote so cast will get here. With these grave objections to the Bill, I think this whole discussion is to be regretted. It is another cause of dissension between the two parties that hitherto have been united on all that is necessary to help the Empire in this crisis. We have voted all the money asked for, and have done everything in our power to strengthen the Government's hands. And now, in the dying hours of the session, when we are about to depart for our homes, we are called upon to enact a law here which may be a dead letter and which bears the suspicion of partisanship and may sow the .seeds of partisan dissension in the ranks over there. For all these reasons, I hope the minister will reconsider his decision and will accept the proposal of the'leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for St. John city, so that we may have the satisfaction of knowing on the night of the general election should it take place-for the Prime Minister told us a few moments ago that we may or may not have an election during the war-that the vote given by the boys at the front is the free expression of those entitled to* vote. By accepting	this	suggestion,	the hon.gentleman	will	close	this	chapterin our history	with	an	agreementon both	sides of the	House,
which, I earnestly believe, will be satisfactory to the Canadian people and to the boys who represent us at the front.

The Minister of Justice seemed to think that I was asking questions that had been answered this morning. I was present this morning, but in my place in the House I do not hear the hon. minister when he is talking in his ordinary tone of voice. I did not hear this matter explained this morning. I desire to make this statement in case he should think that I was trying to badger him.

I may possibly be alone on this side, but I desire to express myself as being opposed to this Bill in its entirety. I am already on record in that way. I do not make excuses, but declare myself whole-heartedly opposed to this measure. My first reason for this opposition is that this Bill is for a purpose which

cannot be carried out. The minister would have saved himself a great deal of trouble, and would have saved this House and this country a great deal of unnecessary confusion had he said to the zealous partisan, whoever he may be, who proposed this Bill, that the measure could not be allowed to pass. He should have told that partisan that the soldiers of this country have no right to demand or expect any greater rights or privileges than the soldiers of the King in the Mother Country, and that whatever provisions or conditions govern the soldiers of the King in the Mother Country and at the front, the like conditions and provisions should govern the soldiers of the Dominion who cast in their lot with them. Speaking for those who agree with me, I say that we are satisfied with the advancement of the Mother Country so far as civil privileges are concerned. Our most advanced legislation in this country is based on similar legislation in the old land, and when any person advocating this new theory comes to the minister and tells him that the intention is to go further than the old land has gone in such a matter as this, he should say:	The officers and soldiers of His
Majesty in the old country have no vote while the ivar is on and they are at the front, and therefore our men should not expect to have votes. One W'ould almost have thought that these considerations would have resulted in the killing of this idea before it got into the shape of a Bill. I can only speak of conditions as they exist in the province from which I come. In Nova Scotia no man may cast a ballot unless his name is duly entered upon the list, after having gone through the regular processes outlined by statute of the local legislature. The franchise is established by the law of the province of Nova Scotia, and that franchise is accepted by the Federal Parliament. This Bill, however, provides an entirely new franchise. It extends the franchise in Nova Scotia beyond the limits which have circumscribed its operations in that province. We have no manhood suffrage in Nova Scotia; every man who gets his name on the list must have certain property or income qualifications. These considerations are, however, thrown to the four winds of heaven by this proposed legislation, and the name of any person who can make the declaration that he was 30 days in Nova Scotia before he enlisted is put on the list. Although we do not know who he is, wrhere he came from or anything 
about his antecedents, he is given at once the same voice in the government of the province of Nova Scotia as the bast citizen in the province. This is a striking departure from the practices to which we are accustomed in Nova Scotia, and it is a departure which should not be undertaken without asking the people of Nova Scotia something about it.
As I read this Bill, the votes are to be placed in one bag, without any special arrangement; the votes for the man in British Columbia are put in the same bag as the votes for the man in Nova Scotia, and no system is provided by which they shall be separated. There is no certainty that the votes will reach their proper destinations, and when they do come to be counted in any particular district, the names are not on any list and no objection can be taken to the ballots. There is no assurance of fair play or justice, so far as I can see. The minister places great confidence in the officers of the militia; out of the honesty of his own heart and mind, I suppose, he thinks that they will be incapable of doing anything dishonest in connection with the recording of these votes. Having had political experience with some of these officers, I think that I would not be doing the minister justice if I did not say something about those experiences. I had occasion less than three months ago to go to an officer, a well-to-do man, whose name it is not necessary that I should mention-a man who would impress the minister, if he saw him, as being a gentleman in whose hands he could safely place the disposition of the ballots. I had occasion to say to him: " Colonel, there is a man in your ranks whom I want as a witness in the Supreme Court in the province of Nova Scotia. I have served a subpoena upon him and paid him his conduct money; I want you to let him go to the court when the day arrives, in order that he may give his evidence." If this man had been desirous of doing the right thing, he would have said: " I see no reason why the man to whom you refer should not be allowed to go to the courthouse and give his evidence." Without hesitation, however, he said:	" No, I will
not allow him to go and give evidence." I had to accept his decision, but I got an order from an officer higher up, at Halifax, directing that the man in question should be sent to the court under an escort. The Minister of Justice; would naturally think that the colonel would instantly have complied with this order-but nothing of the kind. He put

the soldier in the hands of a squad of partisans, stole him out of the country to Newfoundland, and kept him there for ten days. The sitting of the court lasted eleven days, and it so happened that the man, thinking that the court was over, came back on the tenth day. He put himself in hiding, but we sent the sheriff after him, brought him into the court-house and heard his testimony. That is my experience with officers in whom the Minister of Justice has such great confidence. This incident occurred during the progress of the war, when, if there is any honour on the part of these officers, it should be manifested. An officer who is capable of stealing a witness away and keeping him out of the country until he thinks that there is no further chance of his testimony being obtained would not hesitate for a moment to change a ballot or to do something which would prevent the ballot from getting to its proper destination. These are reasons which have influenced me to a great extent in opposing the proposal to put the fate of myself and my party friends in the hands of officers of that kind. The officials are at present on the other side of the water in connection with military matters. Since they left this country some of them have been disqualified yin the Supreme Court of the province of Nova Scotia; they have been proved guilty of fraud and corruption. They are at the front to-day, and if the services of any. men are required for the purposes of an election, these are the very men who will be picked up, because they have had experience in elections when they were at home. The minister, will, therefore, pardon men from Nova Scotia if they do not care to have their political destinies placed in the hands of such men, or that such vast and extensive powers should be vested in such men by Parliament.

This section deals with the affidavit which the voter has to make. The affidavit may be made out in one of two ways. The first form is:
That, within the six months immediately preceding the date when I was enlisted... in the military forces of Canada the last place in which I was resident.
was so and so. And then he has to say that he is not qualified to vote in any other electoral district. I should like to call the minister's attention to the fact that a large number of these volunteers will not know whether they are qualified or not. Except in the western provinces, a man has to be on the voters' lists to be qualified, and 1
am sure that very few of these volunteers will know whether they are on the voters' list or not. The alternative form is
That immediately before I was enlisted .. . in the military forces of Canada I was qualified to be a voter at
such and such a place. Suppose that a voter chooses the second form and swears that he is qualified to vote at a certain place, and that when the affidavit comes back it is found that his name is not on the voters' list, would that vote count?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I have already answered that question. It would appear to me that that is a man who has succeeded in polling his vote by swearing to a false oath. I take it that he would be in the same position as a voter in Alberta who falsely swears that he is a qualified man, and whose vote is taken. I do not see how we could do otherwise than accept such a vote as my ihon. friend refers to subject, however, to the parties having the same remedies that they have in regard to a vote in this country which has been polled upon the strength of a false oath. They would not have any remedy, as I understand it, by way of prosecution for perjury.

I should like to call the minister's attention to an objection that I made this morning. The more I think of it the more impossible I think it will be for the commanding officer to carry out the duties that are imposed upon him by this Bill. A commanding officer has 220 men under him

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is there a commissioned officer who has a smaller unit under his command than a company or a battery or a squadron?

There is indeed. A
company is now divided into platoons under lieutenants, and these platoons are divided into sections under the command of sergeants. Our present company 5 p.m. consists of only 48 men, and is commanded by a captain, three lieutenants and four sergeants. The war service unit is much larger. The platoon now is quite as large as the ordinary company in Canada. Under this Bill the commanding officer has to fake these affidavits, and certify that the document was written in his presence and that he believes the statements made in the affidavit are true. When all these preliminaries have been gone through the commanding officer gives the

soldier a ballot, and, after it has been marked, puts it away in a box. I say that it would not be _ possible for a commanding officer to go through all these preliminaries and take 200 odd votes in a day. For instance, a commanding officer on active service may be under operation orders and be ordered to take his company and put out skirmishers or advance guards or to occupy a certain position. He may be away three or four days or perhaps a week with that particular section. On the other hand, he may have what is called a field officers' day, that is, he has regimental duties to perform in connection with his regiment. This takes him completely away from his company. So it seems to me that it would be impossible for these commanding officers to do this work and their military duties as well. Then there is a provision that if the commanding officer is unable to do the duties imposed by this Bill, the next senior officer shall do what is required. But the next senior officer may be away. It is quite possible that in the Princess Patricias and other regiments, even in the regular service, companies may be commanded by non-commissioned officers during a big engagement. I want the minister to understand that I am not making any criticism except what I consider fair and honest criticism. I should like this Bill to pass if I thought the machinery was effective and workable. I would just ask the minister to consult either with the Minister of Militia or with General Gwatkin, who is the first military member of the Militia Council, and has had a great deal of experence on active service, and take their advice as to whether this is practicable. I should like to see authority given to the commanding officer to appoint any officer he sees fit in case he himself is unable to perform the duties imposed by this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not quite grasp that it would be an improvement. As I understand it, if the designated officer' cannot act, the officer next in rank would act; and if the section does nflt make that perfectly clear we could modify it so that if the commanding officer is prevented from carrying out the work it may be done, not necessarily by the man next in rank, but by any man between the company commander and the junior lieutenant.
But I shall be glad to make that perfectly clear. The difficulty I apprehend is overcome when we provide that if the the officer commanding cannot do it the next in rank available shall do it.
The words are not clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will be glad to make them clear. In order to avoid a difficulty which has been raised it is necessary that we shall cut down the number of men handling these ballots to the smallest number. The hon. gentleman heard the objection that was made this morning on the ground of the number of men that was going to handle these ballots. It is desirable to keep these numbers down as low as we can. While it might be true that if the whole 250 men came to vote on the same day it might be difficult for the captain, or major commanding the company, to take the oaths of all at the same time, we are not fixing the day and we are not limiting the hour. Provided that these ballots are taken in time to get back here for the polling day the officers and men voting can suit their own convenience as to the marking of the ballots and under these conditions I would have hoped that it would have been possible for the votes of a company to be taken by the commanding officer, or failing him, by some other officer who would take his place. I do not like the suggestion of his naming somebody. I think it desirable to have it so operated that it will never be a matter of personal choice in determining what officer shall act. It would seem to me to be the fairer way to let the performance of the function attach to the office held by the officer performing it and let it work out in that way so that there will not be a selected officer who might be a partisan of one party or the other. So long as we leave it to operate in such a manner that the officer takes over the duty simply by reason of his military rank it leaves the chances perfectly fair and equal to both parties as to what the partisanship may be, if there be any partisanship. I would rather see it designated as the officer commanding or the officer next in rank, without reference of the choice to the man who is not in a position to do the work himself. My hon. friend believes that a company is too large a unit for us to try to take the vote under one officer. I understand that a company is divided into-
Four platoons, each of them under a lieutenant.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That there are two parts and that these two parts are subdivided.

That is the present system in Canada. There are eight companies

in a regiment, but on active service we have only four companies. They are like double companies and each of these companies is divided into four platoons just like separate companies. They are almost as large as some of the ordinary regiments we have in camp. These platoons are again divided into sections under the command of a sergeant.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then if we depart from the commanding officer and go a step further we will have to multiply by four the number of officers that may be handling this matter and we will get it down to a situation where each officer who is handling it will only be concerned with 50 or 60 men. It would hardly be necessary to provide an officer for every 50 or 60 men to take these ballots. I would have hoped that it would have been possible to provide for a company through one officer and really
1	would think, in view of the fact that he does not have to do it all on the same day, (that we might trust to his carrying it through. However, I will think about it and if it is necessary I will be willing to go back to the section.

There must be some practical method of carrying this thing out on active service and it would be well for the minister to consult with the Minister of Militia, or with men who have had experience and who would be able to suggest a practical solution of the objections that have been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall do that before the Bill passes its final stage. In the meantime I beg to move that subsection
2	be amended by inserting in the sixth line, after the word "batteries," the words ''or of any line of communication or administrative unit." That is to meet an observation made by the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens this morning.
That will cover it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was pointed out by the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens this morning that "companies, batteries and squadrons" would not cover the army service corps and the medical corps and my hon. friend the Minister of Militia suggested these words.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg also to move that subsection 3 of clause 2 be amended in the eighth line by inserting after the word, "batteries," the words, "or of any line of communication or administrative unit."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
Does the minister provide any form of affidavit to be subscribed to by the officer who takes the vote?

There is no provision in the Bill requiring an officer to be sworn. It occurred to us that we could not prosecute for perjury committed over there, and we have to rely on the moral security. If you swear the officer who takes the vote then somebody would have to administer the oath to him, and you would have to swear that official, too, and finally, unless we got all these men swearing each other we would have to get back to some official on whose certificate we could rely, that the man was sworn. I would be disposed to believe that we can rely on the officer discharging this duty faithfully without exacting from him the additional moral security, because that is all it would be, of his taking the oath. I am not disposed to resist the suggestion, if it is insisted upon, that we should provide a method to swear the officer; but then, of course, we will have to swear the man who swears the officer, and so on, until we get back to some one who is authorized to administer the oath under our own law.

There is no reason why the officer in Bermuda or in England should not take an oath before some functionary, and we can provide in this Bill to that end. With every sincere desire to see a workable Act, I wish the minister would see his way clear to provide for the different conditions which exist in Bermuda and England from those which exist where the fight is going on. All a man has to do in Bermuda is to walk down the street on that beautiful island on a sunny day, drop into the office of a notary public, and subscribe to the affidavit.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the idea the hon. gentleman has in mind be met if we inserted a provision requiring the officers to be =worn before any person authorized to take oaths in the country in which the officer is?
It ought to be made imperative in Great Britain and Bermuda.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no objection to an amendment, if the hon. member desires it, to provide that the officer shall be sworn before an official competent to take oaths in Bermuda or Great Britain.

I think my suggestion is a reasonable one. I.want to say a word now about another matter, and not in any critical sense. We have heard a great deal



to-day about trusting the officers, but yesterday all day we listened to hon. gentlemen on the other side justify their report in regard to the shoes which were furnished to our soldiers, by basing all their speeches on the contention that the report of 75 or 100 regimental boards throughout this country were not worth the paper they were written on, because, forsooth, these men who were sworn to defend their King and country were going about and holding these boards for the mere purpose of getting new boots for the soldiers. It is ratheT a sudden change in doctrine for hon. gentlemen opposite to come down to-day and tell us that we should trust these officers. Certainly I am prepared to trust them the same as I would trust any other decent citizen of this country, with proper limitations; but we have to make laws here for all classes. I regard the military * officers as honourable men, and I regret that hon. gentlemen opposite did not so regard them yesterday. If the minister will only go a little further and give us a sane amendment to this law, so as to provide for a sane system of voting in Great Britain and in Bermuda, he will be carrying out to a legitimate conclusion my proposition to which he has given assent.

It does seem to me that when we are discussing what duties shall be imposed upon military officers, we should have the Minister of Militia present to give us his opinion as to which is the most satisfactory way to have the voting -conducted. We are proposing to exact from officers of the British army certain duties of a civil character which may materially interfere with the performance of their military duties, and surely there is no man who ought to know better than the Minister of Militia and his advisers the best mode to adopt in these circumstances. The committee would like to have the opinion of the Minister of Militia on what is a technical military matter, and in respect to which the Minister of Justice would not be supposed to know.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understood the technical question involved was, how many men had to be dealt with in a company and in a platoon, and I am satisfied to take the information which the hon. member for Queens (Mr. H. H. McLean) has given us on that point. I understand that in a company are included four platoons, and that therefore we -should consider the desirability of going to the officer who commands a platoon -thereby multiplying by four the number of officers. Between the major who commands a company and the officer who commands

a platoon, there is no officer who commands any other section of -a company. I had an impression that in a company there were officers under the commanding officer, each of whom commanded half of the company.

There is the major, then the captain, -and then the four lieutenants each in command of a platoon, which is divided into two sections each under the command of a sergeant. The minister is quite right in regard -to the formation of our regiments in Canada, which are divided into eight companies, but the new British system divides the regiment into double companies, and instead of a captain, there is a major in command.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have said to the hon. member for Queens and Sunbury that before this Bill goes through its final stages, I will consult with the military authorities, with General Gwatk-in in particular, and I shall be very glad to come back to this House and impart the information I received, and if it leads to any action being thought desirable, I shall be glad to take it.
With regard to the amendment that the hon. member for Pietou desires, I have tried to put- it into suitable words. It would apparently properly come at the end of subsection 4, and this is what I understand ought to be -added:
The officer receiving affidavits and taking votes under the above provisions shall in the United Kingdom and in Bermuda be sworn faithfully to perform his duties before an official authorized to administer oaths under the laws of the country where the said duties are performed.
Does that meet with the idea of the hon. member?

There are notaries
public in both England and Bermuda.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the notary public is an authorized officer he would come under this.

It would be better to put:
Before a notary public or some other official authorized to administer oaths.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Even in England or in Bermuda we are creating a situation where, if by any accident it should happen that officers cannot find this qualified officer, all our machinery will fall to the ground. Will the hon. member consider giving in the alternative the right of the officer being sworn, because we are dealing with a company officer, before the commanding officer?	*
If the duty is done by a subordinate, the commanding officer could administer the oath.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are dealing with company officers, so that there will always be above them a higher officer. I beg to move that subsection 4 be amended by adding thereto the words:
The officer receiving affidavits and taking votes under the above provisions shall in the United Kingdom and in Bermuda be sworn faithfully to perform his duties before the regimental commanding officer, a notary public or any official authorized to administer oaths under the iaws of the country where the said duties are performed.
What right has the regimental officer to administer an oath?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The right given by this Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But we have no such power. What power have we to confer upon soldiers who are in England or in France the right to administer oaths?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I have already pointed out, we shall get from this only the moral sanction of the oath. It may be more amusing to hear the statement more frequently, but that is the fact which I concede. As for myself, I have already expressed the view that I entertain upon that subject. I was willing to believe that without the oath we might have trusted the officer.
Might you not just as well do away with the oath altogether, because you are binding the conscience of no one by any oath that you are prescribing in this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not understand how the lion. member appreciates conscience, but I think that the average man, if he takes an oath, binds his conscience just as much if he takes it before a non-qualified man, if he takes it in Bermuda or in England or in France, as he does when he takes it in Canada before the most solemnly constituted officer that can be conceived of. I would have been satisfied with my confidence in the officer's honour; but, to meet the objection, I am willing to go further and give the guarantee of the officer's conscience, and I should think that at least we may feel satisfied in resting on the officer's conscientious respect for the oath by which he binds himself upon all that is most sacred to all of us.

As far as I am concerned, I believe it is as binding on a man's 157i
conscience to tell the truth whether he takes an oath or makes a statement. But the hon. gentleman has brought into this Bill what he says is an oath, which is not an oath in the accepted meaning of the term. A man's statement should be just as binding though it were made under this so-called oath before this officer who is appointed to administer it.

The proposition the
minister is good enough to accept was made by myself in regard to the officers who take the votes in Great Britain and Bermuda. In so far as this amendment provides that the oath should be taken before a notary public or other authorized individual, there is no doubt that in such a case perjury could be assigned. But the minister has added a clause which gives the commanding officer the right to administer the oath. To that alone, I think my hon. friend could take exception, though I think that something might be said in regard to the right of the commanding officer of a regiment in England or in Bermuda to administer the oath with the duties assigned to him under the Bill.
They administer oaths in other respects.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

On a former occasion I
called the attention of the minister to the words " I vote for the Government," " I vote for the Opposition," and " I vote for the independent candidate." Has the minister made up his mind to change these words from " Government " to " Conservative," and " Opposition " to " Liberal?" On a former occasion the hon. gentleman said that he used the terms given here because they were the terms recognized by law. But " independent candidate " is not recognized by law; yet that does not say that a man could not cast a good vote for the independent candidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a general principle that words are to be read in law according to their ordinary significance. I think " independent " is well understood. I said that " Government " and " Opposition " are recognized by lan a">d will not be misunderstood. But if you make it " Liberal " or " Conservative " I do not know how you are going to find either as a matter oi fact or as a matter of law an exact definition. For this reason, which I pointed out on previous occasions, I think it better to keep the terms we have.

There is not a man who is going to cast his vote but knows what is meant by Conservative party and Liberal party." If he does not know it, he is not fit to vote. I do not see why " Government" and " Opposition " should be used in our ballot; it has never been done in our elections, and it is not a fair way to put it. Under this Bill, questions relating to the parties are referred to the discussion of the leaders of the party. I think we should use in this law words that are intelligible and will allow the soldier to give an intelligent vote. As to the independent candidate, I think that should be left blank. The candidate who does not belong to either of the great parties may be a Labour candidate, a Socialist candidate, or a Nationalist candidate, for all I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But a fourth alternative is allowed under which the soldier may vote for the individual. The independent candidate I would understand to be the one who presents himself as independent as between the Government and the Opposition, whether he counts himself a socialist or gives himself some other title.

Suppose there were two Conservative candidates. I suppose the interpretation given to the word " Government " would be in favour of the candidate who was chosen by the convention. And the same with the Liberal candidate. But suppose that the Conservative candidate who has not been chosen by the convention has a majority of votes of those who heard him and saw him, but when these soldiers' votes come in, the votes of men who have not seen and heard, they give the majority to the other candidate. In that case, surely these votes should be eliminated and let the election go to the man who was the choice of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Subsection 7 deals with that.
That provides that the leaders shall elect. I say that is unfair.

I would call the attention of the minister to the case of the two constituencies in Halifax city and county, and St. John city and county. The voter in either of those constituencies would be entitled to two papers and entitled to vote for both a Government and Opposition candidate. I do not doubt that many hundred voted that way in the last election. In Halifax there must have been many who voted both for the Prime Minister and for

my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). Has any provision been made for that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not see how we
can find a method, so long as the men have not sufficient information to justify their picking out any special candidate. While the soldiers may not have official information as to who the candidates are, it is probable that in respect of many constituencies the soldier will know, just as all of us know, who are going to be the candidates. The soldier who has that information will be able to avail himself of the opportunity afforded him to vote for a particular person. Under the provisions of the general act a man is entitled to vote for as many people as there are candidates to be elected, and if a gentleman voting -in the constituency of Halifax should vote for two persons upon that ballot, if they prove to be candidates his votes would be counted. But the person who has absolutely no knowledge of who the candidates are, and is unable with absolute certainty to vote for them by name, has the right to vote for the Government or for the Opposition.

How about giving him
two ballots, and permitting him to split his vote, if he wishes to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is this difficulty; if you hand the man two ballots and he does take his chance on voting for a particular person, we may get two votes for  he same man. I think that the persons who would wish to vote for one candidate on one side and one on the other are not very numerous.

If a voter votes for a
particular person who does not happen to be a candidate, is the vote lost?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The vote is lost. I do
not think we can avoid that; it is the general provision of the law.

I want to have as thoroughly established as possible whether or not the Government has any authority over the officer, whoever he may be, who will handle the ballots in Eurorv-'. in England or in Bermuda.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All these paymasters are our own officers. What we were discussing the other day was the question as to whether we can convict a man in this country for a criminal offence committed outside of this country. The right hon. leader of the Opposition expressed the
APRIL 13, 191 &
opinion that we could not, and I am not prepared to dispute that opinion. Our officers, going into the Imperial army, are officers of the Imperial army for the time being, but when they return to this country, as we hope they will, they will return as officers of our miliary organization. I am not prepared to say what remedy may exist for any misconduct on their part during their absence. I am willing to assume that we shall have no recourse under the criminal law for infractions that they may commit under this particular Act. I do not want to say, however, that we have absolutely no authority that may be exercisable sooner or later by reason of the position which they will have occupied.

I want to find out exactly what the measure of our authority is. The exercise of that right on the part of the soldier, that we are taking some trouble here to give, depends on the conduct of the officer who is to act as returning officer. I think it has already been stated-I only want to have it absolutely defined-that that officer acts, or does not act, as he sees fit, and we have no remedy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think that we can by any means within our power give ourselves a method of compelling a man in England to do something. We are empowering these officers to do these things. I do not want to go further than this: I am willing to concede that we cannot deal with these men under the criminal law in respect to things that they may do outside of this country. These men are, of course, in a peculiar position, and it is not very easy absolutely to define what our powers may or may not be in the direction of increasing their obligations. While they are, for the purposes of military operations, under the control of the Imperial authorities, they are still our officers, and are paid by us. I am not prepared to concede that, so long as we limit ourselves to things that have no concern in actual military operations, our law is not effective to create obligations with regard to them, nor am I prepared to-day to undertake positively to affirm that it is. While I am not asking the committee to pass this Bill upon Ithe expectation of its being carried out by our creating legal obligation, I think we can safely rest assured that when the Parliament of Canada empowers these officers to do these things-and, so empowering them, in effect requests them-in the great bulk of cases the officers will be willing to carry out what they are empowered to do, to put themselves to such pains as may be involved in doing the things that are prescribed here in order to enable the soldiers to register their votes.
It is an absolute fact that it is entirely optional with the paymasters whether they act or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can make no further
declaration than I have made.

From what the minister
has said I am bound to conclude that that is the fact. We are passing this law ostensibly to give the soldiers the right to vote, but we are not providing the means which will ensure their having that right. I will admit that it is because we cannot.

We can by appointing
a commission.

But as this Act stands
we cannot do it. Therefore, let us be honest and say that we are holding out to the soldier a prospect which after all depends not upon our legislation, but upon the officers in charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We can create an obligation just as strong, just as powerful, just as binding upon those gentlemen as any obligation we can create upon a commission appointed by statute. There is absolutely no possible distinction in that regard. I have said that I was not conceding that we have not the power to create legal obligations upon these officers over there. I have conceded, without doing any more than conceding it, that we cannot punish the men for a criminal offence committed outside of this country. I have further stated that it was not in reliance upon our imposing a legal obligation on the officers that we proposed this measure, but that we did believe that they, being empowered to do this, and Parliament putting before them the desire of the people of Canada, would carry it out. I have not affirmed that these are absolutely legal obligations, nor have I conceded that they are not. I do not think it is useful to discuss that now. But I am quite prepared to say that the obligation is just as incumbent upon them as would be the obligation that we, by a statute, would seek to impose upon a commission to perform duties outside o* Canada.

I beg .to differ from the minister, and differ entirely. In the present Bill the minister is proposing to invest certain functions in gentlemen over whom this Government and this Parliament have

absolutely no control. These officers are a part of the British army and under the absolute control of the British War Office, and they have no right to do a single thing outside of the performance of their military duties except with the consent of the War Office or of the officers who are in command of the forces at the front; and no one knows that better than, my hon. friend. But suppose that a commission such as was proposed in my amendment was appointed by the Governor in Council. Those commissioners accept the office, they accept the responsibility, and they accept the remuneration which goes with the performance of their duties. Surely that is a different case from imposing obligations upon gentlemen in England or France or Belgium or Bermuda over whom this Parliament has no authority whatever. The moment those commissioners accept the office they become the'officials of this Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But how will they carry out their duties except through these same people?

With the consent of these people.
Mr. DOHERTY; And so does our Act.

No, this Act imposes the duty upon these people in England or France to perform the obligations. On the other hand the commissioners would go to England, France or Belgium as the appointees of this Government, and they could be sworn in in Canada to discharge their duties. They would perform their duties with the consent of the British authorities. That is an entirely different case. In the case of a .commission you have a proper tribunal, a tribunal appointed by this Government, accepting office under this Government, and undertaking the duties of the position under this Government. In performing their duties on the other side they would be doing it with the consent of the British authorities and of the officers who are acting under the War Office. Under a commission you have a properly constituted body, but in the other case you are professing to impose duties on persons over whom you have not a shadow of jurisdiction.
At six o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, before recess I was speaking of the great advantage [Mx-. Pugsley.]
there would be in appointing a commission, as proposed in my amendment, over the proposition of imposing upon the officers -of the British army duties and obligations which they might or might not be willing to discharge.
