I am satisfied that the proposition of a commission is a very desirable one, and if the minister will nox accept it I beg to give notice that when this Bill comes to its third reading I will move this amendment, and also to strike out the sections which will be unnecessary if the amendment is adopted. The minister stated when the Bill first came before the House that one of the strong justifications for the Government in taking up the measure was that New Zealand had already provided similar legislation, but a careful examination of the New Zealand Bill shows that they did not presume to do any such thing as is sought to be done by this Bill. They did not presume to cast upon the officers of the British army the duty of seeing the ballots marked, taking affidavits and certifying to papers which were to be sent back to that country, but they provided that, in the case of soldiers who were on duty in New Zealand preparing to g-o to the war, they should be allowed to vote by marking their ballots before they left, and that if a general election came on, their ballots could be counted. They also provided that, in the case of soldiers who had left New Zealand as members of any expeditionary force before the passing of the Act, they should be allowed to vote in the manner prescribed, and they provided that electoral officers should be appointed out of New Zealand for the purpose of taking their votes. Section, 8 of the New Zealand Act reads as follows:
Electoral officers may be appointed out of New Zealand for the purpose of enabling any person to record his vote under this Act who is a member of any expeditionary force sent out of New Zealand before the passing of this Act.
This is exactly the same provision which is made by my amendment, with this exception, that this amendment contains a greater safeguard for non-partisanship because it provides that the electoral officers, which the commissioners would be, should be appointed upon the nomination of the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition respectively. Otherwise it is the same. I* seems a strange thing, that modelling this legislation, as the Government pnetend to do, upon the legislation of New Zealand, they should adopt the course of imposing obligations upon the officers of

the British army which the Government and Parliament of New Zealand evidently thought was impracticable and unreasonable, and as (to the undertaking of which -obligations the Government has not the slightest information. The Minister of Justice has frankly informed us that he really *does not know whether the officers of the British army will perform the obligations. It seems a very extraordinary thing to pass this legislation, which may be for that reason alone an absolutely dead letter. The Government could easily provide the machinery, by the appointment of a commission, the members of which would be non-partisan electoral officers, and who could, with the aid of the regulations which they might make, see that the provisions of the Act would be fairly and honestly carried out and that all the soldiers desirous of voting would have a reasonable opportunity of doing so, and who would also see, and that is a most important thing, that the ballots which would be marked by the soldie-s entitled to vote would be returned to Canada and would actually be deposited. On the contrary, this Bill proposes to impose obligations on British officers which this Parliament has no right to impose. There is in the Bill a lamentable absence of ' those safeguards which one would suppose the Government would have had in mind in asking Parliament to assent to the Bill.

I wish to draw the minister's attention to the condition which results from the fact that, I think, we have agreed upon, that the officer who acts as a returning officer does so at his own option. He acts or he does not act, as he pleases. The purpose of the Bill is to give the soldier an opportunity of casting his ballot. That opportunity depends on the whim of the officer appointed; there is no obligation on him to take action and, as the minister put it, there is before him only an expression of the desire of the Parliament of Canada that he should act. Beyond that there is no authority or compulsion or obligation upon him. If I remember rightly, in considering the Bill at its earlier stage, the minister took occasion to say that a certain provision, which it was difficult to give effect to, w'as inserted so that there would not be a dislocation of the voting power of the country. We are making provision for the voting of the overseas contingents. We are assuming to make provision for the full number of the members of that contingent
to exercise their franchise. Ostensibly we are doing that. On the face of the Act we are doing that. We are placing this matter absolutely in the hands, under the control and at the option of the men whom we may name for certain positions which they are under no obligation either legal or moral to fill. It is only reasonable to believe that under these circumstances some soldiers will have the opportunity of voting and some will not. We . have no means of guidance as to what proportion of these will have an opportunity and what proportion will not. Surely, therefore, of necessity, under the conditions laid down in the Bill, there will be just as great a disarrangement of the volting power of the country as there would have been under the terms that my hon. friend objected to at the earlier stage of the proceedings. If we cannot do better than that, if we cannot be reasonably sure that every volunteer is going to have the opportunity of casting his vote, let us not claim that we are doing something that we actually are not doing. It may be that we are showing good-will, it may he that our intentions are all right, but unless we can do what we profess to be doing, let us not claim that we are doing it.
Let us admit that we have undertaken to do something that in the nature of things it is not possible to do. I submit to the minister that when the operation of any law cannot reasonably or measurably be assured it is more than doubtful whether there should be such a law at all. By giving unequal opportunity to one portion of our volunteers to vote while in fact denying to others the same opportunity we are not increasing the share of control of the affairs of Canada by the * volunteers as we profess, but we are endangering the reasonable result of a fair expression of opinion by the people who are not on active service. This cannot be the purpose of the minister, but it is the actual fact. I feel I would not be doing my duty if I did not set that view before the minister for his best consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The officers have been
referred to, and no doubt correctly, as British officers, but in the great majority of cases, if not in all, the officers dealing with our soldiers will be Canadian officers.
It may be possible that some of them may decline to act, but the effect of the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite is that because of the unwillingness of some of the offioers to perform mis duty this law might become ineffective in some instances,

that therefore we should not pass the law at all. Does anybody conceive that more than a small minority (if there be any at all), of our officers having this power conferred upon them, will refuse to exercise it? There is already provision in the Bill that if any officer designated in this Act is prevented from discharging the duty it may be performed by the officer next in rank below him. I would understand that to mean that if the officer next in rank below him was prevented from doing it, then the next below him might act. When we come to that section I shall put in words which will make my interpretation of that absolutely clear. I think it is a very weak argument, that because in some instances this Act may fail of its operation for want of good-will on the part of some officer, we should abandon entirely the project of providing votes for our soldiers on active service. I do not think that our authority over the officers on active service would be in any way enhanced or increased by our naming a commission, which commission would themselves undertake to deal w;th that same class of officers; we cannot delegate greater powers to the commissioners than we ourselves have.

Would the minister transfer his mind to the case of an ordinary constituency and ask himself would he consider it fair that, there being set off certain polling divisions in that constituency, it was optional with those who might be selected as deputy returning officers whether a poll should be held or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If that condition should exist, would the hon. gentleman suggest as a remedy that we should disfranchise the whole constituency and give no one an opportunity to vote?

I am not suggesting that. The minister must admit that such a condition would be unthinkable, looking toward a fair expression of the opinion of people in ordinary circumstances, and is it not absolutely just as unfair in securing a full expression of opinion by the soldiers? While the individual citizen has the right to have his vote recorded, the whole body of citizens has also a right in the election, and that right is that the election shall be so conducted that there shall be no disarrangement of the general body of the vote, and that there shall be a full, and fair, and as complete as possible an expression of opinion of all who are entitled to vote. If the minister, in granting the right

to the individual, must take away from the right to which the whole body of citizens is entitled, he surely should reconsider his position.
His suggestion that my view was that if we could not vote all the men, we should not vote any, is hardly a fair statement to make. Under the proposal of the hon. member for St. John, whereby commissioners who would be under ' the authority of this Parliament would be in bodily presence on the other side of the water, these commissioners would have an opportunity of selecting officers who would be willing to act and whose consent they would have before appointing them, and therefore, although there would not be compulsion, there would be assurance that the action would be taken that was necessary to enable the soldier to poll his vote. That is the difference between the proposal made by the hon. member for St. John and the proposal of the minister, which is simply to issue an order to certain men that they shall take certain action, when there is not a shred nor tittle of authority to compel them to take that action or to lay obligation on them for the taking of that action. The minister has laid considerable stress on the idea that because this Parliament says that an officer should act as returning officer, therefore he is in some way not compelled, but made to feel that he ought to take the action that Parliament desires him to take. I do not look upon the matter in that light at all. The officer as well as the soldier is on the other side of the water for a certain definite, specific purpose, in the carrying out of which discipline is one of the first necessities. As regards action by the officer acting as a returning officer or acting as political agent, or a scrutineer,-because if you are going to have a returning officer you should have scrutineers as well-the large majority of officers will say: this is an undue and improper interference with the important business that we are here to attend to; we do not think the Government or the Parliament of Canada was well advised in imposing this duty upon us, and we decline to act. I think that will be the proper view to be taken by officers on the other side, and I believe it is the view that will be taken by a large majority of them, at any rate by those who have a full appreciation of the duties that they are there to fulfill.

I would not take up any further time on this subsection were it not


for the extraordinary statement made by the Minister of Justice that the Government would have no more control over the commissioners, who might be appointed under the amendment which I proposed, when they reached the other side than it would have over the officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think that is the statement I made. I stated that we would have no greater control in any event over the men on the othqr side because it was exercised through commissioners than we would have by exercising it directly. We cannot give the commissioners a greater power than we ourselves have.
That is putting the case a little differently. When my hon. friend uses the word "men," does he mean the commissioners and their delegates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The people that the commissioners may work through over there. We can have no more control over them, because we have named the commissioners, than we can exercise directly.

My hon. friend is
entirely wrong. Suppose, for instance, that the commissioners go to France or Belgium. Surely they go there under an agreement with this Government to act as electoral officers or commissioners. There is a contractual obligation into which they have entered with this Government to discharge certain duties, and that obligation they are bound in law to carry out. Suppose they want assistance, they appoint delegates to act for them; they make contracts with these people so to act and to discharge the duties which are required to be performed under the statute. Does not that create as against the people so appointed a contractual obligation? Surely it does; but as to those gentlemen who are officers in the British army, some of them are Canadian officers or were Canadian officers until they went under the control of the British War Office, and the moment they go under that control, this Government has no control over them whatever. On more than one occasion in the House that has been the statement made by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Militia. I remember early in the session I asked the Minister of Militia if he had received any complaints from England as to the separation of the units of the troops which had gone from New Brunswick. He said that there had been some correspondence, but that this Government had no control over the men
whatever; that when they landed upon the shores of England, they were absolutely under the control of the British War Office; and that they then formed part of the British army. The same statement was made again' by the Prime Minister, when the case of Col. Struan Robertson came before us, that this Government must not interfere; that there must be no divided authority. Yet this Parliament is asked to impose' an obligation upon these officers who are under the control of the War Office to perform civil duties for this Government in connection with the holding of the elections of this Parliament. Surely the position of these officers, as far as this legislation is concerned, would be entirely different from that of the commissioners, who had undertaken with this Government for a consideration to perform the duties of electoral officers under this legislation, and it would also be entirely different from that of the delegates whom the commissioners might appoint and who would enter into a contract with them. Take the case of the Acting High Commissioner in London, who is outside of the territorial jurisdiction of this country, but who is under the control of this Government, because when he accepted the office of Acting High Commissioner, he became bound under his contract to perform the duties which pertain to the office which he is filling. The same is true as regards the agent of Canada in Paris, who is out of the territorial jurisdiction of this country, but who is under a contractual obligation to perform his duties as agent in Paris. It seems to me that the case is not arguable at all. These commissioners would, as I have said, be like the electoral officers who were appointed under a contract with the New Zealand	Government
that	for	a	certain	consideration
they would discharge their duties. But, as my hon. friend from Edmonton points out, this Government is asking the people to believe that it is making arrangements to enable the soldiers to cast their ballots. If they are not arranging to do that, then they are doing a great injustice to many of the boys at the front. Though this is what they profess, yet the minister himself admits frankly

he is compelled to admit-that there may be cases in which these officers will decline to act and by reason of that the votes of the soldiers under those officers may not be taken. Whether there will be a large number or a small number in that position the minister is unable to give us any idea. In answer

to the hon. member for Edmonton, the minister says: Suppose some returning officer should decline to act, should decline to hold a poll, shall we therefore disfranchise the people? Surely, that is not a parallel case. The returning officer is not relied upon to act unless he has agreed to act; he gets a certain compensation for acting; there is a contractual obligation upon him. And I am inclined to think it would be the law- I think it is undoubtedly clear-that if for any reason a poll is not held-the judges would declare the election void and another election would have to be held. Talk as the minister may, he is imposing upon these officers duties which he knows they cannot be required to perform, obligations which he cannot assure the House they will carry out, yet he is making profession that this Bill will enable the soldiers to exercise their right of franchise. He believes that there may be cases. I believe there will be many, many cases affecting thousands of our soldiers-in which they will not be given opportunity to exerciee their franchise, whereas, if ho took the simple course of following the example of New Zealand, and appointing electoral officers, letting them go to England, France and Bermuda, letting them make arrangements for delegates and assistants to carry out the provisions of the Act, he would be able to give reasonable assurance to the Canadian soldiers that they would all have an opportunity to cast their votes.

I do not rise for the
purpose of discussing any of the articles of the present section. As the Minister of Justice knows, I spoke a few days ago about granting the right to vote to others than soldiers. Every member of the House knows that there is a certain class, a class of labour men especially, who are deprived by their occupation of the opportunity of cast their votes. I refer particularly to the railway men. A year ago, I believe, a letter was presented to the committee and an argument was made in favour of giving these men opportunity to use their franchise which was kindly received by the minister and by the members of the committee. This year a letter was sent and an argument presented which also was well received by the minister and the members of the committee. It seems to me that while we are spending so much time in finding a way to give votes to the soldiers we should add a section to this Bill which would cover the railway men. Of course, everybody will admit that il these men are [Mr. Pugsle'* 7
sent to work early in the morning of election day, it is impossible for them to cast their votes. They are not like nearly all other classes whose occupation enables them to remain near their homes and within easy reach of the polling places. These men must be ready to take out their trains on schedule time, and it is absolutely necessary for the business of the country that they should fulfil that duty. They might be required to take away a train load of soldiers or a train load of munitions of war. They would thus be actually assisting in the carrying on of the war, and yet would be prevented from voting, while the soldiers would have opportunity to vote. The railway men tell me, and I accept it on their authority, that forty per cent of these men are prevented from polling their votes. I have a subsection to propose, which, I think, will overcome this difficulty. I think it should come in after subsection 4, and it might, if the minister wishes, be numbered 4a. I submit it in the form of an amendment and shall be glad if the minister will say whether he is in favour of it or not. He may say that it is a question of establishing the machinery to enable these men to vote. We have talked so much about machinery that it seems to me we ought to be in a position to organize machinery of any kind, especially for a purpose like this, which is to take the votes of people who remain within the country and not as in the case of the soldiers, to take the votes of those who are outside of the country. I do not know that I am absolutely in order in moving this amendment now, but I submit it in the hope that I am in order:
Railway conductors, railway engineers and brakemen, and all other railway employees, who are detailed for train service, shall have the option to cast their vote on polling day in the regular manner provided by law, or on the day before polling day in the following manner, to wit:
The railway employee, at any time between the hours of eight in the morning and six in the evening, shall present himself to the deputy-returning officer of the polling subdivision in which he is or may be, inscribed, who, in the presence of two witnesses, shall administer to him all the oaths required by law and shall then give him a ballot paper. The railway employee may thereupon mark the ballot paper in the usual manner provided by law and the deputy-returning officer Shall then place the same in the envelope, upon the hack of which shall be endorsed a certificate in form " c," mutatis mutandis, which certificate shall be signed by the deputy-returning officer and witnesses, and shall securely close the envelope. The .envelope containing such ballot paper shall then be sent by the deputy-returning officer by post to the returning officer, who shall open the envelopes and count the ballots, and in-

elude them in his returns, in the manner provided by law.
This is submitted as embodying the best way,to enable these men to cast their votes. Of course, there are many different ways by which it could be done, and this is not exactly the way proposed to the minister and the committee. While these are absentee votes, yet they are the votes of men who are in a position to know exactly who are the candidates in their several divisions. The letters sent to the committee a couple of years ago were signed, by 0. Lawrence, legislative representative of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, 200 Elgin street, Ottawa W. L. Best, legislative representative of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Engineers, 576 McLeod street, Ottawa; and J. H. Hall, legislative representative of the O. of R. C., Car-leton Hotel, Ottawa. My hon. friend will observe that the three men who signed that letter had a certain amount of responsibility on their shoulders. One represented the railway conductors, another the firemen and another the engineers. This demand must have reached a good many members of the House; I am sure that any railway man with whom they talked on the subject must have spoken of the manner in which railway men are handicapped on polling day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:

It seems to me that

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. member for Maisonneuve is moving to add a section, 4a, to the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Personally I have no
desire to insist on any point of order; I
am quite willing to answer what tlm_ hon. gentleman has asked. We are dealing with subsection 4 of section 2, prescribing the details of how the soldiers shall register their votes under section 1 and the first subsection of section 2. The amendment which the hon. gentleman proposes is hardly an amendment to the method by which soldiers shall exercise the right of voting. If the hon. gentleman wants to introduce an other section, it ought to come at the end of section 2. However, perhaps that is not material. The hon. gentleman has pointed out, very correctly, that the railway men have pressed for a method by which they may exercise their franchise. He has also very correctly said that I have every sympathy with their endeavour to have a means provided by which they may vote. I may point out in the first place, however, that the remedy which they ask for differs totally and entirely from the method suggested by my hon. friend. I have had many communications on the subject; the matter was dealt with in the committee, and I feel confident that I make no mistake in saying that they made no suggestion oi this particular method of voting that is now asked for on their behalf by the hon. gentleman. If we should provide a method for them to vote, I certainly think that the method they asked for would be very much more effective than this. The committee went into this question in connection with the Dominion Elections Act generally, both last year and this year we gave it a good deal of consideration. The committee, as a whole, came to the conclusion that it was not a practicable method. I am not sure that if I had been alone on that committee I would not have felt it possible to have worked the matter out, but, as the hon. gentleman knows, when we came to deal with the Dominion Elections Act generally at this session, we did not, save as regards one or two separate and distinct things, endeavour to deal with that matter at all. If the hon. gentleman really wants to help the railway men and all other persons who are interested in a further recognition of the right of people who cannot present themselves at the polls during the polling hours to have their vote, it would seem to me that the wisest course to follow would be to aid us in putting forward this first measure for this particular class of men who are away from the country and who are prevented from voting, not because they are attending to their own work, but because they are attending directly to the work of the public. I am sure that railway

men-, would be the first to recognize the difference between the two classes of voters. One is the class of men who, in the exercise of their employment, find themselves prevented from voting. That is a case with which I have the very greatest sympathy, hut at the same time it is not an absolutely analagous case. The hon. member has witnessed in this House the strong feeling of antagonism that has been shown to the idea of trying to provide a method by which people can vote otherwise than with all the formalities in the way which are provided for the public generally. That feeling we have to overcome. We are having, as the hon. member witnessed, some little difficulty in overcoming it, even in this exceptional case of ithe soldiers. Does not the hon. gentleman think that he will do more to aid the cause of those who, for other reasons, seek to have another method of absentee voting adopted, if he will help this Bill to go through, and allow us to demonstrate, in the face of the apprehension and fears that have been expressed, that you can safely provide for absentee voting? I certainly would not favour the adoption of the method suggested by my hon. friend. It is a method that, so far as I know, the railway men have not asked for; it is one which makes it absolutely out of the question that candidates or their representatives should be notified or have any opportunity of being present, It is quite true that that may happen, out of absolute necessity, in the case with which we are dealing, but there is no absolute necessity for it in the case which the hon. member brings forward. The best way to help all persons interested in the recognition of the right of those who cannot present themselves at the polls to vote is to profit by this particular case, which presents a peculiar claim to the exercise of the right, and to allow the results of this proposed legislation to demonstrate the feasibility and practicability of providing for absentee voting. I am satisfied that the passing of this measure and its successful operation will be the most effective method of helping to meet the desire of the railway men.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I understand that last year, when the committee was considering amendments to the Elections Act, the railway men applied to have their case considered; and this is a letter which I understand was addressed to my hon. friend as chairman of the Committee.
Ottawa, March 11, 1914. Hon. C. J. Doherty, Esq.,
Chairman and Member of Committee on the operation of the Election Act,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Dear Sir:
On account of the peculiar nature of their work which necessitates them being away from their home terminal on election day, a large percentage of railway men in train service are disfranchised and we would request that your committee who are considering amendments to the Election Act, take into consideration the adoption of some plan whereby a much larger percentage of railway employees could avail themselves of the privilege that rightly belong to all good citizens, namely, that of using their franchise.
Therefore we desire to submit the following proposition for your earnest consideration: That at all railway centres or divisional points the polling be extended to two days by placing the ballot box in charge -of some responsible person who will be stationed at some convenient point the day prior to the day on which the election is to be held for the purpose of allowing those employees to vote who might be away from home on the regular election day. If there is more than one railway running into an electoral district with more than one terminal, have a separate ballot box for each terminal.
The only difference which exists between the amendment that has just been submitted to the House, and the suggestion contained in the letter addressed to my hon. friend last year, is that the latter suggested that the voting should take place at divisional points, whereas the amendment before the House suggests that the men should vote at their place of residence either on polling day or the day before. This point, however, is not material. If the Government is not disposed to consider the amendment, I would observe to my hon. friend that last year when he and the committee presented to the railway men the difficulties and objections which existed in connection with having a separate law for any class of the community, these reasons seemed satisfactory to the railway men, and they did not press their views further. But this year, when they found that the Government was making a separate law for one class of our fellow citizens, who, whatever may be the reason, will not be able to vote as the rest of the citizens will vote, the railway men naturally came to the conclusion that the same privileges should be allowed to them; and that is the reason for their demand. My hon. friend says:	Oh,
let us pass this law, and it will help the railway men in attaining their object. If it is reasonable to have special legislation for one class of the community what objection can there be to giving the same privi-

leges to another class, which for one reason or another, is also prevented from polling in the regular way? The soldier is at the front doing his duty, but the railway man is doing his duty also, and it is just as important to the community. It is true that he is earning his living in the discharge of that duty, but every citizen ;n the community is working for a living, and every one is performing his duty to the state. It seems to me that my hon. friend is well justified in presenting his amendment ; but if the Government will not accept if that is the end of it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must remind the

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not wish to question the ruling of the Chairman, neither do I wish to insist upon it, but I might just point out that it is perhaps not of material importance whether we discuss it on section 4 or on the present section, for we have already discussed it, to some extent.

speechtext:
After section
4.

speechtext:

As we were discussing

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the minister will not accept it, that disposes of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps it is not quite
fair to say that I do not accept the amendment, but I hardly think it comes within the scope of the Bill. As the matter has been taken up I should just like to say this, with the permission of the Chairman: The committee that reached the conclusion that it did with regard to the difficulties in the
way of providing this form of voting for the railway men dealt with this matter last year, and also considered if again this year, but not in connection with this measure. Hon. gentlemen will remember that the committee was originally constituted to consider the Dominion Elections Act and the Controverted Elections Act, and that later on this question of votes for. soldiers was specially referred to it. Now I cannot quite accept the view of the right hon. gentleman, that because we are making this measure in regard to the soldiers it alters the situation with regard to -the railway men. I have the advantage and pleasure of knowing a great many railway men, and perhaps the men who have shown the most active and intelligent interest in this movement to get votes, and I am satisfied that I shall have their endorsement when I say that they themselves will not pretend that their case, from the point of view of the cause that prevents their voting, is analagous to that ot the soldier. We thought-and I say_ it notwithstanding my very high respect' of the railway men of this country-that the soldier stood in a peculiar position as compared with every other class of 9 p.m. people who are staying at home; and we are trying to deal with that very special and peculiar position. For myself, I am as sincerely in favour of meeting the desire of the railway men in this regard as my hon. friend who has made this amendment, and I say that without any reflection on his (sincerity. But after what we heard pro and con in the committee, and in view of the manner in which the matter was viewed by the committee, and particularly when I think of the difficulties which we met in this House when we did come with a minor proposition, but which looked to a certain extent to facilitating the voting of the railway men-I refer to the proposition to open the polls at an earlier hour in the day-in the face of all those facts I cannot think that one can do better service to the railway men and others who desire that we should arrive at a system whereby a man who cannot actually present himself at the polls may vote, than by giving the system support and a fair trial in this special case, when the opportunity for bringing it into force is furnished by the very special and peculiar position of those on whose behalf it is asked. Under the circumstances I cannot feel otherwise than that the suggestion of this amendment cannot be looked upon as something that can be expected to be acted upon in conne tion with this Bill. I do not think

we should embarrass this measure, when we are ihaving such very great difficulty in having it assented to by this House, by introducing into it at this stage, and without notice of any kind, a proposal in regard to which opinions might be held on lines other than those which would naturally be expected to bear on a Bill such as that before the House.

I hope the minister will believe that I had no intention other than to give the right of voting to railway men. I do not see why this would prevent the present Bill from passing. It has nothing to do with the passage of the measure. It has been stated time and again that the Government are not willing to pass class legislation. Do they characterize legislation of this kind affecting the interests of the railway men as class legislation? We are passing class legislation to-day. Of course, it is for the soldiers but it is class legislation to a large extent. It may be class legislation in the proper sense of the word. If you are going to give soldiers now at Montreal or Valcartieir votes you must pass class legislation for the purpose because there are soldiers at Valcartier who could go to Quebec and other cities and deposit their ballots in their own polling places. These railway men are not in a similar position. They may be away down at Riviere du Loup, and if they want to vote for any hon. gentleman opposite or for myself they cannot do so because they cannot return to their homes in time. If I had been in the House when the Bill to amend the Dominion Elections Agt came up I would have moved this same amendment. I have heard time and again in this House this argument about class legislation. I am sorry to say that whenever we bring a labour measure before the House it is said that it is class legislation. What is there that is not class legislation? Every private Bill is class legislation. Only public Bills are not class legislation, but private members of the House have no chance to put through a Bill during the session because the rules of the House are made to prevent public Bills, introduced by private members, from being passed. The rules are such that you cannot reach a public Bill on the Order Paper. I repeat that private Bills are class legislation, and to facilitate their passage certain days and hours are set apart for them. It is only the Government that can introduce a public Bill and ensure its passing. I know that members on the other side 
of the House, as well as on this side of the House, are not satisfied with the present [DOT]conditions because, while a public Bill may be introduced by a private member and placed on the Order Paper, it is wiped off at the end of the session. I claim that my amendment will <not prevent the present Bill from passing; far from it. It is just my intention to add to this Bill a certain clause which will enable these railway men to record their votes. It may be said that there are other voters who cannot reach their polling places on election day. It is always possible for men, in the majority of cases, to remain for two or three hours in the city where they reside in order to cast their votes. Commercial travellers can do that. With the railway men it is impossible. Fishermen can go out a little later in the morning or come back a little earlier in the evening, but a train must go on schedule time. The lives of the people are at stake, and there are other considerations which make it necessary that running schedules must be maintained. Let me repeat that it is not my intention to prevent the passing of this measure. I am. not-afraid of the measure. My only intention is to give these men a chance of casting their votes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not claim to be any more sincere than the hon. gentleman; so it is evident I did not question his sincerity. I am sorry to hear this legislation spoken of as class legislation. Our soldiers are citizen soldiers, and all classes of people are represented amongst them. I have reason to know that the railway men in particular are represented among our soldiers. They have merged themselves into this great body of men that should not be described as a class in any sense at all. It is composed of people gathered from all ranks and all occupations, and I am sorry to hear this legislation spoken of as class legislation.
I only spoke of those who are in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Those in Canada represent all classes. We can hardly speak of them as belonging to any particular class. I do not want to stand on any technical matter at this stage, when a point of order is raised. I am willing to say quite frankly what I think. This Bill was introduced for a specific purpose, and it required to be preceded by a resolution, which resolution could only be presented to this House after it had been communicated to His Royal

Highness the Governor General and had met with his 'approval. The resolution covered the providing of votes for soldiers. I do not think it would be competent for us to introduce into a Bill of that kind a further extension going beyond what the resolution covers.
It seems to me that the Minister of Justice did reflect upon the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I seemed to do it I want amply and completely to withdraw any reflection. I did not intend to make any reflection.
What I understood the minister to say was that the amendment was introduced for a purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I immediately corrected that.

What I would understand the minister to mean was that my hon. friend was not sincere in speaking and that he was seeking to introduce this amend-[DOT] ment for effect.
borne in mind that the only object of pressing this Bill in the dying hours of this session, and in the face of the many amendments which the Minister of Justice has himself made in it, with a view of removing its defects, is that the Government believes that there may possibly arise before another session of Parliament a psychological moment when they would hope with advantage to throw the country into the turmoil of a general election. Surely it is poor consolation to the railway men to say that the Government may spring an election on them after this Bill is passed, but that next session or the session after, or five years hence, or some time before another general election, the claims of the railway men may be taken up. Call this Bill what you like, it is a Bill to amend the Dominion Elections Act, and it is quite proper that an amendment along the lines suggested by the hon. member should be added to it; the title makes no difference, the title can be changed. My hon. friend (Mr. Verville) only wants provision made so that the railway men may vote at convenient places in Canada under the terms of the present Dominion Elections Act and under the present franchise, and he asks for no important changes at all. On the other hand, this Bill is seeking to make provision for marking ballots in foreign countries under circumstances where it seems impossible to surround the marking of the ballots with the safeguards which the people of Canada have always insisted are to be provided in the case of an election. The Minister of Justice said he was sorry to hear the hon. member refer ito some provisions in this Bill as class legislation. I do not understand there is any ignominy attached to the words "class legislation." All that means is, that you are enacting special legislation which will only apply to one particular class of our citizens, and does not this Bill do that? It provides among other things that so far as the soldiers on active service in Canada are concerned there shall be a special franchise for them; that the law requiring a residence of six months or twelve months as is the case in the different provinces shall not apply to the soldiers who are in Canada, but that a residence of thirty days gives them the right to vote. Surely that is legislation applying to a class of our people who have enlisted for active service. There is no insult in the use of the word "class;" all it means is that it applies to a particular

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Just because I had used these words, and because it occurred to me that such a suggestion might come from somebody, I hastened to add that I did not mean to say that there was any such purpose on the part of the hon. gentleman. I hastened to correct myself by saying that there might possibly be a purpose, but I certainly added what I have said, and if I did not I want to do it now. 1 want to put it as clearly as I can that I did not intend to suggest anything that would lead any one to conclude that I did not attribute perfect sincerity to the hon, gentleman who moved the amendment.
Mr. PUGSLEY; I am very glad indeed to hear the minister making that explanation, because I think every member of the community will recognize that the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) is at all times earnest, sincere and watchful over the interests of the working people. And, as delegations from the railway men have been before this Government on different occasions urging that better opportunities should be given them for casting their votes, 1 can very well understand that my hon. friend felt it his duty to avail himself of this opportunity to move the amendment. The Minister of Justice has told the hon. member that it would be better to let this Bill pass as it might help to forward the object he has in view, but it should be

portion of the community, and (that is all my hon. friend (Mr. Verville) said. If this Bill is to go through this session, I believe there would be no difficulty at all in having the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Maisonneuve added to it.
We are getting along fairly well with the Bill, and if the Minister of Justice can only come a little way towards us and agree to these reasonable amendments, which would make this Bill workable, and which would surround it with safeguards which would assure an honest vote being -taken, we could pass the Bill in a very short time. But if the Minister of Justice shows that he is magnificently stubborn, and that he cannot be made to budge once he makes up his mind, and will not try to improve the Bill unless we all agree to his suggestions, then, of course, it makes it more difficult to consider the measure. Although, of course, at the same time I do not suggest for a moment that the members on this side of the House will not help it along as well as we can.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I desire to express my deep sympathy with any practical effort towards securing for railway men an opportunity to exercise the franchise. We have no more intelligent class of voters in Canada than are the railway men, and I would be very glad to do anything I could to bring about a means whereby all railway men would have an opportunity to vote. I have lived for many years in a railway city, and I have regretted at every election to find that large numbers of our very best citizens are deprived of the opportunity of exercising the franchise. In my city we have for thirty years been trying to think out some practical means for securing to the railway men an opportunity .to vote, but we have never been able to hit upon a plan that did not seam to have so many objections to it that it was found to be impracticable. I quite admit that the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve would enable a larger percentage of the railway men to vote than is the case now when the election is confined to one day instead of two, but his proposition does not at all meet the situation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In my judgment, this discussion is out of order. This amendment is not within the scope of the title of the Bill, and the committee has no power to deal with it nor have a discussion on it on the question under discussion at the pre-

sent time. Therefore it is my duty, after having consulted my best advisers, to rule the amendment out of order at the present time.

Only at the present
time? [DOT]
Will the minister state why the envelopes are to be sent by registered post by the-Clerk of the Crown in Chancery and not by registered post from abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The- reason why we did not speak of registered post from abroad was that tha arrangement with regard to registration on the other side was of such a nature as might expose the ballots to very considerable delay.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Subsection agreed to.

If I might be permitted,
I want to say as regards subsection 4, that it is really a very loose way of handling the ballots that is suggested. The subsection says:
The envelopes containing the ballot paper shall then and there in the presence of the voter be placed in a bag or other suitable receptacle, which shall be carefully kept by tha said officer, and securely closed.
That is the time when the ballot should be placed in a sealed package, the package to be sealed in the presence of the voter and with a notation in some form as to who has voted, so that there will be a permanent record. There is just as great necessity for the ballot to be sealed from the hands of the original returning officer to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery as there is from the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to the returning officer in the constituency. I would very strongly urge that my suggestion be adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The reason why we usa the words "securely closed" instead of the word "sealed," is that it was pointed out to us that in many circumstances it might be difficult or practically impossible for the officer to produce sealing wax to seal up the parcel; after all, sealing is only one method of carefully closing this bag or receptacle, and we are making the requirement that it should be securely closed. If other words can be suggested to be added there that will impress more the necessity of secure closing than the words used, I shall be very glad to add them, but I would like to avoid the word "sealed" simply for the reason I have given. If in addition to "securely closed" we should say "fastened or bound together so that it cannot be opened without that being per-

ceived," or something of that kind, I shall be very glad to add it. I was under the impression that subsection 4 had been passed. I do not want, however, to object to the suggestion of the hon. member.

I am well aware of that, and I am quite willing to submit to the rule; but I am urging that this is the most important stage in the proceeding, and that there should be a more definite wording. Over and above the sealing of the package, which I still think should be done, the returning officer should make a list of the votes cast and put into the package, so that there will be a permanent record of the votes cast and of the number of the votes cast.

I do not think the attention of the minister has been called to the fact that there is no provision in section 2 whereby any soldier who may not be able to read or write will be able to cast his vote. There must be some men in that position, and section 2 is the section that provides the manner of voting.
The Dominion Elections Act provides for that.

Yes, but this is a Bill giving the instructions for the parties who are going to take the vote. Where you have a section like section 2 which deals with the whole voting under these exceptional circumstances, the expression of the method means the exclusion of the more general method contained in the Dominion Elections Act.
I would also like to point out that this section provides .for the volunteer who desires to vote:
In the presence of the said officer, but in such a manner as not to disclose to the officer how he is voting. I
I would like to know how this is possible. The Dominion Elections Act provides that a person who wants to mark his ballot shall go into a separate apartment away from the officer and scrutineers and make his mark there, and there is absolute secrecy. There cannot be absolute secrecy here. Fancy the situation in which a vote of this kind will be taken. You have the commanding officer of the company or squadron, as the case may be, in a tent at the front, and you have his table in the centre of .the tent. Where is the soldier going to go in that tent for the purpose of marking his ballot so that the officer cannot see what he is doing?
These two points seem to me to be entirely weak. If the wish is to preserve the secrecy of the ballot, you are trying to provide an impossibility, in view of the conditions under which the vote would be taken. In the second place, in my judgment, the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act would not apply to the illiterate voter, for all the directions are contained in the Bill, and this would not be covered without some express declaration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a clause in the Bill later on providing that this is to be read-
I know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not wish to discuss that, but if there be any doubt about the applicability, I am prepared to have the Bill amended so as to expressly declare that section 166 of the Dominion Elections Act shall apply, that. being the section applying to those unable to write. Now, with regard to marking the ballot I believe that to require a separate compartment and so on for the marking of the ballot would be to require the impossible. But, for instance, I venture to say, that as the hon. gentleman sits there at his desk, it would be quite possible for him to mark a ballot in such a way that I, standing here, could see him mark it and yet I could not see for which candidate he marked it.
This is a very big chamber.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And fields are large.
I understand that the battle front in Europe extends for miles and miles. If necessary, some of that space could be utilized. I think it is not difficult so to arrange matters. so that one can be seen to mark a ballot without it being seen for whom he marks it. I am not now in a position to quote exact instances, but I may say that this is the method provided for in many systems of absentee voting. As to the "suggestion of the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. H. H. McLean) that a list should be inclosed, I am not going to deny that there would be advantages in having a list made. But we have to remember that if we surround this with too much formality, we shall defeat the very purpose of the measure. After all, the making of the list and inserting it in the package, so far as I can see, would have only this advantage, that if somebody had voted and was entered as one of a certain number on the list and the corresponding ballot did noit turnup you would



know that the ballot had disappeared, which would be an indication that the par-pel had been tampered with. But this would hardly be conclusive, and you would hardly on that basis, reject all the ballots, for it might be that the failure to put the ballot in was the result of an oversight. When these ballots come to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery he is ordered by the next section to make a record. While there would be usefulness in the list, yet I do not think, in view of the conditions under which this law must he carried out, that we ought to impose more formalities than are absolutely necessary.
Referring to the observations of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), if we might be allowed to go back to subsection 4, I would like to have it amended in the sense he suggested. I move:
That subsection 4 be reconsidered, and that it be amended by adding, in line thirty-five, after the word " closed," the words " and fastened in such a manner as to make any tampering with the same evident. '
Is not the minister providing for a list?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I pointed out that the
advantage of having a list, in my opinion, would not counterbalance the disadvantage of the additional formality.
It would be a check on the officer himself. It would be no trouble for him to count the number of ballots.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
means to enter only the number, not the names?

Only the number of the
names or envelopes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no objection to requiring him to enclose a statement of the number of ballots, in the parcel.

That would be a certain check.
. Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Now, to provide for the statement of the number of envelopes, I move:
That the section be amended by adding, at the end of line thirty-four, after the word "receptacle,' the words, "in which the officer shall enclose a slip giving the number of envelopes contained in it."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

If any special place is provided for the voting of the soldiers at the front, in all probability it will be a tent.

I am quite sure that you cannot work out the idea of secrecy in connection with the marking of the ballot if -the soldier has to mark it in the presence of an officer. Why should he mark it in the presence of an officer, if he knows how to read and write? I suggest that words " in the presence of the said officer " be struck out from the fourth Line of subsection 4.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No man gets a ballot until he makes an affidavit. We thought to secure that the man himself shall mark the ballot. If we allow him to go away from the presence of the officer to mark his ballot, we do not know who will mark that ballot. It is suggested to me by my colleague (Mr. Crothers) that after the word " officer " in line 26 of subsection 4, there be inserted the words " or any other person." I beg to move that subsection 4 be so amended.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

In every election there are independent candidates in many constituencies. The Government may have a candidate in a certain constituency, and the Opposition, feeling that they cannot carry the constituency, do not put up a candidate; accordingly, an independent candidate offers for election. On the other hand, in some constituency which is very strongly Liberal, the Government may not put up a candidate, and the result will be that there will be an Opposition candidate and an independent candidate. How will the votes be counted in such oases? If the soldiers vote for the Government, and there is no Government candidate, how will the votes he dealt with? One of the very many exceedingly objectionable features which I see in this Bill is that the voters at the front do not know who the candidates are.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Does the hon. member offer any suggestion to obviate that difficulty?

The first suggestion I
offer-and I think it is an exceedingly sensible suggestion-is that the Bill be dropped The second suggestion that I offer is that you do away altogether with the mention of the independent candidate. I 3imply wish to point out that the soldiers may vote for a Government candidate or an Opposition candidate, and there may be no Government candidate or no Opposition candidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to the suggestion that we drop the Bill, of course I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman in that respect. If a man votes for the Government candidate

in a particular constituency and there is nobody supporting the Government, that man is in the same position as anybody who votes at home for a person who is hot a candidate-he loses his vote. The same thing applies, of course, if he votes for an Opposition candidate or an independent candidate, and there happens not to be any. Speaking personally, 1 have a strong feeling that the opportunity that is now afforded to the voter to say: I vote for John Smith-naming the candidate-will meet a great many cases. I believe that the knowledge will reach the other side in a great many instances as to who the candidates are or will be, and that this knowledge will enable the soldiers to take the chance in registering their votes, that a certain man is going to be a candidate. I think many ballots will come back containing ballots for particular candidates, and I think that in the bulk of cases it will turn out that the person named on the ballot is the real candidate. I am free to admit that there may be cases where a soldier says: I vote for the independent candidate, and there may turn out to be no independent candidate; also there may be cases where a man may vote for the Government or for the Opposition candidate -and there may be no such candidate. These will be exceptional cases, however; I confess that I cannot devise means to avoid that.
They may be exceptional, but they may not be so exceptional in this case as not to affect the whole result of the election. Sometimes majorities are very narrow.

These cases were not exceptional in the province of Quebec during the last election. At that election there were fifty candidates whose platform was opposed to the policies of both the leader of the Government and of the Opposition. They most emphatically disowned any relationship with the present Prime Minister, and one sentence -that is well remembered in my province was, Borden is worse than Laurier.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That was awfully
abusive.

It was well known that most of these gentlemen were Conservatives, and it is well known now that their campaign fund was financed by the Conservative party. I have under my hand the programme of one of these gentlemen, Mr. L. P. Pelletier, now Judge Pelletier, who was 158J
the former Postmaster General in this Administration. This is what he said in his speech at Jeune Lorette in accepting the candidature. I am quoting from L'Eve-nement, the OTgan of the Conservative party, in its issue of August 30, 1911:
" En second lieu je suis candidat parce qu'a votre voix qui m'appelait s'est jointe la voix du chef nationalists de ce district, M. Arma-nd Lavergne."
" Je suis aussi candidat comme protestation cont-re la marine de guerre, et pour contribuer a remedier a cette loi scelerate."
I will try to translate that: Certainly I am a candidate because to your voice-the voice of the people-which is calling me, is united the voice of the Nationalist leader of this district, Mr. Armand Lavergne. I am also a candidate as a protest against the Naval Law, and to help in having that nefarious law repealed.
Surely the Minister of Justice will not say that Mr. Pelletier was an Independent; for, thirty days after he uttered these words, he was a member of this Administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He might meet the description of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German). He was clearly against the Government.
He was not an Independent at all, for he became a member of this Administration thirty days after. I should like to know what the returning officer would do in such a case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Put him on the bench.

Would he count the votes in favour of the Government?' Perhaps under one of the artful clauses of this Bill the right hon. Prime Minister would be the judge. Is that fair? I do not think so. The right hon. gentleman knows by experience what the independence of the so-called Nationalists amounts to. It would be deceiving the electors to call these men Independents. I am sure that at the last election it would have been very difficult to apply this system in my riding; it would have been very difficult to say to whom the vote should go.
I do not know whether there 10 p.m. will be any Nationalists next time, I do not think there are many of them left in the province of Quebec. I think provision should be made in the Bill to cover such a case as I have mentioned. Personally I do not see how this Bill can be worked out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I appreciate the kindly anxiety of the hon. gentleman on behalf of the Nationalists, of whom he says there are no more. We are legislating for the present and the future, not for past conditions. In any event the only ballots that the leader of the Government or the leader of the Opposition can deal with are those that have been given either for the Government or for the Opposition. Their respective power is limited to saying who ought to get that vote, the Prime Minister dealing with votes marked for the Government, and the leader of the Opposition dealing with votes marked for the Opposition. The men who vote will make it quite clear that they want their vote to go to the greatest benefit for the Government or for the Opposition, and I think we .have provided a perfectly fair method of determining who that vote for the Government shall be applied to, or who that vote for the Opposition shall be applied to. As for 'the Independent candidate, in no case will the leader of the Government or the leader of the Opposition be entitled to claim votes given for Independent candidates. Either there will be a person to answer to that description or there will not. If there is such a person he will get the votes. If there is not, the vote will be void.
Mr. MARCH,: Suppose there are two independent candidates.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If there are, I do not know how you are going to arrive at a determination as between them. But all [DOT]our past experience goes to show while -such a case is possible, it is very exceptional.

I think the hon. member for booth York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) -always runs as an independent candidate.
-Mr. DOHERTY: He will get the votes, then.
Suppose the votes are all marked either for the Government or for the Opposition. The hon. member for South York would not get any of the Government votes, as he would not be a Government candidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
Suppose that a great number of ballots are marked Independent, and that there is no Independent candidate in that division. Those ballots would not 
be counted. Is that fair? We are so anxious to give the soldiers an opportunity to vote that we should certainly see that their votes are not lost. Again, a candidate may accept the fiscal policy of a certain party, but be against that party on other questions. Suppose that in his speeches he lets the people know where he stands, where would those ballots go? It is such a technical question that perhaps only a lawyer could decide it. Perhaps it would be better to divide the votes, seeing that the candidate favoured one part of the policy of his leader, but not another part. I suppose my hon. friend would say that those votes would be rejected. As we are so anxious to give votes to the soldiers, we should see that the votes are not thrown away. My hon. friend said that there will be Liberal candidates at the next election. I hope there will be quite a few of them. There may also be some Socialist candidates; I think there will. They might be elected but you could not be sure. It would be a good thing to have a few of them in this House. Will one mark "socialist" on his ballot if there is no socialist or candidate of an independent turn of mind? It has been the custom of many people in this country to mark "socialist" on their ballots and thus spoil their ballots because they want to acknowledge the fact that they -are for -socialism. The more we study this Bill the more we see its defects. I would be sorry to think -that any soldiers should lose their votes on thi-s account. Canadian soldiers have probably' learned more of socialism than they ever knew before. They are now in contact with eiem-ents which probably were not so familiar to them on this side and it may be that a great many of -these men will be willing to cast their votes for socialists. There are many socialists in Belgium, England, and France, they will be associating with those who hold these -ideas at the front and they also may come in contact with German prisoners who are -socialists. Therefore, there may be a very great change of opinion and I am afraid that a large number of votes will be spoiled in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know that my position enables me to give any authoritative solution of the difficulty suggested. But I would take it that if you had in a constituency a Government candidate, an Opposition candidate and, say, a socialist candidate, and you had votes given for an independent candidate, I would understand that under these circumstances -the man who classified himself as a -socialist, or came

under some other designation would thereby announce himself neither as supporting the Government nor the Opposition, and would meet the description of an independent candidate. But it will not do . for me to deal with that. If that question arises the courts will have to determine it. We have provided for people as being for the Government, for the Opposition, or for neither one nor the other and I would be disposed to think that any man who adopted a designation such as the hon. gentleman suggests would be starting out on a line which would place him in the position of being neither for the Government nor the Opposition. That, to my mind, would meet the description of the hon. gentleman.
In 'the case of a deferred election both might be for the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The gentlemen will vote either for the Government or the Opposition. If they vote for the Opposition, and both of the candidates are for the Government, they will be in the position of having voted for no candidate if it turns out that that is the situation.

I have always been opposed to electors being called upon to vote for anything but a personality. If they are asked to vote for the Government or the Opposition there is intimidation. When the officer confronts the voter and asks Rim if he votes for or against the Government it is certainly intimidation especially in the case of the soldier at the front. No one in this country values more highly the sacrifices which our soldiers are making than I do. I value so much the sacrifices of our soldiers and I would think they had so much to do in this terrible war, the results of which must certainly be disastrous to our children at the front, that I would not even attempt to bring in a bill to give franchise to the soldiers until the time when they had returned from the front bearing the laurels of victory. We all expect and hope that this terrible war will be ended favourably to the cause of the Allies before next September or October. It has been a very strenuous war but the most terrible part of it is to come because the Allies are bound to conquer, as they must conquer in the interest of humanity. I would like to ask any hon. members of this House why we should be rushing on an election during the most terrible part of this war. Lord Kitchener told us not , six weeks ago that the war would commence in May. It is about commencing now,
and the sacrifices that our armies have made during the last five or six months are nothing as compared with the sacrifices which they will be called upon to bear within the next six months. The only-encouragement that the soldier has in the trenches is that derived from the comradeship of the man who is beside him. He does not inquire whether he is a Liberal or Conservative, whether he is for the Government or for the Opposition, he knows that he will help to sustain his life and courage in the great struggle that is being waged in the cause of humanity. That is the situation, and unless we can draw up a Bill which will give the franchise in such a form as we all desire, such as will enable the soldier to cast an independent vote, we should not be too eager to expedite this measure. During the discussion this afternoon and this evening the Minister of Justice by his avowals has admitted the impossibility of framing a Bill which will meet all the requirements of the men at the front. I am for votes for the soldiers, but why not wait until another session? We have supplied the Government with all the money they need to carry on the war. We look for British examples. Next December the British Parliament will expire. Is the British Parliament busy to-day passing a Bill providing, votes for the soldiers at the front? It is contemplating the possibility of extending the life of Parliament in order that there may be no election during the war. We have eighteen months yet to go, and I am sure that in that eighteen months the war will be settled satisfactorily to the Allies, or it will never be settled. The discussion having demonstrated the impracticability of the-Bill which we have before us, let us consider it for another year and if the war is-, not settled by that time the Bill can be taken, up again and brought into operation at the-expiration of this Parliament, which will take place in November, 1916. I submit these considerations to the Minister of Justice and I appeal to his judgment.
Has the Bill a provision to meet the case of a soldier who through the action of the enemy has lost th? use of his arms, or is invalided in some way so that he cannot sign the ballot paper?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That suggestion was
made by the hon. member for Pictou and I answered that section 166 of the Dominion Elections Act, which deals with persons who are physically unable to mark the

ballot paper, would be made to apply to this Act.
Will the words "I vote" on the ballot papers be in French and English?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will be very glad to
put them both in French and in English.

I suppose some of the
affidavits should be in French?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We could have some
printed in French and some in English.

Does the ballot bear the
initials of the officer who takes the vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no provision
for that but if it is considered a precaution I have no objection to insert it. We were relying on the fact that the officer saw the man mark the actual ballot. In view of the circumstances under which this vote is to be taken I would like to avoid introducing any complication unless it is of manifest advantage.
What we did rely upon in that regard as to the identity of the ballot was the fact that the officer would see that the whole thing was done simultaneously, and that he was in a position to see the marking of the ballot. Then the ballot as it stands in the form provided in the Rill will have the counterfoil with the number on it which will remain on the stub as it is handed out, and it seems to me that that is sufficient identification that it is the same ballot, because the man does his voting without leaving the sight of the officer. I would like to avoid complicating the matter.
There is no evidence that the same ballot will get back to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the initials of the returning officer be sufficient?
I do not think the initials would be of much use being put on abroad, because if any one wanted to switch the ballot, he could do it.
He could initial the envelope . as being closed.

There is a general provision that if a ballot has a special mark,, it loses its value. Under the circumstances in which the ballots are to be marked, there is a very great possibility that there may be marking that will tend to disclose identity, or that will not be in accordance with the ordinary usage.

It would be very undesirable if the very strict rule that is generally applied to the marking of ballots in their being counted were applied to the making of these ballots. Will that strict rule be applied under the provisions of this Bill to these ballots?
Mr. DOHERTY': That is the rule that provides that if a ballot is marked so that it can be identified, it loses its value?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I understand the [DOT] matter aright, in the application of this section, it becomes a question to be determined by the circumstances of each particular marking, whether a mark in a certain way is a mark by. which a man can be identified. While I have not had occasion very recently to look into the jurisprudence in connection with the subject, I do not think 1 am wrong in saying that the courts have adopted pretty generally the rule that you should lean in favour of the view that will give effect to the vote. I have no doubt that the courts in determining whether a mark, that may be claimed to be a marking that may serve to identify, should be so considered or not, will take into consideration the circumstances under which the ballot is marked. It would not be safe for us to wipe out the provision entirely; the safest course is to leave to the good judgment of the courts to bear in mind the circumstances in which the ballots are marked when determining whether the particular way in which tlie ballot is marked will lead to the identity of the voter.

These ballots will count as much as any other ballot, and sometimes an election turns on the marking of one or two ballots. Therefore you cannot give too great care to determining what shall and what shall not be counted.

I have an amendment
which I would like to suggest to my hon. friend to come as subsection 11 of section 2 which we have been considering. Before reading the proposed amendment, I would like to call the attention of the minister to the fact-and to emphasise it as strongly as possible-that Parliament is proposing to ask officers of the Imperial Army to perform certain duties under this legislation. These officers are all under the control of the British War Office, and of course their military duty is the paramount duty which they are called upon to perform. Therefore

I would suggest to the minister that it would be an act of courtesy; that it would lead to greater harmony in the discharge of their duties by the different officers and to better understanding with the War Office, and that it would be altogether exceedingly desirable that before we give effect to the provisions of this Bill seeking to impose these duties upon Imperial officers over whom this Government has no control, the Secretary of State for War should be consulted and his (approval of the Bill obtained. I throw out this suggestion which I think is worthy of favourable consideration, and it is altogether desirable that it should be added to the Bill. The amendment which I would suggest is:
That there be added as subsection 11 of section 2 the words:
