No action shall be taken under the foregoing provisions of this section until the same have been submitted to and approved by the Secretary of State for War of the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This suggestion, perhaps not precisely in this form but in substance, has been made at different .times throughout this debate. Fot myself, I think it so perfectly obvious that neither the Secretary of State for War on the other side nor any member of the Imperial Government, nor any authority whatsoever over there, would ever imagine -that we meant to force the operation of this law to the detriment of military operations or so as to interfere with anything that -the military authorities could consider necessary, that it would be absolutely out of place that we should put in this Bill -something that would suggest that we thought -that -they might think us endeavouring to do that. I am quite confident that they would never think so. That being so with regard to -this particular case, I think generally speaking, it is a highly objectionable proposition that this Parliament should legislate subject to the permission of -the Secretary of State for War or of any other minister of His Majesty's Government of the United Kingdom. I would like to point out what I said in moving the second reading of -this Bill, that to my mind this-is purely a Bill recognizing the right to the fr-anchise of a certain class of Canadian subjects of the King and providing a method whereby they may exercise that franchise. It is absolutely without question that where availing themselves of that right will interfere in any way with -the par-amount duty of those Canadian subjects of the King as soldiers of the King, they themselves will not allow it to interfere, and that if they were disposed to do so, the military authorities can be absolutely trusted not to allow it to interfere. That is a matter which the military authorities are absolutely in a position to control; but for my part, and with all the respect that I entertain for the military authorities of the United Kingdom- and for His Majesty's Government of the United Kingdom, I, as one member of the. Parliament of -Canada and as one representative of the people of Canada, certainly do not think that it would be the proper thing that we should legislate as to who in Canada should have the franchise and -who in Canada should be afforded the means Of exercising that right, and say in express terms that we subject our judgment upon that question either to the Secretary of State foT War or to His Majesty's Government as a whole of the United Kingdom.
I do think we owe that much recognition to the autonomy of this country, that much respect to this Parliament itself. So completely is it recognized that the power relating to the election of representatives of the people in this country belongs exclusively to the Parliament of Canada and to the courts that the Parliament of Canada constitutes, that His Majesty's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council have consistently declined to entertain applications for leave to appeal in cases bearing upon elections to this House, laying down the doctrine that it was within Canada that matters pertaining to the election of members to the House of Commons of Canada should properly be decided. It therefore appears to me obviously unnecessary that we shorn,* go forward implying in any way to the Secretary of War that we have the faintest idea that our legislation can under any circumstances interfere with his military control of military operations. In the second place, I think it, in principle, undesirable in the strongest sense of that word, that we should in an Act dealing with the Canadian franchise, subject the action of this House to any approval or disapproval outside of this Parliament of Canada. Therefore, I must, for my part, decline to accept the suggested amendment. I may point out, if it is thought that in doing what we are doing here to-night we are overstepping the proper bounds within which the Parliment of Canada should keep itself, that there is in His Majesty a power of disallowance. But I do not think we can go forward with the implied admission that there is something in our legislation which could be objectionable. For my part, I see nothing to give rise to

any well-founded objection on the part of the Secretary of State for War or the Government of the United Kingdom, and I am not ready to go forward with the suggestion, which would be involved in our submitting the legislation to the approbation of this minister, that there is something objectionable in this Bill. An hon. gentleman said to me to-day, " Qui s'excuse, s'accuse". If we go with such excuses we imply that there is lurking in our minds the belief that we have tried to do something which might interfere with the legitimate authority of the Secretary of State for War. I have no consciousness of having done anything of that kind, and the legislation we are dealing with to-night seems to me so obviously and in a very special manner a matter to be dealt with exclusively by this Parliament that I cannot consent that legislation being subjected to the approval of any Minister of the Crown in the United Kingdom.

The hon. minister has entirely misunderstood the amendment I have proposed. I was careful that it should have no reference whatever to section 1, which is the section which establishes the franchise and gives the vote to soldiers on active service, subject only to their having had a residence of thirty days in this country. As to that, I raise no question	by my	amendment. Butsection 2 provides the machinery by which the soldiers are to be permitted to exercise this right, and the minister proposes by the various subsections of this section to exact an obligation from, and impose a duty upon,	officers	of	the	ImperialGovernment, officers who are in the Imperial army. Without a "by your leave" or suggesting that we do him the courtesy to ask the consent of the Secretary for War, we will impose on these officers, who are abroad for military duty and in the interest of the Empire, and' under the absolute	control	of	the	ImperialGovernment,	the duty	of	carrying
out the provisions of this Act. And the minister says that, because I proposed that before exacting this obligation from these officers the Secretary of State for War shall be consulted and shall approve of it, I am in some way humiliating this Parliament, and suggesting that by possibility the Secretary of State for War may not approve of it. Surely the minister must be wrong. All I say by my amendment and my argument is that we are asking these British officers to do what we have no right to ask them to do. We are by statute imposing 
upon them an obligation which we have no earthly right to impose on them. We are saying by our proposed statute that, instead of appointing our own electoral officers and sending them abroad to give to our soldiers the right to exercise their franchise, we will impose this obligation upon an Imperial officer. Is it humiliating to this Parliament-Does it detract from the authority of this Parliament if we say that, before so imposing this obligation upon these Imperial officers, the Secretary of State for War shall be consulted and shall give his consent?-not to the whole Bill, not to that part which extends the franchise, but only to that part which imposes these obligations upon the officers of the Imperial service. Is it detracting from the dignity of this Parliament if I say that before doing that the Secretary for War shall be consulted and shall approve of it? My mind may be different from that of the minister, but to me it seems cheeky and absolutely indefensible for this Parliament to declare by law that this task shall be cast upon the Imperial officers who are at the front to do Imperial dirty, without asking the consent-of the Secretary of State for War under whom they are serving. I cannot but express extreme surprise that my hon. friend regards this amendment unfavourably. I can do nothing furtjier now, but I can say that when the Bill comes up for third reading, I shall have an opportunity of presenting my amendment again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's amendment is to the effect that this Bill shall not come into operation-
No, only section 2.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: I wish to correct the minister so far as my attitude was concerned. I do not recall that I was condemning him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I mean to say, condemning my course.

If I may be permitted, I do not even agree to that. All I wanted was to establish a fact as it existed, and then to draw certain conclusions from that fact. I do not wish to be understood as condemning either the minister or his course; all I wanted was . to know exactly what the course was, and what the consequences of it would be. At this moment I am not going to concern myself with the constitutional side of this question or the maintenance of the dignity of Parliament, but I am still concerned as to the probability of the volnteers overseas exercising the privilege or the right which it is proposed that they shall have an opportunity of exercising. It must be obvious that it is a matter of interest to us, if we are desirous of their
exercising the right that we place within their reach, to know whether the authorities that are supreme on that side of the water are willing that they should exercise that right. It is obvious, -too, that if the authorities there are not willing, the volunteers are certainly not going to be ahle to exercise it. On the other hand, if the authorities are willing, the exercise of the right by the soldiers then depends, as I have said, on the whim of the officers. I do not wish to criticise unduly, but I would have thought that it would have been wise for the Government to become informed as to what the view of the British military authorities is in regard to the -application of this provision. They -have not seen fit to do so, however; we axe passing the legislation, and there is no time to find out now. It seems to me that it is a fair proposition that a saving ol-ause 'shofild be inserted in the Bill such as has been suggested by the hon. member for the City of St. John.

The proposal made
by the hon .member for St. John city is so obviously proper and right that I cannot understand the position taken by the Minister of Justice in regard to it. What did we send these men across the ocean for? We sent them across the ocean to place them at the disposal of King George arid his Imperial officers, headed by the Secretary of State for War, to fight the battles of the Empire. That is their first duty; that is th-eir whole duty; that is that duty the fulfilment of which with credit to themselves will cause us to give ' them the glory of victory when they return. The moment they landed on the soil of Great Britain th^y ceased to be under the supervision of the Government of Canada, except in the -matter of receiving their pay. As to their disposition; as to where they shall go and what they shall do; as to how they shall perform th-eir duties- that is under the direction of Lord Kit-*chener, and no one else. The Secretary of State for War having control of their movements for the purpose of defending the Empire and of attacking the Germans, I agree with the hon. member for St. John that it is cheeky -and impertinent for us to attempt to interfere with his direction and authority by s-aying that his commanding officers and captains shall do this, that or the other thing on a particular day or days when he, perchance, may wish them to be doing -something else. I -think also that the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John that the Minister of Militia should have

been here during the discussion of this Bill is very apt. The Minister of Justice, erudite lawyer that he is, has no special acquaintance with military discipline, military law or military operations.
He was a soldier.
He is an honorary colonel, like myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am a real captain, unlike yourself.

The Minister of Justice will hardly claim that the situation just now with regard to military operations is such that any one on this side of the ocean is possessed of knowledge which would enable him to take any action interfering with the authority and direction of Lord Kitchener in the controlling of the movements of the men under his supervision. When in the committee I ventured to make a suggestion as to what should be done, my hon. friend took the ground at that time that you could not dictate to these men, that it was a matter entirely for the commanding officer to say whether he would do this or that. When some one suggested that the commanding officer should make out a list of the men who came before him to vote, my hon. friend took the ground that we ought not to impose on the officers in that way. All through the discussion my hon. friend recognized the fact that he had no control or authority over these men, and that he could not interfere with them. If that is so, who has the control of them? The Secretary of War, unquestionably. What is the use of us keeping this House sitting day after day in order to pass legation which will be inoperative, absolutely a dead letter, if Lord Kitchener, in view of the issues that are at stake, should take it into his head to say: I am not going to let my commanding officers waste a week or ten days running around picking up votes from the men who ought to be getting ready to fight the Germans. I think the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), that we should say that this legislation is subject to the approval of the man who has control of the commanding officers, is but due recognition by the Canadian Parliament of the fact that our soldiers are under the control of Great Britain. There is no divided authority in this matter. A lot of confusion seems to exist in the public mind; some people think that the Canadian Government have got some kind of a string on our soldiers who have gone to the front. Why, every man that signed the muster roll agreed to serve [Mr. Macdonald.J.
the Empire for three years, and to give his services not to the Canadian Government but to King George, and to obey the Imperial authorities. This legislation practically amounts to saying to our soldiers: You shall not go out and fight; you and your commanding officers must give up your training in England for this war, and turn out for a week or ten days to see whether you cannot get in some votes. I say that any measure of this kind which did not contain in it the stipulation that the consent of Lord Kitchener should be obtained before it became operative would be not merely cheek and impertinence, but an insult to Lord Kitchener as well. That is the situation; and to talk of autonomy under these circumstances only shows that hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have forgotten that there is a war going on; otherwise, they would never have proposed this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has been impressing upon us things that are so absolutely obvious that it would be absurd for us to make a provision in regard to them, as though we did not know that they were perfectly obvious. This law cannot interfere with the military authority of Lord Kitchener.
Because Kitchener will not allow it to interfere.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And it does not pretend to. We simply assume that Lord Kitchener gives us credit for common sense; and we further assume that Lord Kitchener, having at least as much knowledge with regard to military matters, well, perhaps not quite the degree of knowledge of my
11 p.m. distinguished friend and cohonorary colonel the hon. member for Pictou, will look upon this matter with common sense; and so we leave it in his hands with absolute confidence that he will see to it that if anything under this Act interferes with the performance of military duty it shall not be done.	-

Why do you not say
so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Because it is so entirely unnecessary to say so;,because the Act as it stands, without those words, is neither intended to interfere nor can it interfere with the authority of Lord Kitchener; and because I think it would be an unfortunate thing for us to intimate that we were passing legislation that would so interfere with his great work as to make it necessary for

us to first ask his leave. As I have said several times in the course of this discussion we are perfectly willing, if need be, that the Act should lie there a dead letter, rather than that there should be interference with the paramount duty of the soldier. Just let me point out the degree to which the hon. member for Pictou has found it necessary to read into this Bill things that are not in it. He tells this House that in this Bill there is said to the officers of Canada; "You shall not go out to fight; you shall take ten days for running around to pick up votes." When I propose a Bill of that kind I shall recognize that I am proposing something so utterly and entirely indefensible that I cannot conceive of any man being so cheeky and so impertinent as to do what the hon. gentleman suggests, namely, that we should present ourselves to Lord Kitchener and say: My dear Lord Kitchener, we are passing a law saying to your soldiers, you shall give up your fighting, you shall abandon your military duties and take a week or ten days off for the purpose of running around and picking up votes; and we have come, Lord Kitchener, to ask your leave to pass that law. Could anything be more offensive to Lord Kitchener than that anybody should suggest that he could possibly give leave for that kind of legislation? If I ever dreamed of proposing legislation of that kind I certainly should not like to be the gentleman delegated to ask Lord Kitchener's leave to give effect to it. This legislation proposes nothing of that kind. It is purely enabling legislation making it possible for the soldiers to vote, subject of course to the performance of their military duties; and I think it would be as offensive to our soldiers for us to suggest that they were willing to abandon their duties in order to pick up votes as it would be to suggest to Lord Kitchener that we thought it possible that he would give us leave to have legislation of that sort made operative. The moment the operation of this legislation runs counter to the performance of the military duties of the soldiers, automatically it ceases to have operation.

My hon. friend is
arguing in a kind of a circle. He says that this legislation will be inoperative unless Lord Kitchener consents, and yet he says that this legislation is only for the purpose of enabling the soldiers to vote. Why, those soldiers can vote only if Lord Kitchener lets them. When we suggest a provision that the Bill shall not become operative unless
Lord Kitchener consents to it, my hon. friend argues that the autonomy of Canada is in peril. Now what sense is there in passing legislation for the purpose of enabling men who are on active service to vote, unless Lord Kitchener gives his consent to it? It is no use our fooling away time here passing legislation which is not to be operative.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Why do you do it?

The hon. gentleman
knows that the session came to a conclusion naturally a few days ago. The hon. gentleman knows that he never could draft a Bill to provide in any practical way for the soldiers on active service easting their votes. For what reason, in process of time, have we had this measure evolved ? My hon. friend does not meet this issue at all by saying what he does say in answer to the objection. It is held up to the country that they are proposing a method by which the soldiers can vote. Either the measure is a successful and practical one, and one under which the soldiers can vote, or it is not. My hon. friend says to-night that it is not a practical measure, that it is not one under which a man' can vote, that it is an enabling measure only if Lord Kitchener chooses to call a halt to operations so that under section 2 some of these men can vote. I would like to know what my hon. friend does say if he does not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I said that if it does
not interfere with the performance of any military duty nobody will interfere to prevent it taking effect. It does not interfere in any of its provisions with the performance of military duties.

It does interfere.
Every line of section 2 interferes with the performance of some duty by the commanding officers of the army whose business it is to fight the Germans. Otherwise all of this section 2 is nonsense. If this section does not mean that the commanding officers are going to take some time to do this work correctly, and if these officers are not to be diverted from their duty preparing for and taking this vote, I do not know what this measure means. It is an enabling measure, says my hon. friend; it is not compulsory. That means that if any one of these officers attached to the Canadian contingent chooses to say:	I do not want to
take the votes of my men and I am not going to do it, that you are not going to have the

votes of that branch of the service taken at all. Then there is this further consideration. General orders are issued either in England, Bermuda or France, providing that various duties shall be undertaken by the commanding officer. Except in times of extraordinary emergency these general orders are always issued a couple of days before the actual performance of the duty assigned to the officer, and it may be that an officer's time is fully taken up in pursuance of one of these general orders. Under the circumstances must he disregard the general orders and pay attention to an Act of the Canadian Parliament? Are these officers going to pay attention to the orders of General Alderson or are they going to pay attention to an Act of this Parliament? My hon. friend says that they will pay attention to the orders of General Alderson. The result is that this measure is of no use unless his superior officer, his commander, and the Secretary of State for War, definitely intimate to Gen-Alderson that it is his duty to see that sufficient time is allowed on various days for the taking of this vote. Unless this legislation is to be subject to the direction of General Kitchener it is mere waste paper. We are wasting time talking about it. The position of the Minister of Justice indicates that. That being so, is it not ordinary politeness to say to Lord Kitchener, the man to whom the whole Emipre looks, and who has the responsibility of seing us through this war: Having control over our troops at the front, is it possible for you to arrange for them to vote under the proper method? That being the fact, we should say so and it should be put in the Act .

I have every respect for the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), but I am sorry to see that the position he takes to-night is not one in keeping with the general attitude of the Government. From the very outbreak of the war we were told in all the declarations of the Prime Minister and of his colleagues that the Government, in connection with every move that was being taken, were in close consultation with the home Government.
It was stated that nothing was done unless the War Office was consulted. Yet the minister has declared to-night that the amendment proposed .by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) places us in a position of inferiority in such a way that it would make us subservient to the wishes of a minister in Great Britain in the exercise of what the hon. gentleman considers to be a free right of the Canadian Gov-
eminent-the granting of the franchise to whomsoever it pleases. It is a long time since Downing street rule has been battered out of Canada and there is no intention of reviving it, but at the present time every move in our war policy is subservient to the wishes of the Imperial Government. It could not be otherwise. The only way in which we can take an active part in this great war is by co-operating with the British authorities. Instead of passing a measure which would be accepted unanimously by the Canadian Parliament and the people, we find that we have only a measure which has been tattered and torn, which has been amended in every respect, and which is going out of this House in such a condition as to threaten it with falling into contempt because it cannot be enforced. A law which cannot be enforced, a law which is allowed to fall into contempt, is of no advantage to the public or to the people for whose benefit it was especially intended. I think the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from St. John is elementary and should be accepted by the Government. In order to make sure that the soldiers on the other side will really have a chance of casting their votes the Government should neglect no opportunity, they should do everything that is possible to be done to show their sincerity in the matter and to make it certain that this Act shall not become a dead letter. I regret that the minister has not accepted this amendment and I hope that before the Bill reaches the stage for its third reading better counsels will have prevailed, and that it will be accepted, if only in the interest of the soldiers themselves. The Government have assured us that they are very anxious that the Canadian soldiers shall have an opportunity of casting their votes but inasmuch as they have neglected to enter into communication with the War Office through the proper channels the right of our Canadian soldiers to exercise the franchise may be placed in jeopardy.
I wish to express my opinion of the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). I am glad to know that the Minister of Justice is a convert to Canadian autonomy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A convert?

Unfortunately his plea for Canadian autonomy does not work in with this proposed legislation. If the Canadian soldiers were acting under the Canadian Militia Act I would understand

the plea of my hon. friend, but we have given all (that away by allowing our volunteers to go beyond the boundaries of our country and serve in the Imperial army.
I am in favour of giving votes to our soldiers if we can provide proper machinery for them to exercise the franchise. The moment our .soldiers leave the shores of Canada, they are under British Army regulations. Their prime duty is to fight for the liberties of the British Empire, and the Canadian Government cannot impose any other duty on them without first obtaining the sanction of the British military authorities. Not only must we require the goodwill of Lord Kitchener to carry out the provisions of this Bill, but Lord Kitchener himself may have to consult the officers commanding the Canadian troops, and possibly also the French and Belgian generals with whose armies the Canadian soldiers may at the time be intermingled. It is quite possible that General Alderson or Sir John French may have to consult General Joffre and other French general, operating in northern France or in Belgium, where the Canadian, soldiers may be. The Minister of Justice shakes his head, but he has served with honour im the North-West rebellion and knows what military discipline is, for both officers and men. Will he tell me that when a regiment is in action any outside civil authority, no matter how high, can interfere with the direction of the commanding officer? The Minister of Justice will not deny that proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I certainly will not
deny it.

Then, the hon. gentleman should not hazard passing this legislation without having first obtained the sanction and goodwill of the British War Office. Should this Bill become law, it is quite possible that some officers will agree that the soldiers may vote, while others may be opposed to it, and may answer that having received no orders from the War Office they shall ndt allow their men to play politics when the fate of the Empire is at stake. I submit that it is not beneath our dignity to insert a provision in this Bill that it shall only come into operation after the British military authorities have given their consent to it. I may be all wrong, but it occurs to me that the proposed amendment of the hon. member (Mr. Pugsley) is mo>st deserving of the approval of the committee. I repeat that I shall be proud to see our soldiers enabled to exercise their franchise, but the machinery provided for in this Bill is obscure, and it lends itself to serious
irregularities, I will not say corruption. Nevertheless, if the Government desires to pass it, they should at least take care, when this franchise is to be exercised in a foreign country, by our soldiers who are fighting under the direction of the British War Office, that the approval *of the British military authorities should be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to contra diet the description of affairs with regard to the operation of this legislation which the hon. gentleman has just made. 1 think his description is a conclusive de-nionstration of the entire absence of any necessity for the suggested amendment. Our soldiers are soldiers absolutely and undoubtedly, and I do not quite understand what the hon. gentleman's suggestion could do to produce a different situation as regards the carrying on of any war-like operations under the control of the British War Office authorities. It has not entered into my mind to conceive that this legislation of ours could in its operation under any conceivahle circumstances be allowed to interfere with the performance of their duties by our soldiers. If it does interfere, then if we go to Lord Kitchener to ask his leave to let it interfere, I have no doubt that it will be his duty to refuse that permission just as it will certainly be utterly cheeky and impertinent for us to ask for it to operate under conditions where it will interfere. On the other hand, under conditions where it will not interfere, which are the only conditions under which it can operate, I really cannot bring myself to see that Lord Kitchener is of such a disposition that we shall forfeit his good-will because simply we allow something to go on that in no way interferes with the performance of the military duties of our men. In other words, according to conditions, one thing will happen or the other. If the conditions are such that the carrying out of this voting will interfere with military duties, Lord Kitchener neither would nor should grant us permission, and we certainly should not go asking a permission which he neither would nor should grant. On the other hand, conditions may be such that all this will interfere in no way with military operations, and I for my part decline to assume that it will be considered necessary for us to go and ask leave, and objectionable if we do not ask leave, when we are simply allowing a law, having to do not with the performance of the soldier's duty but with the exercise of the citizen's right, to take its course and to operate with regard to our own citizens.

I am sure the discussion that has taken place during the last two or three days on this subject must have satisfied the hon. Minister of Justice that it is very difficult to lay down conditions under which the vote of the Canadian soldiers can be taken at the front. The very fact that the Bill now before us is an altogether different Bill from the one introduced by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice some two or three days ago is proof of what I say, and the minister must surely see now that the longer it is discussed, the more difficulties arise in the way of carrying out this proposition. If that is the case, why not go back to the proper course? My hon. friend must be particularly anxious to have the soldiers vote when he is going to all this trouble and proposing a Bill that cannot be carried out in any reasonable manner. If my hon. friend and the Government, are so anxious to have the votes of the soldiers, why not do the decent, fair and honest thing, and say that there will be no election at the present time? Why not w'ait until the war is over and let the soldiers come back, and then all those who are entitled to vote will be allowed to vote? Would not that be better than putting forward a half-baked Bill such as the one we are now discussing which proposes ways and means of having the votes taken and sent back here, when neither the minister nor any one else knows how his proposition can be carried out? Why go on with a proposition of this kind when the whole trouble can be obviated by doing the proper thing? There is more than a year and a half for this Parliament to run; and if the war is not over in a year from now, although in all probability it will be, if my hon. friend still wants to give the soldiers votes, -we shall have a year to consider the matter. But now in the declining hours of the session to put forward a measure of this kind; to try to force it through to give votes to men who are in another country and who are out of our jurisdiction altogether, and then to try to do it without the authority of the one man who has charge of the whole matter and to object to ask the consent of that man, all this is something that I cannot understand. The minister a minute ago seemed to think it would be something unheard of for us to ask that Lord Kitchener should be consulted, or that we should make the Bill inoperative until he gave his consent. On the other hand he thinks it is all right for us to pass legislation instructing different men to 
carry on certain wrork when they cannot do anything at all without getting the consent of Lord Kitchener. The whole matter is too absurd for sane men to be arguing over it for two or three days, and to keep the House here in session on a matter of this kind, when tne work is all practically done. There are two or three ways- in which to get. over the difficulty. I have asked my hon. friend once or twice already w'ho has asked that the soldiers be given an opportunity of voting.
Every one.

I venture to say that
not a single organization in Canada nor any individual has asked that the soldiers be given an opportunity to vote. It is the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches wrho are anxious to get the votes-perhaps not so anxious to get the votes as to manipulate tnem. My hon. friend now must see the difficulties in the way, and he still refuses to make the Bill inoperative until Lord Kitchener gives his consent. Imagine Lord Kitchener consenting to an election being taken on a certain day, and on that day word comes for a general advance against the enemy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Just imagine asking
Lord Kitchener leave for a thing like that!

That is exactly what my hon. friend will be asking under this Bill, that is, lor authority to take a vote at the front when he does not know at what moment after that authority is given orders may come for a general advance, with the result that the vote may be taken at one part of the front and not at another part. It is quite likely, as some hon. gentlemen have pointed out, that the officers commanding in certain cases will say: I am not here to make politics; I am not here to peddle around begging votes from this man or from that man; I am here to fight the battles of the Empire, and I will take no part in this whatever, therefore you will have some sections of the army voting and other sections not voting. Although I have been in this House for a good many years, I have never before seen such a crude piece of legislation introduced.
I would sincerely ask the Minister of Justice to withdraw this Bill. It is an impracticable proposition. If he wants to get the votes of the soldiers let him put off the elections until the war is over. If the war is not over next year we can easily get authority from the Imperial Parliament to extend this Parliament until the war is over.

Then, when the soldiers come back, every one who is entitled to vote will be able to cast that vote and cast it in the proper manner.

I desire to say just one word in answer to the Minister of Justice. Impressed as he must necessarily be by the force of the argument that this Parliament has no -right to impose a duty on the officers of the Imperial army, he said that this measure imposed no duty, that it is merely an enabling law. Let us see the evidence. Subsection 3 of section 2 provides that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall notify the secretary of the High Commissioner by cable of a general election, -and the secretary shall thereupon send a sufficient number of ballot papers and envelopes to the chief paymaster of the Canadian expeditionary force, who shall forward the same to the several regimental paymasters who shall deliver the same to the officers commanding squadrons, companies and batteries. Now, let us -see the "enabling" part of it; "and such officers shall give each volunteer under their respective command making the affidavit in form (b) before such officer a ballot paper, and shall fold it in a certain manner and place it in the envelope. It is then provided (that the certificate in form (c) shall be signed by the officer who shall also securely close the envelope containing the ballot paper which shall then be sent by such officer by post to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.	,
If that is not imperative language, I fail to know how imperative language can be framed. That is not permissive; it is not an enabling clause but declaring what their duty shall be in connection with the taking of these votes. The Minister of Justice says that this has not the effect of imposing on these officers any duty which would interfere with their military duty. Who is to be the judge of that? This Parliament has said that these Canadian soldiers are to have a vote and that these Imperial officers shall give the opportunity to vote to every man who makes the affidavit before them. Does not that impose duties upon the officers that might interfere with the discharge of their military duties? If not, I fail to know how language could be employed to do so. We heard the suggestion that was made yesterday by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) or some other hon. gentleman on that side. From this side it was suggested that the Secretary for War might not permit
this. The hon. gentleman whom I am quoting said he could not imagine the Secretary of State for War taking such a stand, because it would create a deplorable and unfortunate situation. What did that mean? It meant that, this Parliament having declared that it should be the duty of these Imperial officers to allow a vote to be taken and make an affidavit and distribute the ballots, if Lord Kitchener should say that this should not be done it would create an unfortunate situation-that is it would create a conflict between the Secretary of State for War and this Parliament. That would indeed be unfortunate. But all that could be avoided if it were provided that these sections shall not be acted upon until submitted to the Secretary for War and approved by him. If the Secretary for War were consulted and thought that the voting could be carried out, it would create harmony, whereas in the present form it is likely to create friction and entire want of harmony. It seems to me that in taking the stand he has taken in regard to this amendment, the Minister of Justice is taking a position which cannot be justified and is likely to create friction and lead to great dissatisfaction.
Amendment (Mr. Pugsley) negatived.
I give notice that I will move this amendment on the third reading of the Bill.

I think where a man is entitled to claim that he is a voter, it would be only right that he should ndme the electoral district as well as the place of residence. I can see the possibility of difficulty under the section. If a man is a voter, he ought to know in what district he is a voter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That generally is true. This subject is one that was a good deal discussed in the committee-this form of affidavit. The first instance given was with regard to the city of Montreal. It was stated that both as regards the men who reside for thirty days, and as regards men who have been voters perhaps for years, in view of our redistribution there would be great danger of men misapprehending the electoral district in which their places, of residence had	been	situated, thoughquite aware	that	by virtue of
their residence they are qualified voters. My own constituency is now very largely made up of people who heretofore never 
were in the electoral division of St. Anne; people whose, knowledge on the subject, derived, perhaps, from years of being settled there, would be that they "were in the county of Jacques Cartier. I have reference at the moment to the city of Ver dun. A man in that situation might be expected to fall into error, but if the soldier swears that he was entitled to vote in the city of Verdun at the time he was enlisted, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery will have no difficulty, with the Redistribution Act in front of him, in determining where the vote belongs. What applies to my own constituency applies, I think, to all constituencies as at present constituted in the city of Montreal. The same thing would be true of the city of Toronto and the city of Edmonton, which, 1 understand, has been divided into two electoral districts. Persons who are not informed as to where the line runs between East Edmonton and West Edmonton, might be very much puzzled to know in which electoral district they were when they enlisted, but they would know that they had qualifications in the city of Edmonton and that they resided at some particular place in the city of Edmonton. In view of that situation, instead of requiring the de signation of the electoral district, we pro vided for a designation of the place at which the man had been accustomed to vote, from which the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery will have no difficulty in settling the question of the electoral district.

On section 3-officers who are candidates not to act:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Carrying out a promise I made to the hon. member for Sudbury and Queens this afternoon, I beg to move that this section be amended by adding to it the words "and failing him for any of the causes aforesaid, the next below him in rank, and so on." Further, in view of some suggestions that were made as to the possibility of the commanding officer declining to perform the duties prescribed under the Act, I think we should make section 3 apply in the case of the officer designated ot next in rank declining to perform the duty as well as in the case of the officer who is prevented from acting. To produce that result, I beg to move that the section be further amended by inserting in line 18, after the word "it" and before the-words "the duty," the words "or declines to perform it."
The first amendment proposed might produce a condition where the sergeant would be the responsible officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The question is whether it is better t-o leave it possible that the sergeant may sometimes perform this duty than to leave it possible that it shall not be performed :at all. If the Act operates as I hope it will operate, I do not think that a case of this kind will happen very often. If there should be ground for anticipating that the officers generally would refuse to do the duty assigned to them, then, of course, this position would come into general operation. If it is thought preferable, I would limit the operation of the section as amended so that the duty should not be performed by 'an officer who is subordinate to a commissioned officer. If we do that, however, we may create a condition where, merely for want of an officer, the mem may lose their votes. It seemed to me that we might with perfect safety, in the few cases where this would arise, allow the non-commissioned officer to do the work rather than cause the soldiers to lose their votes because of there being no officer to perform this duty.
One of the results of the provision might be that the officers would turn their work over to the sergeants.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Even if it be a violation of obligation on the part of the officers not to fulfil this duty, we cannot make them do a thing if they do not want to do it. The case which I had in anticipation was that of an officer who might happen to be a candidate in an election or who might be prevented from acting. The latter case, I think, will be more frequent than the case where he may decline to act. If he declines to perform the duty, we leave it to the next officer in rank. We start with the company officer, who has under him, before you get to the non-commissioned officer, five officers. I think we may fairly assume that some one of these six officers will be able and willing to perform the duty.

As a civilian, speaking
from what I have read, I suggest that the sergeants do all the work 'any way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not prepared to say anything about that. When I was in the army we used to find something to do.

I think this is another argument in support of the suggestion 159
that a superintendent of some kind should be appointed. Has the minister arrived at any solution of the difficulty that was suggested to-day in this respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I pointed out that, if it were considered that my suggestion would provide for what was desired, I was prepared to let it go to a small committee for consideration. That offer met no response, and at the present moment I do not think that we are prepared to re-open that consideration. The amendment suggested did not provide for persons who would have the receiving of the ballots.
It only looked to provide for representatives of the different parties to be present when the voting took place. It did not look to provide machinery for taking the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They refer to the sections of the Dominion Act prescribing the duties of returning officers and poll clerks. We are trying to make the duties of the returning officers and poll clerks at the camps in Canada approach as nearly as possible to the duties that have to be discharged by the ordinary returning officers and poll clerks at an election in Canada.

The section does not make clear that this returning officer is not the returning officer of an electoral district. If, as I understand, he is a returning officer specially appointed, I would suggest that words be used to convey that idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am quite willing to make that clear. It follows the wording of the Dominion Elections Act. As regards the issuing of the writ, the Dominion Elections Act says:
Every writ for an election shall be in form A and shall be dated and be returnable on such days as the Governor General determines, and shall be addressed and forwarded by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to the person appointed by the Governor General, as hereinafter provided, and shall he transmitted to such person by mail, unless otherwise ordered by the Governor General.
And then 76 provides that:



The person to whom a writ for an election is so addressed shall he the returning officer at such election.
I took it ithat these definitions provided for the issue of the writ and for the holding of the poll at each military camp.

I am perfectly satisfied with the explanation although on reading the section it was riot quite clear. There are two regiments in barracks in the constituency of East Edmonton and there is a squadron of cavalry in the constituency of Strathcona within the limits of greater Edmonton, but in different constituencies and having no connection. The squadron of cavalry has no connection with the infantry regiment. Would each be considered a base which would be given to a returning officer or would one returning officer handle both establishments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My impression would be, if these forces have no connection one with the other, that we would have to provide a separate returning officer for. each.

What would be the result if a man is not on the list in the place that he chose to describe as his place of residence six months prior to the date of his enlistment? My hon. friend knows the position we are in in the cities of the province of Quebec. He knows that registration takes place in December. A man might not be on the list because he went before the list was made. Will a man who is in a position to swear that he lived within a certain polling subdivision for six months prior to the time of his enlistment have the right to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the cities' system if the lists were prepared at the time they were enrolled, or if they were on an electoral list that was still in force-it may not have been a new one-they would be entitled under this Act to vote in that electoral district wherein they would have been qualified to vote if the election had taken place the day that they enrolled. If I understand the city system aright in Montreal, there is always a list in force. Their lists are revised every two years and one list remains in force until the next one is revised. In the case suggested the fact that the voter was on the list of two years previous if that were still in force or on the newly made list would entitle him to claim as having been a person qualified to vote in ithe district on the day he enlisted. If, on the other hand, he was not on that ex-

isting voters' list he would not be in a position to say at the time he was enrolled he was a qualified voter in the district, but he might claim, if that was the place where he had lived for thirty days, within the six months before enlistment, that he was entitled to vote in that district because of his thirty days prior residence.

What list will be in
force in five or six weeks from now in Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If I am not mistaken,
the electoral lists that were prepared in December were revised in January and are actually in force now.
They were supposed to be in force on April 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know the
exact day, but I know there was a period of time which I think will now have elapsed. It will be in force for two years or until there is another revision.
On section 4, subsection 4-at expiration oi ten days returning officer to prepare lists of volunteers:
The question arises as to what are the terms of the revision of this list.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no provision for the revision of the list. What is arranged is that the returning officer shall make a list of the people who have given him notice. This is useful, because it informs him of who are the people who pretend to be voters in that district and it enables him to know the electoral districts he has to handle. The Act does not expressly provide for making it a final list in such a manner as to determine the right of the voter. A man who has arrived at camp after ten days have gone by, or who is precluded from sending his name should not be prevented from voting on polling day. I do not think it would be fair to make any list which the returning officer is able to provide an absolute settlement of a man's right to vote by reason of the existence of his name upon it, or the absence of his name from it. The provision requiring the prepartion of the list is really a measure of convenience, but there is no provision to make the presence of the man's name on the list essential to his right to exercise the franchise. The provision for the making of this list is for the purpose of facilitating and making more convenient the holding of a poll, but it is not provided that the list shall be treated as de-

termining whether or not a person has the right to vote.
Can the returning officer refuse a man his vote after he has made the affidavit?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If nobody requires him to be sworn he will vote.
Has the returning officer the right to strike his name off?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no provision by whiclh, he is entitled to strike the name off. We have to have qualification by affidavit, but I think it is fair not to make that affidavit sent in in writing to the returning officer conclusive in the event of a question being raised. For example, in a camp like Valeartier there might be a large number of voters from a certain constituency, and the candidates might find it desirable to send representatives, so that I do not think it would be fair that because a man has handed in an affidavit ten or fifteen days before, the representatives of the candidates should not be entitled to swear the voter to the essentials of his qualifications in the presence of a returning officer.
There is no provision for that in the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; the Act is subject to all the provisions of tlhe Dominion Elections Act which are applicable.
I find no provisions here, after the returning officer has made the list, for adding to or striking off any names that may be on the list.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because being on that list is not essential to the right to vote.
Where do you provide for anything outside that list?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think I understand the idea of the minister, although I do not approve of it. The idea is that the moment a person has taken the affidavit he becomes an elector, and his vote can be challenged, but there is no provision in the Act for challenging his vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The provision that makes it possible to swear a man in the presence . of the returning officer and the scrutineer is that in subsection 6 of section 4 which says that except as herein otherwise provided, the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act relating to the power and duties of the returning officer and other officers shall so faT as applicable apply.
159i
Section 153 says:
Except in the province of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the Yukon Territory, an elector, if required by the deputy-returning officer, the poll clerk, one of the candidates, or an agent of a candidate, or by an elector present, shall before receiving his ballot paper, take such oath of qualification as by the law of the province he may in the like case at a provincial election be required to take, such changes having been made in the form of oath as are necessary to make it applicable to the election being held, and shall also, if required, take the oath in form Y.
I am free to admit that we are not dealing with an oath that is required for a provincial qualification. There are other provisions and I am pretty confident that I could lay my hands on them; but to make the matter absolutely clear, we will put it in so many words so that there can be no possible doubt about it. At tlhe time I examined the Act I was satisfied that, by referring back to these provisions, we would make it possible for a man to be sworn at the time as to his qualifications, but as there may be some doubt about it, we will put it in.

Is the general language used in subsection 6, where you are adopting the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, sufficiently broad to cover the appointment and presence of scrutineers at the polls?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is a subdivision of
the statute called " the polling." Section 137 says:
In addition to the deputy-returning officer and the poll clerk, the candidates and their agents, not exceeding two in number for each candidate in each polling station, and, in the absence of agents, two electors to represent each candidate at the request of such electors, and no others, shall be permitted to remain in the room where the votes are given during the time the poll remains open.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The trouble
is this, that you may have thirty or forty candidates represented at one poll, and you may have 230.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is barely possible, but it is assumed that the returning officer in adjusting his poll will make as many polling places as are necessary. We assumed that if he had a knowledge of the different electoral districts with which he had to deal, in cases where there might be only a few voters in each electoral district, he would probably endeavour to subdivide his polls so as to include them in one poll. If he have a large number on one electoral

[DOT]district, he may have to provide several polls for that district. We leave it to the judgment of the returning officer so to dispose of these things as to make the matter workable. One cannot say in advance how many electors a returning [DOT]officer may have to deal with. In one camp he may have only one or two, while in another camp he may have half a dozen. The provision is:
The returning officer shall proceed to hold such number of polls upon the day fixed for the holding of the election in the several electoral districts, within such camp or base, and appoint such deputy-returning officers and officers as may be necessary' therefor.
I think we can leave it to the returning officer to make the necessary arrangements. I hardly think that any returning officer will arrange to hold polls for twenty electoral districts all in the same polling booth unless he has secured very large accommodation. If there are half a dozen voters from one electoral district, I doubt if there is any reason to anticipate that there will be representatives of candidates there. If the voters are numerous, there will probably be representatives of candidates there, but it seems that it might properly be left to the returning officer for his owm comfort if for no other reason to provide sufficient accommodation.
I would like to say in plain words whatever right the candidates have with regard to the scrutineers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If it is desired to have it copied in, I shall have it copied in, but I would ask my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), for instance, if he has any doubt that, when this Bill says that the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act relating to the polling shall apply, all of those sections which are in the Dominion Elections Act under the title polling apply.
. Sir WILFRID LAURIER: The difficulty is this: we have -now over 230 constituencies, and it is not an extravagant supposition that there may be at a camp the electors of perhaps thirty or forty constituencies. In the camp at Montreal, or at Ottawa or at any other central place, there may be candidates from British Columbia, Nova Scotia, and other parts of Canada. IJndeT the law as it is, at present electors can be scrutineers without any authority from the candidate. Any two electors in a constituency [DOT]can go and be scrutineers; but it might be impossible to get authority from a candidate in British Columbia to have representatives

at the poll at Montreal or at Ottaw'a, and I believe some provision should be inserted that any two electors in any constituency can be scrutineers for all on the one side or on the other side of politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no objection to that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Two electors in. the city of Montreal could go as scrutineers, and if they were to be scrutineers for one candidate, they could be scrutineers for all the candidates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The matter will
really work out in that way, because the right hon. gentleman will remember that if no person is appointed as scrutineer for the candidate, any two electors can undertake to represent him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
They can represent one candidate, but not all the candidates.
SiT ROBERT BORDEN:	I think they
can.

There are a great
many deputy returning officers who will say that this legislation does not provide for candidates' representatives. It would be wise if the minister would draw up some section to meet the suggestion of my right hon. friend to provide for two agents of the same political party as the representatives for alii the candidates who may be voted for at the .same poll.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would be inclined to think, if it happened that in the same polling booth votes were being polled for more than one electoral district, that two electors coming in there would be entitled to represent candidates from different electoral districts. Now, as regards the possible ignorance of returning officers that the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act apply with regard to polls, I would like to point out that in addition to that we have a provision :
This Act shall be construed as one with the Dominion Elections Act.
The duties of returning officers as well as others are to be governed by that. It would be his duty under the Dominion Elections Act, and under this Act, to furnish the deputies not only witih this Act but with the Dominion Elections Act, and furthermore to furnish them with the instructions that are got out. Of course, if considered necessary, the Dominion Elections Act could be copied instead of telling

the deputy returning officers and the returning officers that the provisions. of the Act apply. But I should hope-as these returning officers are to instruct the deputies-that we should be able to find men of sufficient intelligence, that when told that all the provisions about the duties of returning officers and deputy returning officers, and about the polling and the taking of the vote, would apply, they would be able to understand that without it being nee sary to print these sections; but I will get them printed if-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is not necessary. It was only to understand the Bill and to put it as intelligibly as possible. I appreciate that we should have, perhaps, more legislation about scrutineers. But. scrutineers are chiefly useful to prevent personation. There cannot be much personation here, because there is means of identification. Two electors can see that the formalities are followed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it will work out that way. Let that section stand.

Many people who will have to work out this Act will find great difficulty in referring to the Dominion Elections Act and reading one into the other. There are not nearly so many people learned in the law on the outskirts of civilization as in the city, of Ottawa, and it is surprising how difficult it is for a man who is not used to such work to go through such an Act and read one section in the light of another. For that reason, I would ask that whatever is required in	regard to scrutineers
and the voter getting his name on the list up to whatever time is allowed him- that these provisions be made perfectly clear on the face of the Bill. Another thing: Are the returning officers and deputy returning officers to be civilians or military men?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They will be appointed as other returning officers and deputy returning officers are appointed. The returning officer will appoint his deputy just as other returning officers and deputy-returning officers are appointed. There is nothing to [DOT] require xior to prevent him selecting mili-"tary men if he wants to.

But he does not need to
choose military men?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, the Governor General will appoint the returning officer for the camp just as he appoints the deputyreturning officer for an electoral district.

The minister says that the Dominion Election Act is to be followed. But in these places there is a certain military rule. Is the minister going to do anything under this clause to make sure that the military rule shall not override the Elections Act? I know that has been done in other cases and probably would be done in this.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think there is room for the slightest doubt that the Parliament of Canada controls soldiers in Canada. And where this Act, if it is passed, says that a certain thing shall be done, the soldier has- to obey as much as any other man. Here we have an express direct clause, providing what is to be done in the camp, and there is no military rule that can override Parliament's expressed provision.
Section stands.
On subsection 7,-reporting vote to several electoral districts:
On section 4, subsection 8-poll at which to vote:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In all cases, except under this proposed legislation, the electoral list determines whether or not a man has a right to vote. If he is on the list, he has a right to vote; if not, he has not a right to vote. In this case, what constitutes the right to vote is the affidavit of the soldier.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A man whose name has been put upon the list must vote at the place where ihe is allotted, and not elsewhere. I would not have it understood that this section implies that the man who is not allotted at all should not vote anywhere.
There should go with that the correlative provision that the military authorities shall see that facilities are provided to enable the volunteer to vote at the poll to which he is assigned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am willing to insert a provision to that end, although I had not thought it necessary.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Subsection agreed to.
Section 4, subsection 9-obtaining certificate that voter is on list where voting on previous qualification:

Under this provision a soldier from a western constituency who is in an eastern camp would have to communicate with his friends in the far-distant
-!526

constituency in order that the certificate of the returning officer might be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There might be some difficulty about that. The provision makes it a duty for the returning officer in a certain electoral district who receives notice that somebody has claimed to be qualified in that district, to send the electoral list there. The returning officer who receives the list may ascertain whether the name of the man in question is upon it. Perhaps it would he well to put in some words providing that if the returning officer fails to find that name on the list, he should have power to reject the vote.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Subsection agreed to.
On section 4, subsection 10-procedure when volunteers leaving Canada before election day:
I wish to ask again whether the amendment which I proposed at eight o'clock would be in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Inasmuch as the Bill which we are dealing with provides for an expenditure out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, it had to be preceded by a resolution assented to by His Royal Highness the Governor General. That resolution was looking to a provision being made for votes being given to the military forces, the expenses in connection therewith to be paid in the manner which I have indicated. I do not think that it is open to us to introduce into this Bill an amendment extending the scope of the proposed legislation, and introducing an entirely different subject matter, unless we have a new resolution assented to by the Governor, and re-introduce the Bill. For that reason, I do not think it is advisable to accept an amendment providing for something entirely different from that which was originally contemplated.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am not sure that that is a good reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In my own experience I have found myself precluded from the possibility of providing-not in connection with a Bill exactly like this, but in connection with a Bill that required a resolution-for something not contemplated in the resolution, and which would involve the cost or charge of carrying out the thing not contemplated. If it is necessary that the Governor General should assent, surely he must assent to what he understands. He has assented to a charge being created for the purpose of providing funds for
	, j
soldiers, and, under guise of that assent, to provide for votes for large numbers of other people, with a possible expenditure connected therewith, would be legislating in respect of something that the resolution did not contemplate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It seems to me that there can be no expenditure in connection with the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Maisonneuve. It is simply to provide that railway officials who are engaged in train service shall be enabled to vote either on the polling day or on the day preceding.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It may not be a very
heavy charge, but you are imposing new duties on the deputy returning officers; and either you are going to compel them to do two days' work for one day's pay, or you must provide them with remuneration for two days' work. However, without insisting over much on that, I have said what I desire to -say in regard to the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In my judgment the Bill referred to the committee by the House is an Act to enable Canadians on active military service during the present war to exercise their electoral franchise. Bourinot says-, at page 546:
It is a clear and indisputable principle of parliamentary law that a committee is bound by, and is not at liberty to depart from, the order of reference.
I understand that the only thing referred to the committee from the House was the Bill under consideration, and accordingly I 'think it my duty to declare the amendment out of order.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-distribution of Act:
I thought the minister had agreed to strike out the word " enrolled?"

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We struck out the words " enrolment or " enlistment " in places where it might possibly create some confusion. I do not think it can do any harm here, but as I have no desire to insist on its staying there, I move that the word " enrolled " be struck out.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 10-when voter cannot vote under this Act:
Mr. ^MARCIL: This is when he has to leave camp and go to the polling booth?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, if he is a voter qualified for that electoral district.
If this will interfere with his military duties, has he to obtain permission from 'the military authorities?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If his voting at the camp interfered with his military duties, 'he would have to get permission from the military authorities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-termination of Act:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I see' that the minister has passed over the clause he prepared as clause 4, providing for the appointment of scrutineers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I explained this morning what happened with regard to this clause, and I am sorry if I did not make myself understood. That clause, as I have explained two or three times, was drafted with a view 'to having some conference as to whether it should be carried out. It was inserted in that first reprint of the Bill by a misunderstanding, and that fact was one of the principal reasons that led me to make the second reprint. I said this morning with regard to the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. John that if something on the line of the suggestion that 1 a.m. is contained in that section, modified as to the number of commissioners and providing for the appointment of scrutineers, would in any way be satisfactory I should be glad to consider it, and even have a special committee to deal with something on those lines. As I understood it, the response that was made to that suggestion was an insistence on the proposition of the hon. member for St. John, and I said in answer to some hon. member that I was not making a proposition on the subject, but endeavouring to meet the suggestions, and that if anything on that line would be acceptable I should be glad to try and work it out. This morning I put before the House this corrected reprint, with the explanation that the insertion of that clause as nrinted in the Bill distributed yesterday was* the result simply of a misunderstanding, and I am sorry if I have created the impression that I proposed to go on with the first reprint which has been corrected by this corrected reprint, which does not' contain that suggestion.

The minister should
state one further thing. He was asked whether these scrutineers would have any
notice of when and where the votes would be taken, to which the minister replied in the negative. Therefore, it seems to me that was simply an empty proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not discussing the value of the proposition at all. I was explaining that I did not put forward that clause as a provision of my Bill, but was endeavouring to see if a suggestion carried out on those lines would be acceptable. The hon. member for St. John, for reasons he thought sufficient, did not consider it acceptable.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We understood the whole thing very differently. The hon. member for St. John suggested that we should have scrutineers, and have some check upon the voting. He suggested a commission and my hon. friend agreed to that and he suggested that we should proceed with the Bill. We thought that, before we proceeded with the Bill as to the manner of voting, we should be able to provide some check preferably by way of a commission, and we offered some suggestions as to that. If the idea of a check upon the voting in the form of a commission should be adopted it would be necessary to modify the clauses accordingly. That is the reason why we did not press the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not want to take
advantage of anything that may have been a misunderstanding. The hon. gentleman will bear me out when I say that hon. gentlemen opposite did not consider my suggestion satisfactory. At three o'clock, with this matter standing in that shape, I did state that we were not prepared to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John, but that if something on the line of carrying out what was printed there, with the necessary modifications if we were to subtitute two commissioners, and if they were to have power to appoint scrutineers, would be acceptable, I would be glad to consider it and to refer it to a committee. There was some discussion as to how that was to work out, and I was asked whether I would consider whether there should be a provision that every officer, before he proceeded to take the votes, should call in the scrutineers. I said I did not think that would be workable, and I understood that was a proposition that was entirely unacceptable.

Only to myself; I did
not speak for the leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I put the proposition
in the most general terms to the hon. member for St. John. However, I do not want tc draw any consequences from anything that may have been a misunderstanding. If that was understood in the other way, I shall be glad to consider some provision for the appointment of scrutineers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think we might consider one or two matters that have been allowed to stand a little later in the forenoon, and I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House adjourned at 1.12 a.m. Wednesday.
Wednesday, April 14, 1915.
